No install, no clone, and for public repositories no sign-in. They split into three jobs: read a repo (github1s), feed a repo to an LLM (GitIngest, GitMCP), and understand a repo (GitDiagram, DeepWiki). GitHubBox is the odd one out: it runs a repo, and only helps if the repo is a JavaScript project. Every screenshot in this post comes from one real repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments: 280 text files, Scala and Java, Maven build. That choice exposes the limits as well as the wins. Two of the tools did not work for this repo, and the post says so and shows why. Why read a repository without cloning it A pull request link, a Stack Overflow answer or a colleague’s message lands you in a repository you have never seen. The default move is git clone, then an IDE import, then a Maven or sbt dependency download, all to answer a question like “where does this job write its output?”. For a repository you will not touch again, that is minutes of setup for a thirty-second question. A family of small sites removes the setup by taking the GitHub URL itself as input. You change github.com to another host, or put another host in front of the path, and the page you land on has done the work: an editor with search, a single text file ready to paste into a chat, a diagram, or a server your AI assistant can query. This post runs each of them, in order, on the same repository so the outputs are comparable. It is a tutorial first: each tool has numbered steps and a screenshot taken during the run. It also records where each tool stops, because “works on any repo” is only true of some of them. The test repository All runs use rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. It is a good subject because it is awkward in the ways real repositories are: Property Value Why it matters Files 280 text files analysed by GitIngest Large enough that a naive dump is cropped Layout 34 top-level folders, 32 of them Maven modules (each has a pom.xml), one per Spark integration A diagram has to summarise, not list Languages Scala 153,704 bytes, Java 41,228, Shell 23,514, Python 5,074 (GitHub languages API) Not JavaScript, which matters for GitHubBox History 102 commits, one branch, last commit eaf9e23 Small enough to read, old enough to be unmaintained What the URL rewrite actually does None of these sites is magic. Each one is a web application that receives owner/repo in the URL, fetches the repository from GitHub on the server side (or, for github1s, in your browser), and renders a different view of it. The rewrite is the cheapest possible interface: you already have the GitHub URL, so the only thing you type is the part that changes. https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments | | swap the host, keep owner/repo v github1s.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> VS Code in the browser gitingest.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> one text file for an LLM gitdiagram.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> architecture diagram gitmcp.io /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> MCP server URL githubbox.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> redirects to CodeSandbox deepwiki.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> generated wiki, if indexed All six take the same two path segments. Only the host differs, so the habit to build is: open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host. Three jobs, three places the work happens The tools differ less in what they show than in where the computation runs and what they cost you. Tool Job Where the work runs What you get Needs sign-in github1s Read and search Your browser, which loads a VS Code web build A read-only VS Code workbench No GitIngest Feed an LLM Server One text file: summary, tree, file contents No GitMCP Feed an LLM, live Server, over MCP A URL your assistant calls as tools No GitDiagram Understand Server, using an LLM A Mermaid diagram of the architecture No DeepWiki Understand Server, using an LLM A wiki, after an indexing job Email to index GitHubBox Run CodeSandbox A cloud dev environment Not to open “Needs sign-in” is for a public repository, as observed in this run. Private repositories need tokens or accounts on most of these, and none was tried here. The trade-off all six share Each tool trades privacy and completeness for speed. The server-side ones receive the repository name, and GitHubBox, GitIngest and GitDiagram each run on someone else’s infrastructure, so none of them belongs anywhere near a private repository you have not cleared. The model-backed ones (GitDiagram, DeepWiki) also summarise: they read a slice of the repository, which the sections below quantify (GitDiagram reported reading 40 source files out of 280). The alternative is the tool you already have: git clone --depth 1, then tree, rg and your IDE. It is complete, private and offline, and it costs the clone plus the import. The six tools win on the first minute and lose on everything after it. Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository Every step below was run on 12 November 2026 in Chrome against the repository above, signed in to nothing but GitHub. The screenshots are from those runs, unedited apart from file size. Each tool section ends with what it did not do, because that is the part the landing pages leave out. Tool 1: github1s, a read-only VS Code in the tab What it is for. Browsing and searching code with a real editor’s tree, tabs and search panel, without cloning. It is the right first move when you want to read, not run. Steps Open the repository on GitHub: https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. Edit the host in the address bar: replace github.com with github1s.com. The full URL is https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. Wait for the workbench to load. It opens the README as a preview tab and the whole folder tree in the Explorer. The status bar shows master, the branch the URL resolved to. To land on a file directly, keep the whole GitHub path and change only the host. This opens the Delta Lake example: https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments/blob/master/spark-delta-lake-integration/src/main/scala/com/ranga/spark/delta/lake/SparkDeltaLakeIntegrationApp.scala Search across the repository. Click the magnifier in the activity bar, or press Cmd+Shift+F on macOS (Ctrl+Shift+F elsewhere), and type format("delta"). The panel reported 2 results in 1 file, and both matches are highlighted in the open editor. Where it stops No syntax highlighting for Scala. The status bar showed Plain Text for the .scala file. Navigation and search work; colour does not. Read-only. The Search view has a Replace box, but this is a viewer for a public repository. There is nothing to run, build or debug. A “Leave site?” prompt. After I used Search, Chrome asked for confirmation before navigating away from the page. It is a browser prompt from the editor page, not data loss, because nothing can be saved. Tool 2: GitIngest, the whole repository as one prompt What it is for. Pasting a repository into an LLM chat. It produces a summary, a directory tree and the file contents as a single text document. Steps Open https://gitingest.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The path is the same owner/repo, so the page starts processing immediately. Wait for the spinner. This run took under half a minute for 280 files. Read the Summary panel. For this repository it reported: Repository: rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments Commit: eaf9e23df97e7f3dbe720223b027fb24352f3f5f Files analyzed: 280 Estimated tokens: 173.5k Use the controls above the result before you ingest, not after. The form has an Exclude (or Include) pattern box such as *.md, src/, an Include files under slider that defaults to 50 kB, and a Private Repository checkbox. Typing *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties into the Exclude box and clicking Ingest again took the result from 280 files and 173.5k estimated tokens to 151 files and 64.1k tokens, with the same commit. Click Copy all to put the document on the clipboard, or Download to save it as a file. Paste it into a chat with the question you actually have, for example “Which modules write to Kafka and which read from it?” Where it stops The on-page view is cropped. The panel begins with (Files content cropped to 300k characters, download full ingest to see more). The 173.5k-token estimate is for the whole repository, so only Download gives you everything. 173.5k tokens does not fit everywhere. It is a large prompt even for long-context models. Exclude patterns are not optional for a repository this size. A snapshot, not a live view. The summary pins commit eaf9e23. A later push is not in the document you copied. Tool 3: GitDiagram, an architecture diagram from the file tree What it is for. The first ninety seconds with an unfamiliar repository: what are the parts and how do they connect. Steps Open https://gitdiagram.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. Watch the progress panel. It shows Understanding the architecture with a timer and an Info line, 40 source files read. The diagram appeared after roughly half a minute. The first render fits the whole diagram into the page. For this repository it is too wide to read: Click Enable zoom. The diagram becomes pannable and zoomable (the first view opened at 467%), with -, + and FIT controls. Scroll and drag to read a cluster: The toolbar also has Export and Regenerate. For use in your own notes, add .md to the URL: https://gitdiagram.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.md That returned 200 with text/markdown, about 15 KB, containing an Overview, the diagram as a Mermaid block, a Components list with links to source files, and Connections. It is built for pasting into an agent’s context instead of screenshotting the page. Where it stops It reads a sample. Forty files out of 280. Its own markdown says it is generated “from its file tree, README and a sample of source files” and that it “is an AI-made overview: check details against the source.” It invents hubs. The top node, Example runner, fans out to every cluster. This repository is a set of independent examples, and the generated overview itself says each is “independently initiated”. The hub is the model’s way to draw a tree, not a program in the repo. Read diagrams like this as a table of contents, not a call graph. Wide repositories shrink. Thirty-two sibling modules produce a diagram that only works zoomed. A repository with a deeper structure would read better than a flat monorepo of samples. Tool 4: GitMCP, the repository as a tool your assistant can call What it is for. Instead of pasting a snapshot, give an AI assistant a URL that it queries on demand, so it reads current files rather than a stale dump. Steps Open https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The page is a setup guide titled GitMCP Documentation Server, with the server URL: https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments Pick your client from the tabs: Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, VSCode, Cline, Highlight AI, Augment Code or Msty AI. For Cursor, add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json: { "mcpServers": { "ranga_spark_experiments Docs": { "url": "https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments" } } } For Claude Desktop the page gives a different shape, because that client starts a local process and bridges to the remote server with mcp-remote. Add this to claude_desktop_config.json: { "mcpServers": { "ranga_spark_experiments Docs": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "mcp-remote", "https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments" ] } } } Restart the client and ask a question that needs the repository, such as “In ranga_spark_experiments, how does the graceful shutdown example stop a streaming job?” Where it stops Not run end to end in this post. The configuration above is exactly what the page shows. I did not connect an assistant to the server or list its tools, so what the assistant does with the URL is not claimed here. Claude Desktop needs Node. npx mcp-remote means a local Node.js install, which cancels some of the “no install” appeal for that client. Editing the config file is the install. A remote MCP URL means the assistant sends your questions, and what it fetches, to a third-party server. Tool 5: GitHubBox, a running dev environment, for the right repo What it is for. Opening a repository as an editable, runnable project in CodeSandbox, which suits JavaScript and Node projects. Steps Open https://githubbox.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. It redirects to https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/github/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments, shows “Fetching details…”, then opens the editor. It opened without a sign-in, with a Sign In button still available. Where it stops, and this one stopped. The preview pane is blank. The template label reads nodebox, a Node runtime in the browser, and this repository is Scala and Java built with Maven: no package.json, nothing for a Node sandbox to start. It is a useful negative result. GitHubBox is for JavaScript repositories, and nothing in this post is evidence that it works for anything else. I did not test it on a Node repository. Tool 6: DeepWiki, a generated wiki, if someone has indexed it What it is for. An LLM-written wiki of a repository, with pages by topic. Steps Open https://deepwiki.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. For this repository the page showed Repository Not Indexed: “This repository hasn’t been indexed yet”, with the estimate “Indexing typically takes 2-10 minutes”. Indexing requires an email to notify (required) and a click on Index Repository. I stopped here. Submitting someone’s email address to a third-party service is not part of a read-only demonstration, so the wiki itself is not covered in this post. Where it stops. It does not work on first visit for a repository nobody has indexed, and the index step has a cost in personal data. For well-known projects that are already indexed it is the lowest-effort tool of the six, but I have not shown that here. Real-world scenarios and production failures These tools are for reading, so “production failure” here means the moment a workflow built on one of them gives a wrong answer or quietly stops working. Each case below was observed in this run unless it says otherwise. Failure 1: the prompt is bigger than the model can use The GitIngest summary for the unfiltered repository says Estimated tokens: 173.5k. Pasting that into a chat either fails the length limit or, worse, fits and leaves little room for the answer. The page does not stop you. It crops its own preview to 300k characters and leaves the decision with you. The fix is to cut before copying, not after. Excluding build files, shell scripts, Markdown and properties files removed 129 of 280 files and cut the estimate from 173.5k to 64.1k tokens at the same commit. Mind what you removed: that exclude list also drops the pom.xml files, so a question about dependencies now has no evidence to read. Run Files Estimated tokens Defaults (50 kB file limit) 280 173.5k Exclude *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties 151 64.1k Failure 2: the diagram says something the repository does not GitDiagram’s top node is Example runner, with a labelled runs edge to every cluster. Read at face value it says one entry point launches all the examples. The same tool’s text overview says the opposite: “Each example is independently initiated.” Both statements came out of one generation. The root cause is structural. A diagram needs a root, a flat collection of 32 independent modules does not have one, and the model supplies a hub. The tool also states it read 40 files, so any behaviour that lives in the other 240 is a guess from names. Treat the diagram as an index of where to look, then confirm in the source (github1s is the quickest way to do that). Failure 3: the same URLs refuse a script All of these loaded in the browser. Requested from a shell with curl, the same hosts answered differently: URL (path /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments) Browser curl status githubbox.com Redirected to CodeSandbox and opened 403 deepwiki.com “Repository Not Indexed” page 429 uithub.com Not opened in the browser 401 gitmcp.io Setup page 200 gitingest.com Result page 200 gitdiagram.com Result page 200 The page-level 200 for GitIngest, GitDiagram and GitMCP only proves that a page was served. I did not trace how each one fetches its results, so a bare curl of the page is not shown here to be a way to automate them. If you want repeatable output in CI, use the repository’s own tooling: git clone --depth 1 and a local packer, not these sites. The one exception observed is GitDiagram’s .md endpoint, which returned the generated text over plain curl with a 200. Failure 4: a stale snapshot treated as current GitIngest pins the commit in its summary (eaf9e23...). Anything pushed after that is not in your document, and nothing in the pasted text tells the model so. If you are asking an assistant about a fast-moving repository, put the commit hash into the prompt and refresh the dump before a long session. This repository last changed in December 2023, so staleness did not bite here, and I did not test a repository that changes daily. Failure 5: what you paste and what you sign up for Everything included is sent to the model. GitIngest includes every file under the size limit that your pattern does not exclude. If a repository has a committed credential in a config file, it is in the dump. Scan or exclude before copying. This is a general risk with any dump tool, not something I found in this repository. Private repositories. GitIngest has a Private Repository checkbox and GitDiagram has API Key and Private Repos entries in its header. I did not test either, and handing a private repository’s code to a free third-party service is a decision for your security team, not a URL trick. DeepWiki asks for an email. To index a repository you must give an address. The post stopped there on purpose. Ads and sponsors. GitIngest shows Carbon ads and GitDiagram a sponsor banner. This is how free tools pay for the servers that read your repository, and a reason to keep them off pages with sensitive context. Failure 6: wrong tool for the repository GitHubBox is the clean example. For this Scala and Java repository, the editor opened and the preview was empty, which looks like an error on your side, not a mismatch. The test before you open any of these tools is one question about the repository: what is its main language, and what do I want out of it? If the repository is Reach for Skip JavaScript or Node, and you want to run it GitHubBox Nothing, but expect to wait for installs Any language, and you want to read it github1s GitHubBox Any language, and you want to ask an LLM GitIngest for a one-off, GitMCP for repeated use Pasting the unfiltered dump Large, unfamiliar, and you want the shape GitDiagram, then verify in github1s Trusting the hub node Popular open source project DeepWiki, if already indexed Indexing someone else’s repo with your email Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices The tools have few settings, so the tuning is mostly about what you decide before you open them and what you do with the output afterwards. Pick the tool by the question, not by the novelty What do you want to know? | +-- "Where is X, and how is it written?" ---------> github1s | (read, search) +-- "What are the parts and how do they connect?" -> GitDiagram | (then verify in github1s) +-- "Answer questions about it, once" ------------> GitIngest | (scope with excludes first) +-- "Answer questions about it, repeatedly" ------> GitMCP | (the assistant fetches on demand) +-- "Does it run?" (Node/JS only) ----------------> GitHubBox +-- "A wiki for a well-known project" ------------> DeepWiki (only if already indexed) Walk the diagram top to bottom. The first two branches need no AI at all for the answer: github1s is plain browsing. The AI-backed branches (GitIngest, GitMCP, GitDiagram, DeepWiki) are where you should check the result. A pipeline that uses three of them For an unfamiliar repository, in this order: GitDiagram for the shape. Open the .md version if you want to paste the overview and component list into your notes. Write down the two or three clusters that matter to you. github1s to confirm. Open one file from each cluster and read it. This is where the Example runner hub gets caught. GitIngest, scoped for the deep question. Exclude everything outside the clusters you picked, so the token count matches the question. GitMCP if you will keep asking. A configured MCP URL beats re-pasting a dump every session, and does not go stale the way a pinned dump does. (Configuration shown above; not exercised end to end in this post.) Scope before you paste GitIngest’s controls are the only real tuning surface in the set. Control Default seen What it does Use it when Exclude / Include pattern empty Glob patterns, comma separated, e.g. *.md, src/ Always, for anything over a few dozen files Include files under 50 kB Skips larger files Generated or data files dominate Private Repository off Checkbox for private repositories Not tested here Measured on this repository, one exclude list changed the result like this: Exclude list Files Estimated tokens None 280 173.5k *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties 151 64.1k Patterns worth trying, as starting points and not measured here: exclude test folders when the question is about production code, exclude *.json and *.csv for data-heavy repositories, and use Include mode to keep only one module’s directory. Verify the file count after each change, because a pattern that matches more than you meant removes the evidence for your question. Check what you are about to send Before pasting a dump anywhere, run two local commands on a shallow clone. They cost almost nothing and they are the check the web tools do not give you: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments cd ranga_spark_experiments git ls-files | wc -l grep -rIn --exclude-dir=.git -E 'AKIA|password *=|secret' . On this repository that printed 313 tracked files, and the grep produced a handful of hits that were all configuration key names and placeholders: Hadoop fs.s3a.secret.key settings that read the value from a variable, a usage string with the literal arguments ranga_aws_access_key ranga_aws_secret_key, and a spark.datasource.hive.warehouse.password=hive line in a run script. No real credential. That outcome is the point of the exercise: a pattern search finds names, so a person has to triage it, and it is quicker to do that on a terminal than after the text is in a chat. The file counts differ by tool and the post did not reconcile them: git ls-files says 313, GitIngest analysed 280, and 151 after excludes. Different tools count binary files, ignored files and size limits differently. Compare counts within a tool, not across tools. Prompt template for a dump A pasted repository answers better when the prompt says what the text is. Below is a snapshot of github.com/<owner>/<repo> at commit <sha>, filtered to <what you kept>. Answer only from this text. If the answer is not in it, say which file you would need. Quote file paths. Question: <your question> The commit hash comes from the Summary panel (eaf9e23... here). It tells the assistant, and your future self, which snapshot the answer is about. The “which file you would need” line is the cheap guard against a cropped or filtered dump producing a confident answer from missing evidence. Cost and trade-offs against a local clone Browser tools (this post) git clone --depth 1 plus local tools Setup None Network fetch and disk Disk used None 1,812 KB for this repository, of which 304 KB is .git Completeness Sampled (GitDiagram read 40 files) or cropped (GitIngest preview at 300k characters) Everything tracked Privacy The repository name and content go to a third party Stays on your machine Repeatable in CI Not shown to work (see Failure 3) Yes Freshness A snapshot, or live through GitMCP git pull Cost Free, with ads or sponsors Free For this 313-file repository the clone is 1,812 KB on disk, with a 304 KB .git. The browser tools do not save you bytes at this size. They save you the decision to set anything up, which matters for a repository you will open once and does not matter for one you will work in. Timings are left out on purpose: they depend on the network and the day. Key takeaways The trick is the same in every case. Open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host. github1s.com, gitingest.com, gitdiagram.com, gitmcp.io, githubbox.com and deepwiki.com all take owner/repo after it. Match the tool to the question. Reading and searching: github1s. Shape of an unfamiliar repository: GitDiagram. One-off questions to an LLM: GitIngest. Repeated questions: GitMCP. Running a JavaScript project: GitHubBox. Scope before you paste. One exclude list took the test repository from 280 files and 173.5k estimated tokens to 151 files and 64.1k. Verify the AI-generated views. GitDiagram read 40 of 280 files and drew a hub node the repository does not have. Use it as a table of contents and confirm in the source. Know what did not work. GitHubBox showed a blank preview for a Maven project, DeepWiki had not indexed the repository and asks for an email, and GitMCP was configured from its page but not run end to end here. Do not use these on private code unless cleared. The server-side tools run on someone else’s infrastructure. For anything repeatable, clone. A shallow clone of this repository is 1,812 KB on disk, runs offline, and scripts cleanly. References github1s, the VS Code web viewer for GitHub repositories GitIngest, which turns a repository into a prompt-ready text file GitDiagram, which generates an architecture diagram and a Markdown overview GitMCP, which serves a repository as a remote MCP endpoint GitHubBox, which opens a repository in CodeSandbox DeepWiki, which hosts generated wikis for indexed repositories The test repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments Model Context Protocol for what an MCP server and client are Trademarks GitHub is a trademark of GitHub, Inc. Visual Studio Code is a trademark of Microsoft Corporation. CodeSandbox, Cursor, Claude and DeepWiki are trademarks of their respective owners. Apache Spark, Apache Kafka, Apache Hive and Apache Maven are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries.

entry.title: Spark 4 in four releases: the features worth knowing and what they cost

link.title: Spark 4 in four releases: the features worth knowing and what they cost

entry.content:
• Three shifts behind the features
    • SQL becomes the main surface again
    • Batch and streaming converge on one declarative layer
    • Python and Connect move off the JVM path
  • The features, release by release
    • Spark 4.0: the break, and a far more expressive SQL
      • ANSI mode on by default (SPARK-44444)
      • VARIANT, a type for JSON you do not want to schema
      • SQL pipe syntax (SPARK-49555)
      • SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057)
      • Session variables (SPARK-42849)
      • String collation (SPARK-46830)
      • The built-in XML data source (SPARK-44265)
      • The Python Data Source API and Python UDTFs (SPARK-44076)
    • Spark 4.1: pipelines, procedural SQL, and real-time mode
      • SQL scripting (SPARK-54499)
      • Recursive common table expressions (SPARK-24497)
      • VARIANT generally available, with colon paths (SPARK-54454, SPARK-52494)
      • Smaller additions: sketches, parameter markers and Arrow UDFs
      • Spark Declarative Pipelines (SPARK-51727)
      • Structured Streaming real-time mode (SPARK-53736)
    • Spark 4.2: new types, new joins, and a clearer SQL surface
      • Geospatial types: GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY (SPARK-51658)
      • The QUALIFY clause (SPARK-31561)
      • NEAREST BY top-K ranking join (SPARK-56395)
      • SET PATH: where unqualified names are looked up (SPARK-54806)
      • Metric views (SPARK-54119)
      • Smaller addition: time_bucket and IGNORE NULLS (SPARK-56594, SPARK-55256)
    • Spark 4.3: stateful real-time mode, semi-structured SQL, and history tracking
      • JSON_TABLE (SPARK-58366)
      • ASOF JOIN (SPARK-58092)
      • UNNEST in the FROM clause (SPARK-58419)
      • VARIANT editing functions (SPARK-57804 and others)
      • TIME(p) and nanosecond timestamps (SPARK-57551, SPARK-56876)
      • Stateful real-time mode (SPARK-58635, SPARK-57228, SPARK-58508)
      • Auto CDC with SCD Type 2 (SPARK-58321, SPARK-58247, SPARK-58261)
      • New functions (SPARK-56820, SPARK-57253, SPARK-58399, SPARK-58295)
      • Faster queries on small data (SPARK-57851, SPARK-57268)
  • Run every example yourself
    • What you need
    • Download and verify
    • Four things that went wrong first
    • A runner that executes a SQL file
    • One SQL file per release
    • The PySpark examples
    • Real-time mode against Kafka
    • Cleaning up
  • When these features bite
  • Which upgrades are worth it
    • Settings that gate these features
    • What to budget for
    • Upgrade by upgrade
    • Before you upgrade
  • All features at a glance
    • Spark 4.0
    • Spark 4.1
    • Spark 4.2
    • Spark 4.3
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • Four minor releases in about seventeen months, each with its own centre of gravity: a break with the past and a far more expressive SQL (4.0), pipelines and procedural SQL (4.1), new data types and joins (4.2), stateful low-latency streaming and history tracking (4.3).
  • About eight features per release, each with what it is, why it exists, the syntax and the output of a real run on the release that introduced it.
  • Several headline features are off by default or need a connector. The text names the exact setting rather than implying they work out of the box.
  • Removals, default changes and upgrade risks are in the release history post.

A Spark release note lists hundreds of tickets, and most of them have nothing to do with the job you run on Monday. This post picks the features a data engineer meets in daily work across 4.0 to 4.3 and shows, for each, the syntax and what it printed when run.

Release Date Tickets resolved What the release note leads with
4.0.0 23 May 2025 over 5,100 Scala 2.13 and Java 17 as the baseline, ANSI mode on by default, VARIANT, SQL user-defined functions, session variables, pipe syntax, collations, a built-in XML source, a Python data source API, a lightweight Spark Connect client
4.1.0 16 Dec 2025 over 1,800 Spark Declarative Pipelines, Structured Streaming real-time mode, SQL scripting and VARIANT generally available, Arrow-native Python UDFs, recursive CTEs
4.2.0 14 Jul 2026 over 1,700 Geospatial types, change data capture, Arrow-optimized Python UDFs on by default, NEAREST BY joins, SQL path resolution, metric views
4.3.0 30 Oct 2026 over 1,100 Stateful real-time mode, SCD Type 2 in Auto CDC, JSON_TABLE, ASOF JOIN, VARIANT editing functions, faster queries on small data

The last gap is half the size of the first two, and 4.3.0 shipped with no preview builds.

That last point matters when you pick a release. 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 went through two, four and five preview builds. 4.3.0 had none (no 4.3.0-preview exists on Maven Central or the Apache archive), so it has had the least outside testing, and the patch releases that follow it are where the first corrections will land.

Every example ran on the release that introduced the feature, on an official Docker image and, for the SQL and Scala examples, on the plain release tarball too. The setup is in Run every example yourself. Where a feature needed a flag, a connector or a second tool to run at all, that feature’s section says so.

Three shifts behind the features

Read the four release notes in order and they look like four unrelated lists. Read them as one line and three decisions run through all of them, which is also why some features arrive in pieces over two or three releases.

Each lane is one shift; each box is what that release added to it.

SQL becomes the main surface again

For a decade the work went into the DataFrame API. The fourth line turns back to SQL and adds constructs that other SQL engines have and Spark did not.

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3
New query syntax Pipe syntax (SPARK-49555) Recursive CTEs (SPARK-24497), query parameter markers anywhere (SPARK-53573) QUALIFY (SPARK-31561), NEAREST BY join (SPARK-56395) ASOF JOIN (SPARK-58092), JSON_TABLE (SPARK-58366), UNNEST in FROM (SPARK-58419)
Procedural SQL Session variables (SPARK-42849), SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057) SQL scripting, enabled by default (SPARK-54499) Cursors in scripting (SPARK-54759) none in the headlines
Data types VARIANT (SPARK-45827), string collations (SPARK-46830) VARIANT generally available (SPARK-54454) GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY (SPARK-51658) VARIANT editing functions (SPARK-57804), nanosecond timestamps in preview (SPARK-56876)
Name resolution none none SET PATH and CURRENT_PATH() (SPARK-54806, behind a flag) none

Teams used to write logic in Python or Scala because SQL could not express it, and paid for it in code analysts could not read and the optimiser could not see through. Putting the constructs into the language fixes that. The cost is that each one is another thing the parser, analyzer and optimiser must keep correct, and several arrive behind a flag first.

Batch and streaming converge on one declarative layer

Streaming and batch meet in one declarative layer, and the streaming side gets a second, lower-latency mode.

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3
Pipelines none Spark Declarative Pipelines (SPARK-51727) Auto CDC, SCD Type 1 (SPARK-56249) Auto CDC, SCD Type 2 (SPARK-58321 and others)
Change data none none CHANGES clause and DataFrame APIs for row-level changes (SPARK-55668) consumed by Auto CDC SCD Type 2
Streaming latency Arbitrary state API v2, state data source Real-time mode, stateless (SPARK-53736) none in the headlines Real-time mode with state: aggregation, dropDuplicates, transformWithState (SPARK-58635 and others)
Writes none stored procedures API for catalogs (SPARK-44167) Data Source V2 transaction management (SPARK-55855) dynamic table options for UPDATE, MERGE, DELETE

A pipeline used to need an orchestrator for ordering, a streaming job for freshness and hand-written merge logic for change data, written in different dialects by different teams. Declaring the datasets and letting Spark derive the graph removes that, and the cost is that you hand the execution graph to the framework: when a run behaves oddly, the schedule is not code you wrote. An external orchestrator with micro-batch triggers is still the better fit for pipelines that mix many engines.

Python and Connect move off the JVM path

The client and the language runtime change shape, not just the API.

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3
Spark Connect A lightweight Python client, ML over Connect JDBC driver for Connect (SPARK-53484), ML on Connect generally available for Python (SPARK-51236) RDD API compatibility (SPARK-55227) REST endpoints for sessions and operations (SPARK-57941), more complete JDBC driver
Python UDFs Python UDTFs, unified UDF profiling Arrow-native UDF and UDTF decorators (SPARK-52214, SPARK-52979) Arrow-optimized UDFs and Arrow IPC on by default (SPARK-54555) Python performance work
Python data Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), plotting API (SPARK-49530) filter pushdown for Python data sources grouped-aggregation UDFs in Arrow and pandas none in the headlines
Small data none none none opt-in single-task execution and Arrow-native caching (SPARK-57851, SPARK-57268)

Python was the most used language and the slowest path through Spark, because every row crossed the JVM boundary through pickling, and a client that only talks to a server still needed a full PySpark install. The fix is Arrow end to end, a thin client (4.0 added a 1.5 MB pyspark-client), and a server reachable by JDBC and REST. A default that changes how data crosses the boundary changes behaviour at the edges, in types, nulls and timestamps, which is why 4.2 is the release to test on your own UDFs.

The features, release by release

Every entry has the same shape: what it is and why it exists, the syntax, a run, and a maturity tag.

Tag Meaning
Default Works with no configuration on the release that introduced it
GA, on by default Was experimental earlier and is now enabled and supported
Behind a flag Present, but off until you set a configuration
Preview The release note says so; syntax or behaviour can still change
Needs a connector The engine defines the syntax; a data source has to implement it

The last tag is the one that surprises people. A feature that exists in Spark SQL does not exist for your table until the connector for that table supports it, which is true of change data capture, data source transactions and several INSERT extensions.

The sample data is a four-row orders view (id, region, amount) unless an entry says otherwise, and the output shown is what the release printed.

Every example is a runnable file in ranga-spark4-examples, organised by release: spark-4.0/, spark-4.1/, spark-4.2/ and spark-4.3/. ./run.sh 4.2 spark-4.2/02_qualify.sql runs one in Docker. All features at a glance at the end of the post lists every feature with its example.

Spark 4.0: the break, and a far more expressive SQL

All 4.0 examples ran on apache/spark:4.0.5-python3, which reports Scala 2.13 and Java 17. Those two facts are themselves the baseline change: Scala 2.12 and JDK 8 and 11 are gone, which is covered in the release history post.

ANSI mode on by default (SPARK-44444)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 01_ansi_mode.sql.

Before 4.0, an invalid cast returned NULL and a divide by zero returned NULL, silently. With ANSI mode on, both fail loudly, and the error message names the function that tolerates the bad value instead. Data you used to lose without noticing now stops the job.

SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled;          -- true

SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT);           -- [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] ... Use `try_cast` to tolerate malformed input
SELECT try_cast('abc' AS INT);       -- NULL
SELECT 1/0;                          -- [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO] ... Use `try_divide` to tolerate divisor being 0
SELECT try_divide(1, 0);             -- NULL

Watch for: this is the change most likely to turn a green pipeline red. Run your own data through it before the upgrade, and use the try_* functions where a NULL was the intended answer.

VARIANT, a type for JSON you do not want to schema

Maturity: Default in 4.0, generally available in 4.1.

Example in the repo: 02_variant.sql.

A VARIANT holds a semi-structured value, such as JSON, in an encoded binary form, so a query reads a path out of it without re-parsing text and without a fixed schema up front. The alternative is a STRING column and get_json_object on every read.

SELECT parse_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3],"c":{"d":"x"}}') AS v;
-- {"a":1,"b":[1,2,3],"c":{"d":"x"}}

SELECT variant_get(parse_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3]}'), '$.b[1]', 'int');   -- 2

SELECT schema_of_variant(parse_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3]}'));
-- OBJECT<a: BIGINT, b: ARRAY<BIGINT>>

The v:field colon shorthand is not in 4.0. The same statement fails on 4.0.5 with PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR ... at or near ':', and works from 4.1.

SQL pipe syntax (SPARK-49555)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 03_pipe_syntax.sql.

Pipe syntax lets a query read top to bottom, one step per |>, instead of inside-out. It is the same logical plan, written in the order you think it.

FROM orders
|> WHERE amount > 5
|> AGGREGATE sum(amount) AS total GROUP BY region
|> ORDER BY total DESC;
-- eu  40.0
-- us  20.0

FROM orders |> EXTEND amount * 2 AS doubled |> SELECT id, doubled |> LIMIT 2;
-- 1  20.0
-- 2  40.0

SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 04_sql_udf.sql.

A function written in SQL, scalar or table-valued. Because it is SQL, the optimiser can see through it, which a Python or Scala UDF does not allow.

CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION add_tax(x DOUBLE) RETURNS DOUBLE RETURN x * 1.18;
SELECT id, add_tax(amount) AS gross FROM orders;        -- 1  11.799999999999999 ...

CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION big_orders(min_amt DOUBLE)
  RETURNS TABLE (id INT, amount DOUBLE)
  RETURN SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= min_amt;
SELECT * FROM big_orders(20.0);                          -- (2, 20.0), (3, 30.0)

Session variables (SPARK-42849)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 05_session_variables.sql.

A typed variable that lives for the session, set with DECLARE and SET VAR and usable anywhere an expression is. It is the typed alternative to splicing a value into SQL text.

DECLARE OR REPLACE VARIABLE threshold DOUBLE DEFAULT 15.0;
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount > threshold;          -- 2, 3

SET VAR threshold = 25.0;
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount > threshold;          -- 3

String collation (SPARK-46830)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 06_string_collation.sql.

A collation controls how strings compare and sort: case-insensitive, accent aware, by locale. Before collations, case-insensitive matching meant wrapping both sides in lower().

SELECT 'Apple' = 'apple';                                -- false
SELECT 'Apple' COLLATE UTF8_LCASE = 'apple';             -- true
SELECT collation('x' COLLATE UNICODE_CI);                -- SYSTEM.BUILTIN.UNICODE_CI

-- values: 'Ana', 'ana', 'ANA', 'Bob'
SELECT count(DISTINCT n COLLATE UTF8_LCASE) FROM names;  -- 2

The built-in XML data source (SPARK-44265)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 07_xml_functions.sql.

XML reads and writes without the old external package, plus from_xml, to_xml and schema_of_xml for XML held in a string column.

SELECT from_xml('<p><name>Ana</name><age>30</age></p>', 'name STRING, age INT');
-- {name: Ana, age: 30}

SELECT schema_of_xml('<p><name>Ana</name><age>30</age></p>');
-- STRUCT<age: BIGINT, name: STRING>

df = spark.read.format("xml").option("rowTag", "person").load("/tmp/xmlin")
# age: long, name: string  ->  (30, 'Ana'), (41, 'Bob')

The Python Data Source API and Python UDTFs (SPARK-44076)

Maturity: Default, but needs the pyarrow package.

Example in the repo: 09_python_data_source.py.

You can write a data source in plain Python, register it, and read it by name, including from SQL. A Python user-defined table function returns several rows per input row. On the official image both fail until pyarrow is installed: the Python data source worker raises ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyarrow'.

from pyspark.sql.datasource import DataSource, DataSourceReader
from pyspark.sql.functions import udtf

class CounterDataSource(DataSource):
    @classmethod
    def name(cls): return "counter"
    def schema(self): return "n INT, square INT"
    def reader(self, schema): return CounterReader(self.options)

class CounterReader(DataSourceReader):
    def __init__(self, options): self.limit = int(options.get("limit", 3))
    def read(self, partition):
        for i in range(1, self.limit + 1):
            yield (i, i * i)

spark.dataSource.register(CounterDataSource)
spark.read.format("counter").option("limit", 4).load().show()
# n=1..4, square=1,4,9,16

@udtf(returnType="word: string, length: int")
class SplitWords:
    def eval(self, text: str):
        for w in text.split():
            yield (w, len(w))

spark.udtf.register("split_words", SplitWords)
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM split_words('spark four point zero')").show()
# spark 5, four 4, point 5, zero 4

Also in 4.0, not run here:

  • transformWithState for custom stateful processing in Scala, Java and Python, the state data source reader, and state store improvements such as SST file reuse
  • Polymorphic Python UDTFs whose output schema is decided at call time
  • Named and unnamed parameter markers for parameterized queries
  • Structured JSON logging, seen in every error the 4.0 runs logged
  • A 1.5 MB lightweight Python client, spark.api.mode to switch Connect on, and community Spark Connect clients for Go, Swift and Rust
  • Native Plotly-based plotting on PySpark DataFrames (SPARK-49530)
  • Java 21 support, the Spark Kubernetes operator (SPARK-45923), Spark ML on Connect, and unified PySpark UDF profiling

Spark 4.1: pipelines, procedural SQL, and real-time mode

The 4.1 examples ran on apache/spark:4.1.3-python3, apart from real-time mode, which used the playground’s Spark 4.1.3 image because it needs Kafka.

SQL scripting (SPARK-54499)

Maturity: GA, on by default (spark.sql.scripting.enabled is true).

Example in the repo: 01_sql_scripting.sql.

A script is a BEGIN ... END block with variables, loops, conditions and error handlers, run as one statement. It moves logic that lived in a Python driver into SQL that an analyst can read.

BEGIN
  DECLARE total INT DEFAULT 0;
  DECLARE i INT DEFAULT 1;
  WHILE i <= 5 DO
    SET total = total + i;
    SET i = i + 1;
  END WHILE;
  SELECT total, i;
END;
-- 15, 6

BEGIN
  DECLARE result DOUBLE DEFAULT 0;
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR DIVIDE_BY_ZERO
  BEGIN
    SET result = -1;
    SELECT 'caught divide by zero' AS status, result;
  END;
  SET result = 1 / 0;
  SELECT 'not reached' AS status, result;
END;
-- caught divide by zero, -1.0

BEGIN
  DECLARE msg STRING DEFAULT '';
  FOR r AS SELECT region, sum(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY region DO
    SET msg = msg || r.region || '=' || CAST(r.total AS STRING) || ' ';
  END FOR;
  SELECT trim(msg) AS summary;
END;
-- eu=40.0 us=25.0

A script returns the result of its last query, which is what spark.sql handed back in each run above.

Recursive common table expressions (SPARK-24497)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 02_recursive_cte.sql.

A CTE that refers to itself, for hierarchies and graph walks that used to need a loop in application code.

WITH RECURSIVE t(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM t WHERE n < 5
) SELECT n FROM t;
-- 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

A four-level org chart walked from the root (boss IS NULL) returned ceo 0, vp 1, dir 2, mgr 3, one row per level, by joining each employee to the previous level’s output.

VARIANT generally available, with colon paths (SPARK-54454, SPARK-52494)

Maturity: GA, on by default.

Example in the repo: 03_variant_colon_paths.sql.

4.1 declares VARIANT generally available and adds the v:path shorthand, with ::type to cast the result. The release also adds shredding for faster Parquet reads of variants; that part was not run here.

SELECT v:user::string AS user,
       v:tags[0]::string AS first_tag,
       schema_of_variant(v:n) AS n_type
FROM ev ORDER BY 1;
-- a  x     BIGINT
-- b  NULL  STRING

The n field is a number in one row and a string in the other, which a typed column could not hold, and schema_of_variant reports each row’s own type.

Smaller additions: sketches, parameter markers and Arrow UDFs

Maturity: Default. The Arrow UDFs need pyarrow.

Example in the repo: 04_sketch_functions.sql, 05_parameter_markers.py, 06_arrow_udf.py.

Sketch functions (SPARK-52515, SPARK-54199, SPARK-52407) are approximate aggregates that can be stored and merged: top-k frequent items, KLL quantile sketches and Theta set-cardinality sketches. A sketch column can be rolled up later without rereading the raw rows.

SELECT approx_top_k(page, 2) FROM clicks;
-- [{item: a, count: 3}, {item: b, count: 2}]

SELECT kll_sketch_get_quantile_bigint(kll_sketch_agg_bigint(ms), 0.5D) AS p50,
       kll_sketch_get_quantile_bigint(kll_sketch_agg_bigint(ms), 0.99D) AS p99
FROM lat;                      -- ms = 1..1000
-- 499, 989 on 4.1.3 (500, 990 on 4.1.4)

SELECT theta_sketch_estimate(theta_union_agg(s)) FROM (
  SELECT theta_sketch_agg(x) s FROM VALUES (1),(2),(3) AS a(x)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT theta_sketch_agg(x)   FROM VALUES (3),(4)   AS b(x));
-- 4

The exact median of 1 to 1000 is about 500 and the exact 99th percentile about 990. The sketch returned 499 and 989 on 4.1.3 and 500 and 990 on 4.1.4 for the same input, so assert a tolerance on sketch results in tests, not an exact value.

Parameter markers (SPARK-53573): :name markers used to work in a few expression positions. In 4.1 a pre-parser substitutes them nearly anywhere, including identifiers and inside scripts, so a value from application code never has to be spliced into the SQL text.

spark.sql("SELECT * FROM IDENTIFIER(:t) ORDER BY id LIMIT :n", args={"t": "orders", "n": 2})
# (1, eu, 10.0), (2, us, 20.0)

spark.sql("""BEGIN
  DECLARE x INT DEFAULT :start;
  SET x = x + 1;
  SELECT x;
END""", args={"start": 41})
# 42

Arrow-native UDFs (SPARK-52214, SPARK-52979): @arrow_udf and @arrow_udtf pass a function whole PyArrow arrays instead of converting to pandas first, so a vectorised function stays vectorised.

import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import arrow_udf, col

@arrow_udf("double")
def with_tax(amount: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.multiply(amount, 1.18)

df.select("id", with_tax(col("amount")).alias("gross")).show()
# 1  11.799999999999999
# 2  23.599999999999998

Spark Declarative Pipelines (SPARK-51727)

Maturity: Default, driven by the spark-pipelines CLI. The official image needs extra Python packages.

Example in the repo: 07_declarative_pipelines.

You declare datasets, and Spark works out the order. A pipeline project is a spark-pipeline.yml and a folder of Python or SQL files. This one has a materialized view in Python and another in SQL that reads it:

name: orders_pipeline
libraries:
  - glob:
      include: transformations/**
storage: file:///work/sdp/storage

# transformations/orders.py
from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.active()

@dp.materialized_view
def orders() -> DataFrame:
    return spark.sql("SELECT * FROM VALUES (1,'eu',10.0D),(2,'us',20.0D),"
                     "(3,'eu',30.0D),(4,'us',5.0D) AS t(id, region, amount)")

-- transformations/revenue.sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW revenue_by_region AS
SELECT region, sum(amount) AS total, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;

spark-pipelines dry-run      # catches syntax, analysis and cycle errors without writing
spark-pipelines run

The run log shows both flows queued together and orders running first, because revenue_by_region reads it. Nothing in the files states that order. The output tables were:

orders:                          revenue_by_region:
 id region amount                 region total orders
  1 eu     10.0                   eu      40.0  2
  2 us     20.0                   us      25.0  2
  3 eu     30.0
  4 us      5.0

Nothing in the files states the order; Spark reads it from the dependency.

The official image does not contain the Python packages the CLI needs. The first run fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml', and the CLI works through Spark Connect, so grpcio and its companions are needed too. Install pyyaml grpcio grpcio-status protobuf googleapis-common-protos zstandard, or use pip install pyspark[pipelines], which the 4.3 documentation recommends.

Structured Streaming real-time mode (SPARK-53736)

Maturity: Default for stateless queries, Scala only, Kafka source.

Example in the repo: 08_real_time_mode.scala.

Real-time mode runs a streaming query as long-lived tasks that process records as they arrive, instead of cutting the stream into micro-batches. You choose it with a trigger. In 4.1 it supports stateless queries and a short allowlist of sources, sinks and operators; the Kafka source is the supported source, and console, memory, foreach and Kafka are the supported sinks.

import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming.Trigger
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions._

val out = spark.readStream.format("kafka")
  .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:29092")
  .option("subscribe", "rtm_demo_in2").option("startingOffsets", "latest").load()
  .select(upper(col("value").cast("string")).alias("v"))

val q = out.writeStream.format("console").outputMode("update")
  .trigger(Trigger.RealTime("5 seconds")).start()

Messages hello, real and time produced to the topic came out as HELLO, REAL and TIME in a single batch. Python does not accept the trigger on 4.1.3: trigger(realTime="5 seconds") raised TypeError: DataStreamWriter.trigger() got an unexpected keyword argument 'realTime', matching the release note’s “Scala stateless support”. Stateful queries wait for 4.3.

Also in 4.1, not run here:

  • CONTINUE HANDLER and multi-variable DECLARE in SQL scripting, and shredding for faster VARIANT reads
  • Spark ML on Connect generally available for Python, zstd compression for protobuf plans, chunked Arrow result streaming, and no 2 GB limit on local relations
  • python_worker_logs() to query Python worker logs, and filter pushdown for Python data sources through pushFilters
  • A JDBC driver for Spark Connect (SPARK-53484)

Spark 4.2: new types, new joins, and a clearer SQL surface

The 4.2 examples ran on apache/spark:4.2.1-python3. Three of the release’s headline items, change data capture, INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and Data Source V2 transactions, are defined by the engine but implemented by a connector, so the built-in sources cannot show them. They are listed at the end of this section.

Geospatial types: GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY (SPARK-51658)

Maturity: Default in 4.2. The same call on 4.1.3 fails with GEOSPATIAL_DISABLED.

Example in the repo: 01_geospatial_types.sql.

Two first-class types for spatial values, each carrying an SRID (spatial reference id), so a geometry knows its coordinate system instead of being an anonymous BINARY. The release notes mention ST_* functions, WKB and WKT, and Parquet I/O. On 4.2.1 the function surface is small: SHOW FUNCTIONS lists five, and 4.3.0 lists the same five.

-- the five: st_asbinary, st_geogfromwkb, st_geomfromwkb, st_setsrid, st_srid
SELECT typeof(ST_GeomFromWKB(X'0101000000000000000000F03F0000000000000040'));   -- geometry(0)
SELECT typeof(ST_GeogFromWKB(X'0101000000000000000000F03F0000000000000040'));   -- geography(4326)

SELECT ST_SRID(ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromWKB(X'0101000000000000000000F03F0000000000000040'), 4326));
-- 4326

CREATE TEMP VIEW places AS
SELECT 'a' AS name,
       ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromWKB(X'0101000000000000000000F03F0000000000000040'), 4326) AS g;
DESCRIBE places;        -- name string, g geometry(4326)

Watch for: a GEOMETRY defaults to SRID 0 (unknown), a GEOGRAPHY to 4326, and there are no distance or containment functions in this release, so the types are a storage and interchange foundation rather than a spatial query engine yet.

The QUALIFY clause (SPARK-31561)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 02_qualify.sql.

QUALIFY filters on a window function directly, so “the top row per group” no longer needs a subquery around the window.

SELECT id, region, amount FROM orders_t
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC, id) = 1
ORDER BY region;
-- 3  eu  30.0
-- 2  us  20.0

SELECT id, region, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) AS r
FROM orders_t QUALIFY r = 1 ORDER BY id;     -- aliases work; ties all qualify
-- 2 us 1,  3 eu 1,  5 eu 1

The condition must contain a window function, and aggregates are not allowed in it.

NEAREST BY top-K ranking join (SPARK-56395)

Maturity: Default. Evaluation is brute force today.

Example in the repo: 03_nearest_by_join.sql.

For each row on the left, return the K best rows on the right under a ranking expression. It is the join shape behind “closest store”, “most similar item” and fuzzy matching, written as one clause instead of a cross join and a window.

-- pts:  (q1, 1.0), (q2, 9.0)       base: (a, 0.0), (b, 2.0), (c, 8.0), (d, 20.0)
SELECT q, x, name, y
FROM pts JOIN base EXACT NEAREST 2 BY DISTANCE abs(x - y)
ORDER BY q, abs(x - y);
-- q1 1.0 a 0.0
-- q1 1.0 b 2.0
-- q2 9.0 c 8.0
-- q2 9.0 b 2.0

SELECT q, name FROM pts JOIN base EXACT NEAREST BY DISTANCE abs(x - y);   -- K defaults to 1
-- q1 a,  q2 c

Syntax: { APPROX | EXACT } NEAREST [ k ] BY { DISTANCE | SIMILARITY } expr. INNER and LEFT OUTER are the supported join types, and k is between 1 and 100000. APPROX lets the optimiser use a faster strategy when one exists. The 4.2.1 documentation states the cost plainly: the current implementation evaluates the full cross product of the two sides, so pre-filter a large right side.

SET PATH: where unqualified names are looked up (SPARK-54806)

Maturity: Behind a flag (spark.sql.path.enabled, default false).

Example in the repo: 04_set_path.sql.

The SQL path is an ordered list of schemas Spark searches to resolve an unqualified table, view, function or variable. SET PATH changes it for the session, and current_path() reads it. Persistent views and SQL functions capture the path when they are created.

SELECT current_path();    -- system.builtin,system.session,spark_catalog.default

SET PATH = DEFAULT_PATH;
-- [UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.SET_PATH_WHEN_DISABLED] SET PATH is disabled.
-- Set spark.sql.path.enabled to true to enable it.

SET spark.sql.path.enabled = true;
-- two schemas each holding a table named facts: ref.facts (2,'ref'), sales.facts (1,'sales')

SET PATH = spark_catalog.ref, DEFAULT_PATH;
SELECT current_path();    -- spark_catalog.ref,system.builtin,system.session,spark_catalog.default
SELECT * FROM facts;      -- (2, 'ref')

SET PATH = spark_catalog.sales, DEFAULT_PATH;
SELECT * FROM facts;      -- (1, 'sales')

DDL does not use the path: CREATE TABLE t always creates t in the current schema.

Metric views (SPARK-54119)

Maturity: Default, on the built-in catalog.

Example in the repo: 05_metric_views.sql.

A metric view defines dimensions and measures once, in YAML, so every consumer computes the same number. You query a measure with MEASURE(...) and group by a dimension.

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sales.revenue_mv WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML AS $$
version: "0.1"
source: spark_catalog.sales.orders
dimensions:
  - name: region
    expr: region
measures:
  - name: total_amount
    expr: sum(amount)
  - name: order_count
    expr: count(1)
$$;

SELECT region, MEASURE(total_amount) AS total, MEASURE(order_count) AS n
FROM sales.revenue_mv GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;
-- eu  70.0  3
-- us  25.0  2

The 4.2.1 documentation has no page for this syntax. The statement form comes from the project’s own test suite, and the YAML layout above is the one that ran.

Smaller addition: time_bucket and IGNORE NULLS (SPARK-56594, SPARK-55256)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 06_time_bucket_ignore_nulls.sql.

time_bucket(size, ts[, origin]) returns the start of the bucket a timestamp falls into, replacing the date_trunc or epoch-division arithmetic everyone writes for fixed-width windows. collect_list and array_agg now take IGNORE NULLS and RESPECT NULLS.

SELECT time_bucket(INTERVAL '15' MINUTE, TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-11-01 11:27:00');
-- 2026-11-01 11:15:00

SELECT time_bucket(INTERVAL '1' HOUR, ts) AS hour, count(*) AS n, sum(v) AS total
FROM (VALUES (TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-11-01 10:05:00', 1),
             (TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-11-01 10:40:00', 2),
             (TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-11-01 11:10:00', 5)) AS t(ts, v)
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
-- 10:00  2  3
-- 11:00  1  5

SELECT collect_list(x) IGNORE NULLS, collect_list(x) RESPECT NULLS
FROM VALUES (1), (CAST(NULL AS INT)), (3) AS t(x);
-- [1, 3]    [1, NULL, 3]

Also in 4.2, not run here:

  • Items that need a connector: the CHANGES clause and CDC APIs (SPARK-55668), INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and REPLACE ON/USING (SPARK-54971, SPARK-56001), and Data Source V2 transactions (SPARK-55855)
  • Vector distance and similarity functions, cursors (DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE) in SQL scripts, tuple sketches, and broader TIME support across file formats
  • SYSTEM.BUILTIN and SYSTEM.SESSION qualification for built-in functions and temporary views
  • Arrow-optimized Python UDFs on by default (SPARK-54555), so test your own UDFs before trusting it, and zero-copy hand-off of DataFrames to Polars or DuckDB through the Arrow C Data Interface
  • Auto CDC with SCD Type 1 (SPARK-56249), and stateless PySpark queries in real-time mode
  • Spark Connect: RDD API compatibility, YARN cluster mode, and DataFrame inputs to spark.read.*
  • Faster MERGE INTO, operation summaries for UPDATE and DELETE, a web UI rebuilt on Bootstrap 5 with dark mode, heterogeneous Kubernetes executors, Spark History Server scalability, and JDK 25 support

Spark 4.3: stateful real-time mode, semi-structured SQL, and history tracking

All 4.3 examples ran on apache/spark:4.3.0-python3, which reports Scala 2.13 and Java 21. The release shipped without preview builds, and several features below are behind a flag or labelled preview.

JSON_TABLE (SPARK-58366)

Maturity: Default. Flat form only.

Example in the repo: 01_json_table.sql.

The SQL-standard way to turn a JSON document into rows and typed columns. It is the construct that migrated Oracle, DB2 and MySQL queries expect.

SELECT t.* FROM JSON_TABLE(
  '{"items":[{"id":1,"n":"a"},{"id":2,"n":"b"}]}',
  '$.items[*]'
  COLUMNS (
    seq  FOR ORDINALITY,
    id   INT    PATH '$.id',
    name STRING PATH '$.n'
  )
) AS t;
-- 1  1  a
-- 2  2  b

SELECT * FROM JSON_TABLE(
  '{"rows":[{"id":10,"opt":1},{"id":20}]}',
  '$.rows[*]'
  COLUMNS (id INT, hasOpt BOOLEAN EXISTS PATH '$.opt')
) AS t;
-- 10  true
-- 20  false

-- against a column, with LATERAL
SELECT d.id, t.k, t.v FROM docs d,
LATERAL JSON_TABLE(d.doc, '$.tags[*]' COLUMNS (k STRING PATH '$.k', v INT PATH '$.v')) AS t;
-- 1 x 1,  1 y 2,  2 z 3

NESTED PATH columns are not supported yet, so a document nested more than one array deep still needs two steps.

ASOF JOIN (SPARK-58092)

Maturity: Behind a flag (spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled, default false).

Example in the repo: 02_asof_join.sql.

For each left row, take the closest preceding row on the right: the quote in force when a trade happened, the price list valid on an order date. Without it you write a window function plus a join.

SELECT t.id, t.sym, t.ts, q.ts AS quote_ts, q.bid
FROM trades t ASOF JOIN quotes q
  MATCH_CONDITION (t.ts >= q.ts)
  ON t.sym = q.sym
ORDER BY t.id;

With the flag off the statement fails at parse time with [UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.ASOF_JOIN] ... Set "spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled" to true. With it on, using trades at 10:00:05 and 10:00:20 for AAPL and 10:00:07 for MSFT, against quotes at 10:00:00 and 10:00:10 for AAPL and 10:00:06 for MSFT:

id  sym   ts        quote_ts  bid
1   AAPL  10:00:05  10:00:00  100.0
2   AAPL  10:00:20  10:00:10  101.0
3   MSFT  10:00:07  10:00:06  200.0

Three trades matched to their quotes: 100.0, 101.0 and 200.0.

Only INNER and LEFT OUTER are supported. In streaming, micro-batch supports a streaming left side joined to a static right side, and real-time mode does not support it.

UNNEST in the FROM clause (SPARK-58419)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 03_unnest.sql.

The ANSI way to expand arrays into rows, in place of explode and LATERAL VIEW. Several arrays expand in parallel and the shorter ones pad with NULL.

SELECT * FROM UNNEST(array('a','b')) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(value, pos);
-- a 1,  b 2

SELECT * FROM UNNEST(array(1,2), array(10,20,30)) AS t(a, b);
-- 1 10,  2 20,  NULL 30

SELECT id, elem
FROM VALUES (1, array(10,20)), (2, array(30)) AS data(id, arr),
     LATERAL UNNEST(arr) AS t(elem);
-- 1 10,  1 20,  2 30

VARIANT editing functions (SPARK-57804 and others)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 04_variant_editing.sql.

Until now a variant could be read but not changed without rebuilding it. These return a new variant with a path set, inserted, deleted or appended to.

SELECT variant_set(parse_json('{"a":1,"tags":["x"]}'), '$.b', 3);
-- {"a":1,"b":3,"tags":["x"]}

SELECT variant_insert(parse_json('["a","b","c"]'), '$[1]', 'z');
-- ["a","z","b","c"]

SELECT variant_delete(parse_json('{"a":1,"b":2,"items":[1,2,3]}'), '$.a', '$.items[0]');
-- {"b":2,"items":[2,3]}

SELECT variant_array_append(parse_json('{"a":[1,2]}'), '$.a', 3);
-- {"a":[1,2,3]}

SELECT variant_strip_nulls(parse_json('{"a":1,"b":null,"c":[1,null]}'));
-- {"a":1,"c":[1]}

variant_set and variant_insert differ on an existing key: set replaces it, insert is an error. try_ forms exist too (try_variant_set and others).

TIME(p) and nanosecond timestamps (SPARK-57551, SPARK-56876)

Maturity: Behind flags, and preview for the nanosecond timestamps.

Example in the repo: 05_time_and_nanosecond_types.sql.

TIME(p) goes up to nanosecond precision, and TIMESTAMP_NTZ(9) and TIMESTAMP_LTZ(9) add nanosecond timestamps. Two flags guard them: spark.sql.timeType.enabled for TIME, and spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled for the timestamps, which the release notes call a preview.

SET spark.sql.timeType.enabled = true;
SET spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled = true;

SELECT typeof(CAST('10:15:30.123456789' AS TIME(9)));        -- time(9)

SELECT CAST(CAST('2026-11-01 10:00:00.123456789' AS TIMESTAMP_NTZ(9)) AS STRING),
       typeof(CAST('2026-11-01 10:00:00.123456789' AS TIMESTAMP_NTZ(9)));
-- 2026-11-01 10:00:00.123456789   timestamp_ntz(9)

SELECT CAST('2026-11-01 10:00:00.123456789' AS TIMESTAMP_NTZ);   -- default keeps microseconds
-- 2026-11-01 10:00:00.123456

Without spark.sql.timeType.enabled, CAST(... AS TIME(9)) fails with UNSUPPORTED_TIME_TYPE, so TIME itself is still behind a flag in 4.3.0. The Python client in this release cannot materialise a TIMESTAMP_NTZ(9) result: selecting the column raised CANNOT_PARSE_DATATYPE ... timestamp_ntz(9), which is why the example casts to a string.

Stateful real-time mode (SPARK-58635, SPARK-57228, SPARK-58508)

Maturity: Default for the supported operators; needs one task slot per shuffle partition.

Example in the repo: 07_stateful_real_time_mode.scala.

4.1 gave real-time mode to stateless queries. 4.3 adds streaming aggregation, dropDuplicates and transformWithState. The trigger is the same.

val counts = spark.readStream.format("kafka")
  .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:29092").option("subscribe", "rtm43_demo3")
  .option("startingOffsets", "latest").load()
  .select(col("value").cast("string").alias("word"))
  .groupBy("word").count()

counts.writeStream.format("console").outputMode("update")
  .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/rtm43_ckpt3")
  .trigger(Trigger.RealTime("5 seconds")).start()

Producing a, b, a, a printed the running counts as the records arrived:

Batch 2
|word|count|
|   a|    1|
|   a|    2|
|   a|    3|
|   b|    1|

The word a appears three times in one batch because real-time mode emits each update as it happens, not one row per key at the end of the batch.

Watch for: the first attempt, with Spark’s default 200 shuffle partitions on a local[2] session, failed:

[CONCURRENT_SCHEDULER_INSUFFICIENT_SLOT] Cannot run the pipelined stage group:
it needs 201 concurrent task slots to run all its stages together, but only 2
are currently free.

The stages of a real-time query run at the same time, so the cluster needs a free slot for every task in all of them. Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to a number the cluster can run concurrently (2, on a local[6] session, worked) before you size the job.

Auto CDC with SCD Type 2 (SPARK-58321, SPARK-58247, SPARK-58261)

Maturity: Needs a connector. Spark’s built-in file formats are refused.

Example in the repo: 08_auto_cdc_scd2.sql.

Auto CDC applies a stream of change events to a target table inside a Declarative Pipeline. Type 1 keeps only the latest row per key. Type 2, new in 4.3, keeps the history of every change. The SQL form is a streaming table with an Auto CDC flow:

CREATE STREAMING TABLE customers_history
FLOW AUTO CDC
FROM STREAM(cdc_events)
KEYS (id)
APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'DELETE'
SEQUENCE BY version
COLUMNS * EXCEPT (op)
STORED AS SCD TYPE 2;

On a pipeline whose target is a default Parquet table, the syntax parses and the flow fails to start:

[AUTOCDC_TARGET_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_MERGE] Cannot start AutoCDC flow: the target table
`spark_catalog`.`default`.`customers_history` (format: parquet) does not support
row-level operations.

Each micro-batch is applied with a MERGE, so the target must be a table whose connector implements Data Source V2 row-level operations. The 4.3 documentation names lakehouse connectors such as Apache Iceberg as the usual choice, and it notes that its own page for SCD Type 2 is still to be written. This is the clearest case in the line of an engine feature that does nothing until a connector supports it. A pipeline run against an Iceberg catalog was not done here.

New functions (SPARK-56820, SPARK-57253, SPARK-58399, SPARK-58295)

Maturity: Default.

Example in the repo: 06_new_functions.sql.

-- counter_diff: turn a cumulative counter into per-interval deltas
SELECT t, c, counter_diff(c) OVER (ORDER BY t) AS delta FROM VALUES
  (TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00', 100),
  (TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:01:00', 130),
  (TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:02:00', 190) AS m(t, c);
-- 00:00  100  NULL
-- 00:01  130  30
-- 00:02  190  60

SELECT collect_union(col) FROM VALUES (array(1,2)), (array(2,3)), (array(1)) AS tab(col);
-- [1, 2, 3]

SELECT jaro_winkler_similarity('MARTHA', 'MARHTA');              -- 0.9611111111111111
SELECT to_base32(CAST('spark' AS BINARY)),
       CAST(from_base32(to_base32(CAST('spark' AS BINARY))) AS STRING);
-- ONYGC4TL   spark

Faster queries on small data (SPARK-57851, SPARK-57268)

Maturity: Behind flags. Not demonstrated here.

Two opt-in settings aim at laptop-sized data. spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled (default false) lets eligible fragments that read a small single-partition scan run in one task and skip the shuffle before a sort or aggregation. spark.sql.execution.arrow.cache.prefetch.enabled (default false) prefetches and decompresses the next batch of a compressed Arrow cache in a background thread. A trivial single-partition aggregate showed no plan difference with the first flag on, since it needed no exchange either way, so there is no number to quote. Measure it on your own small queries.

Also in 4.3, not run here:

  • Project Feather: opt-in shuffle-free single-task execution and Arrow-native caching for small data (the two flags are in the settings table below)
  • Items that need a connector: @ time travel on table names (SPARK-57421, SPARK-58012) and dynamic table options for UPDATE, MERGE and DELETE
  • Spark Connect REST endpoints (SPARK-57941), operation IDs for tracing, and a JDBC driver that returns ARRAY, MAP and STRUCT
  • BIN BY (SPARK-57133), behind spark.sql.binByRelationOperator.enabled; timestamp_nanos and unix_nanos; and VARIANT field-extraction pushdown for aggregate, sort and join queries
  • DataFrame.zip, opt-in reading of tar, zip and 7z archives, default whole-stage code generation for eligible UNIONs, opt-in null join key spreading for outer and anti joins, and pruning of unused fields inside arrays of structs

Run every example yourself

Everything in the previous section ran on one of two setups: an official apache/spark Docker image, and the plain release tarball from Apache with nothing else installed. This section gives you the second one, because it needs only Java and shows what a clean install does.

What you need

These are the latest releases of each line at the time of writing. The Python column comes from each tarball’s own Requires-Python, and all four ran on the same Java 17 (Temurin 17.0.20), including 4.3.0.

Line Release Tarball Python for PySpark Scala
4.0 4.0.5 523 MB 3.9 or newer 2.13.16
4.1 4.1.4 546 MB 3.10 or newer 2.13.17
4.2 4.2.1 529 MB 3.10 or newer 2.13.18
4.3 4.3.0 535 MB 3.11 or newer 2.13.18

The Python column decides which examples you can run from a tarball. A machine with Python 3.9 can run the SQL and Scala examples on all four releases and the PySpark examples on 4.0 only.

Download and verify

The tarball comes from the Apache CDN and the checksum from the main Apache distribution site, so the two come from different hosts. The CDN keeps only current releases; an older patch release is under https://archive.apache.org/dist/spark/. This is the script that fetched the four files above, each one verified:

mkdir -p ~/spark-4.x && cd ~/spark-4.x
for v in 4.0.5 4.1.4 4.2.1 4.3.0; do
  f=spark-$v-bin-hadoop3.tgz
  curl -sSf -C - -O "https://dlcdn.apache.org/spark/spark-$v/$f"
  curl -sSf -o "$f.sha512" "https://downloads.apache.org/spark/spark-$v/$f.sha512"
  got=$(shasum -a 512 "$f" | awk '{print $1}')
  if tr -d ' \n\r' < "$f.sha512" | tr 'A-F' 'a-f' | grep -q "$got"; then
    echo "OK   $f"; tar -xzf "$f"
  else
    echo "BAD  $f"
  fi
done

Four things that went wrong first

Each of these cost a run, so they are worth knowing before you start.

A different Spark answers. The first run printed SPARK 2.4.4. The shell had SPARK_HOME pointing at an older install, and the spark-shell script honours it over the directory it lives in. Every result from that run was invalid. Start Spark with a clean environment (env -i) and print spark.version first.

spark-shell -i script ran nothing. On this setup the REPL started and quit without executing the file. Feeding the script on standard input (< script.scala) worked on all four releases.

The driver address. Without pinning the driver to localhost, a run hung and logged RpcEndpointNotFoundException: Cannot find endpoint: spark://CoarseGrainedScheduler@.... With spark.driver.bindAddress and spark.driver.host set to 127.0.0.1 every run completed.

Python is too old. The 4.1 and 4.2 tarballs declare Python 3.10 or newer and 4.3 declares 3.11. On 4.2.1 with Python 3.9 a Python worker failed with a TypeError, so a stock macOS Python runs only the 4.0 PySpark examples.

A runner that executes a SQL file

The runner reads a file of statements separated by a line containing only ;;. A line starting with -- ### is printed as a heading, and the SQL after it runs. It uses only spark.sql, so any statement from the previous section works in it.

import scala.io.Source

val specPath = sys.env("SPEC")
val statements = Source.fromFile(specPath).mkString.split("\n;;\n").map(_.trim).filter(_.nonEmpty)
println("SPARK " + spark.version + " | Scala " + scala.util.Properties.versionNumberString + " | Java " + System.getProperty("java.version"))

statements.foreach { block =>
  val lines = block.linesIterator.toList
  // A leading "-- ### title" line is printed as a heading; whatever follows it is the SQL.
  val (heading, sql) =
    if (lines.head.startsWith("-- ###")) (Some(lines.head.drop(7)), lines.tail.mkString("\n").trim)
    else (None, block)
  heading.foreach(h => println("\n### " + h))
  if (sql.nonEmpty) {
    println(sql.linesIterator.next().take(110))
    try spark.sql(sql).collect().take(12).foreach(r => println("   " + r.mkString(" | ")))
    catch { case e: Throwable => println("   ERROR: " + e.getMessage.linesIterator.next().take(200)) }
  }
}
sys.exit(0)

Save it as runner.scala, and run any SQL file with a function like this, where JAVA is a JDK 17 home:

run() {   # run <release> <sql-file>
  env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH=/usr/bin:/bin JAVA_HOME="$JAVA" SPEC="$2" \
    ~/spark-4.x/spark-$1-bin-hadoop3/bin/spark-shell --master 'local[2]' \
    --conf spark.ui.enabled=false --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false \
    --conf spark.driver.bindAddress=127.0.0.1 --conf spark.driver.host=127.0.0.1 \
    --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2 < runner.scala
}
run 4.0.5 smoke40.sql

One SQL file per release

Each file runs the headline features of its release from the previous section. They are the four files that were run, one per tarball, and the results listed under each are what the run printed.

Parameter markers need bound arguments, so they go through the Scala API rather than a SQL file. This ran on the 4.1.4 tarball:

println("P2 " + spark.sql("SELECT * FROM IDENTIFIER(:t) ORDER BY id LIMIT :n", Map("t" -> "orders", "n" -> 2)).collect().mkString(" "))
println("P3 " + spark.sql("BEGIN DECLARE x INT DEFAULT :start; SET x = x + 1; SELECT x; END", Map("start" -> 41)).collect().mkString(" "))
