        "Expiration": {"Days": 2555},                        # about 7 years
        "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {"NoncurrentDays": 30},
    }]},
)

Watch the minimum storage durations (30 days for Standard-IA, 90 for Glacier Instant Retrieval) and the per-GB retrieval charges. Moving files that are read every day into an infrequent-access class costs more, not less. Never tier the files a table format still references, unless the class allows instant reads.

DynamoDB vs RDS: DynamoDB is a managed key-value store for single-digit-millisecond reads by key at any scale, with the access pattern designed up front. RDS is a managed relational database for joins, constraints and transactions:

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("order_status")
table.get_item(Key={"order_id": "o-123"})                  # one key, one read

table.put_item(                                            # write only if newer
    Item={"order_id": "o-123", "status": "SHIPPED", "event_seq": 7},
    ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(order_id) OR event_seq < :s",
    ExpressionAttributeValues={":s": 7},
)

The conditional write is question 65’s “never go backwards” rule, enforced by the database.

Behavioural and managerial rounds

These came up at nearly every company with a managerial round (PwC, KPMG, Deloitte, Cognizant, TCS, Infosys, Atlassian, Amazon, PayPal). The questions merge into eight:

  1. Walk through one end-to-end project: design, your decisions, challenges and impact.
  2. Tell me about a production failure you owned and what you changed afterwards.
  3. A technical decision you disagreed with. What evidence did you use?
  4. A time you took ownership beyond your role.
  5. How you handle conflicting requirements from stakeholders.
  6. Delivering under a tight deadline: what you cut, and the consequence.
  7. Explaining a technical problem (for example, data lag) to a non-technical client.
  8. A teammate’s mistake caused data loss. How do you handle it?

Prepare two or three real stories and adapt them, rather than one answer per question. Use situation, action and result, and put a number in the result. Amazon’s bar raiser will test each story against its leadership principles, so expect “what data did you use” and “what would you do differently” follow-ups.

Interview questions by component

The sections above follow what the 29 companies asked. This section follows the component being tested instead, so you can drill one skill at a time: SQL, Python, Java, Scala, Spark, streaming, data modeling, system design, Airflow, Databricks, Snowflake, dbt, data quality, and LLM pipelines.

These questions are not tied to a company. They come from the round types that recur in 2026 interview-preparation guides and public interview reviews (listed under References), and they skip anything already answered above. Numbering continues from question 75.

 component round        what the interviewer is really checking
 ─────────────────      ─────────────────────────────────────────────
 SQL                ──► correct results with ties, NULLs, duplicates
 Python             ──► memory-safe processing, retries, clean code
 Java / Scala       ──► JVM behaviour behind Spark, Kafka and Flink
 Spark / streaming  ──► plans, failure modes, state and late data
 Data modeling      ──► grain, history, keys that survive change
 System design      ──► trade-offs, backfill, failure, cost over time
 Airflow            ──► idempotent, re-runnable scheduled work
 Databricks         ──► Delta, Unity Catalog, pipelines, compute cost
 Snowflake and dbt  ──► storage, incremental models, cost control
 Data quality       ──► catching bad data before consumers do
 LLM pipelines      ──► rate limits, retries and budgets as design inputs

SQL

76. Sessionize a clickstream: start a new session when a user is idle for more than 30 minutes.

Pattern: sessions. The signal is “idle for more than N minutes” or “group events into sessions”. Flag each event that starts a session, then number the sessions with a running sum of the flags:

WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts,
         CASE WHEN LAG(event_ts) OVER w IS NULL
                OR event_ts > LAG(event_ts) OVER w + INTERVAL '30 minutes'
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
  FROM clicks
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts)
)
SELECT user_id, event_ts,
       SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
                                 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_no
FROM flagged
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts;

 user_id |      event_ts       | session_no 
---------+---------------------+------------
       1 | 2026-10-01 09:00:00 |          1
       1 | 2026-10-01 09:10:00 |          1
       1 | 2026-10-01 09:55:00 |          2
       1 | 2026-10-01 10:05:00 |          2
       2 | 2026-10-01 12:00:00 |          1
       2 | 2026-10-01 12:20:00 |          1
       2 | 2026-10-01 12:50:00 |          1
(7 rows)

User 1’s 09:55 click comes 45 minutes after the previous one, so it starts session 2. The 10:05 click is 10 minutes later and stays in session 2. User 2’s 12:50 click is exactly 30 minutes after 12:20 and stays in session 1, because the rule is “more than 30 minutes”.

One row per session. The common follow-up asks for each session’s start, end and event count, which is one more GROUP BY:

-- One row per session: a gap of MORE than 30 minutes starts a new one
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts,
         CASE WHEN event_ts - LAG(event_ts) OVER w <= INTERVAL '30 minutes'
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new_session      -- first event: LAG is NULL, so 1
  FROM clicks
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts)
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT *, SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
                                      ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_id
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT user_id, session_id,
       MIN(event_ts) AS session_start, MAX(event_ts) AS session_end,
       COUNT(*) AS event_count
FROM numbered
GROUP BY user_id, session_id
ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

 user_id | session_id |    session_start    |     session_end     | event_count 
---------+------------+---------------------+---------------------+-------------
       1 |          1 | 2026-10-01 09:00:00 | 2026-10-01 09:10:00 |           2
       1 |          2 | 2026-10-01 09:55:00 | 2026-10-01 10:05:00 |           2
       2 |          1 | 2026-10-01 12:00:00 | 2026-10-01 12:50:00 |           3
(3 rows)

The comparison is written as <= 30 minutes for “same session”, so the boundary case is explicit, and the first event of each user falls into the ELSE branch because its LAG is NULL. Clarify “more than” versus “at least” before writing it; the two give different session counts on exactly this row.

The trap: the first event of each user has a NULL previous timestamp. If the IS NULL branch is missing, the comparison is unknown, the flag is 0, and the first session is numbered 0 instead of 1. The follow-up is late events: a late click can merge two sessions, so a streaming version needs a watermark and F.session_window("event_ts", "30 minutes"), not this query.

77. Funnel analysis: how many users reach each step, and where do they drop off?

Pattern: funnels. The signal is “drop-off”, “conversion at each step” or “how many made it to”. The technique is one row per user with a conditional count for each step, then one row per step with its share of the previous step and of the top.

Five users signed up. User 5 never came back, user 4 only logged in, user 3 bought without ever adding to the cart, and users 1 and 2 went through views and the cart, but only user 1 bought.

Each step counted independently, which is what most interview versions ask:

-- Each stage counted on its own across all users, as most interview versions ask
WITH per_user AS (
  SELECT u.user_id,
         COUNT(e.user_id)                                         AS events,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'view')            AS views,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'add_to_cart')     AS carts,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'purchase')        AS purchases
  FROM app_users u LEFT JOIN app_events e ON e.user_id = u.user_id
  GROUP BY u.user_id
),
stages AS (
  SELECT 1 AS step, 'signup' AS stage, COUNT(*) AS users FROM per_user
  UNION ALL SELECT 2, 'active', COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE events > 0)    FROM per_user
  UNION ALL SELECT 3, 'viewed', COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE views > 0)     FROM per_user
  UNION ALL SELECT 4, 'carted', COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE carts > 0)     FROM per_user
  UNION ALL SELECT 5, 'bought', COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE purchases > 0) FROM per_user
)
SELECT stage, users,
       ROUND(100.0 * users / NULLIF(LAG(users) OVER (ORDER BY step), 0), 2) AS pct_of_prev,
       ROUND(100.0 * users / FIRST_VALUE(users) OVER (ORDER BY step), 2)    AS pct_of_signup
FROM stages
ORDER BY step;

 stage  | users | pct_of_prev | pct_of_signup 
--------+-------+-------------+---------------
 signup |     5 |             |        100.00
 active |     4 |       80.00 |         80.00
 viewed |     2 |       50.00 |         40.00
 carted |     2 |      100.00 |         40.00
 bought |     2 |      100.00 |         40.00
(5 rows)

The LEFT JOIN from users is what keeps user 5 in the signup count. Starting from the events table would silently remove everyone who never came back, and every percentage would be too high. FIRST_VALUE gives each row the signup count to divide by, and LAG gives it the previous step’s count.

A strict funnel, where a user counts at a step only after passing the previous one, in order:

-- A strict funnel: a user counts at a stage only after passing the previous one, in order
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT u.user_id,
         MIN(e.event_ts) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'view')        AS t_view,
         MIN(e.event_ts) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'add_to_cart') AS t_cart,
         MIN(e.event_ts) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'purchase')    AS t_buy
  FROM app_users u LEFT JOIN app_events e ON e.user_id = u.user_id
  GROUP BY u.user_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                         AS signed_up,
       COUNT(t_view)                                                    AS viewed,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t_cart > t_view)                          AS carted_after_view,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t_cart > t_view AND t_buy > t_cart)       AS bought_after_cart
FROM firsts;

 signed_up | viewed | carted_after_view | bought_after_cart 
-----------+--------+-------------------+-------------------
         5 |      2 |                 2 |                 1
(1 row)

The independent version says 2 users bought, and 100% of carters converted. The ordered version says 1: user 3 bought without carting, so they are a buyer but not a funnel conversion. Ask which one the product team means, because the difference is the whole point of a funnel. For a time limit (“bought within 7 days of the first view”), add AND t_buy <= t_view + INTERVAL '7 days'.

78. Compute the median, and the 90th percentile, of salary per department, with and without percentile functions.

Standard SQL uses an ordered-set aggregate:

SELECT dept,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS median_cont,
       PERCENTILE_DISC(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS median_disc,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS p90
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;

 dept  | median_cont | median_disc |  p90   
-------+-------------+-------------+--------
 ENG   |      180000 |   180000.00 | 226000
 HR    |       90000 |    90000.00 |  90000
 SALES |      120000 |   120000.00 | 120000
(3 rows)

PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between neighbouring values (ENG’s p90 of 226,000 is between 190,000 and 250,000), while PERCENTILE_DISC returns a value that exists in the data.

Without percentile functions, average the one or two middle rows. For an odd count both positions are the same row; for an even count they are the two middle rows:

-- Median without percentile functions: average the one or two middle rows
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS median
FROM (
  SELECT dept, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY dept)                 AS n
  FROM emp
) t
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;

 dept  |       median        
-------+---------------------
 ENG   | 180000.000000000000
 HR    |  90000.000000000000
 SALES | 120000.000000000000
(3 rows)

In Spark SQL use percentile(salary, 0.5) for an exact answer, percentile_approx(salary, 0.9) for bounded memory, or median(salary), added in Spark 3.4. An exact percentile needs all of a group’s values in one task, which is a memory problem on a skewed group. That is why the approximate function exists.

79. Pivot monthly revenue into one column per month, then unpivot it back.

Pattern: pivoting. The signal is “one column per” or “turn rows into columns”. Portable pivot with conditional aggregation:

SELECT product_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-01-01' THEN revenue END) AS jan,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-02-01' THEN revenue END) AS feb,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-03-01' THEN revenue END) AS mar,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-04-01' THEN revenue END) AS apr
FROM monthly_revenue
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY product_id;

 product_id |  jan   |  feb  |  mar  |  apr   
------------+--------+-------+-------+--------
          1 | 100.00 |  0.00 |       | 150.00
          2 |  40.00 | 60.00 | 90.00 |       
(2 rows)

Product 1 has no March row, so mar is NULL, not 0. Most reports want zeros, which is COALESCE around each column. PostgreSQL’s FILTER clause reads more cleanly than CASE, and a row total is one more SUM:

-- Missing cells as 0, with PostgreSQL's FILTER clause instead of CASE
SELECT product_id,
       COALESCE(SUM(revenue) FILTER (WHERE month = '2026-01-01'), 0) AS jan,
       COALESCE(SUM(revenue) FILTER (WHERE month = '2026-02-01'), 0) AS feb,
       COALESCE(SUM(revenue) FILTER (WHERE month = '2026-03-01'), 0) AS mar,
       COALESCE(SUM(revenue) FILTER (WHERE month = '2026-04-01'), 0) AS apr,
       SUM(revenue)                                                  AS total
FROM monthly_revenue
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY product_id;

 product_id |  jan   |  feb  |  mar  |  apr   | total  
------------+--------+-------+-------+--------+--------
          1 | 100.00 |  0.00 |     0 | 150.00 | 250.00
          2 |  40.00 | 60.00 | 90.00 |      0 | 190.00
(2 rows)

Unpivot back with a LATERAL VALUES list (PostgreSQL), or UNPIVOT in Spark 3.4+, Snowflake and SQL Server:

WITH wide AS (
  SELECT product_id,
         SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-01-01' THEN revenue END) AS jan,
         SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-02-01' THEN revenue END) AS feb
  FROM monthly_revenue GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT w.product_id, v.month_label, v.revenue
FROM wide w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('jan', w.jan), ('feb', w.feb)) v(month_label, revenue)
ORDER BY 1, 2 DESC;

 product_id | month_label | revenue 
------------+-------------+---------
          1 | jan         |  100.00
          1 | feb         |    0.00
          2 | jan         |   40.00
          2 | feb         |   60.00
(4 rows)

Spark has both as clauses:

SELECT * FROM monthly_revenue
PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR month IN ('2026-01-01' AS jan, '2026-02-01' AS feb));

The trap: pivot columns are fixed when the query is written, so a new month needs new SQL. A dynamic pivot belongs in the application or the BI tool.

80. Build a monthly cohort retention table: of the users who signed up in each month, what share were active in each later month?

Pattern: retention cohorts. The signal is “of the users who joined in month X, how many came back”. Three steps: assign each user a cohort month, compute each activity’s month offset from it, and divide by the cohort size.

WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_ts)::date AS cohort_month FROM users
),
size AS (SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size FROM cohort GROUP BY 1),
activity AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', event_ts)::date AS active_month FROM events
)
SELECT c.cohort_month,
       (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(a.active_month, c.cohort_month)) * 12
        + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM AGE(a.active_month, c.cohort_month)))::int AS month_offset,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active_users,
       s.cohort_size,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct
FROM cohort c
JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = c.user_id AND a.active_month >= c.cohort_month
JOIN size s ON s.cohort_month = c.cohort_month
GROUP BY c.cohort_month, month_offset, s.cohort_size
ORDER BY 1, 2;

 cohort_month | month_offset | active_users | cohort_size | retention_pct 
--------------+--------------+--------------+-------------+---------------
 2026-01-01   |            0 |            2 |           2 |         100.0
 2026-01-01   |            1 |            1 |           2 |          50.0
 2026-01-01   |            2 |            1 |           2 |          50.0
 2026-02-01   |            0 |            1 |           2 |          50.0
 2026-02-01   |            1 |            1 |           2 |          50.0
 2026-02-01   |            2 |            1 |           2 |          50.0
(6 rows)

The cohort size comes from the cohort table, not from the month-0 activity count, and the February cohort shows why. User 4 signed up in February but was not active until April, so only one of two February users was active in month

  1. Using month 0 as the denominator would report 100% retention for a cohort that is really at 50%.

Cohort by first activity. A frequent variant has no signup table, so the cohort is the month of each user’s first transaction. That is a MIN before anything else:

-- Cohort by the month of the first activity, not the signup date
WITH first_month AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_ts))::date AS cohort_month
  FROM events GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size
FROM first_month GROUP BY cohort_month ORDER BY cohort_month;

 cohort_month | cohort_size 
--------------+-------------
 2026-01-01   |           2
 2026-02-01   |           1
 2026-04-01   |           1
(3 rows)

User 4 signed up in February but first appeared in April, so the two definitions put them in different cohorts. Say which definition the business uses; “acquisition month” and “first-purchase month” are both common.

The month-difference function is dialect-specific: AGE arithmetic in PostgreSQL as above, DATEDIFF(month, a, b) in Snowflake and SQL Server, months_between in Spark.

81. Month-over-month revenue growth as a percentage, without dividing by zero and without skipping missing months.

Pattern: period-over-period change. The signal is “compared with last month” or “growth rate”. Aggregate to the period, then compare each row with the previous one using LAG:

WITH cal AS (
  SELECT generate_series(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-04-01', INTERVAL '1 month')::date AS month
),
rev AS (
  SELECT c.month, COALESCE(SUM(r.revenue), 0) AS revenue
  FROM cal c LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue r ON r.month = c.month AND r.product_id = 1
  GROUP BY c.month
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_pct
FROM rev
ORDER BY month;

   month    | revenue | prev_revenue | mom_pct 
------------+---------+--------------+---------
 2026-01-01 |  100.00 |              |        
 2026-02-01 |    0.00 |       100.00 |  -100.0
 2026-03-01 |       0 |         0.00 |        
 2026-04-01 |  150.00 |            0 |        
(4 rows)

Two traps, both visible above:

  • A missing month. LAG takes the previous row, not the previous calendar month. Product 1 has no March row, so without the calendar CTE April would be compared with February. The calendar join puts March in as 0.
  • Division by zero. NULLIF(previous, 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL, so March and April’s growth is NULL instead of an error. Growth from zero is undefined; report it as “new” in the dashboard rather than as infinity.

Year over year, and “previous available” versus “previous calendar” year. A common version, “annual growth in new marketplace sellers”, compares each year with the preceding year that has data. The sample sellers have no signups in 2023, which is where the two definitions split:

-- New sellers per year and growth over the previous year that has data,
-- plus the calendar-correct comparison when a year is missing
WITH yearly AS (
  SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM signup_date)::int AS signup_year, COUNT(*) AS new_sellers
  FROM sellers GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT y.signup_year, y.new_sellers,
       LAG(y.new_sellers) OVER w AS prev_available,
       ROUND(100.0 * (y.new_sellers - LAG(y.new_sellers) OVER w)
             / NULLIF(LAG(y.new_sellers) OVER w, 0), 2) AS growth_vs_prev_available,
       p.new_sellers AS prev_calendar_year
FROM yearly y
LEFT JOIN yearly p ON p.signup_year = y.signup_year - 1
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY y.signup_year)
ORDER BY y.signup_year;

 signup_year | new_sellers | prev_available | growth_vs_prev_available | prev_calendar_year 
-------------+-------------+----------------+--------------------------+--------------------
        2021 |           2 |                |                          |                   
        2022 |           5 |              2 |                   150.00 |                  2
        2024 |           3 |              5 |                   -40.00 |                   
(3 rows)

LAG compares 2024 with 2022, a two-year gap, and reports -40%. The self-join on signup_year - 1 finds no 2023 row, so the calendar-correct comparison is undefined. Both are defensible; which one is right is a question for the interviewer, and asking it is part of the answer.

82. A report's totals doubled after someone added a join. Why, and how do you find it?

The join fanned out. Order 1 has two shipments, so joining orders to shipments repeats order 1, and its amount is counted twice:

SELECT SUM(h.order_amount) AS total_after_join
FROM order_header h
JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = h.order_id;

 total_after_join 
------------------
           400.00
(1 row)

The real total of shipped orders is 300. Find it by checking the key’s uniqueness on the joined side (GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) and comparing COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) after the join. Fix it by not joining at all when you only need existence, or by aggregating the many side to the order grain first:

SELECT SUM(h.order_amount) AS total_correct
FROM order_header h
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM shipments s WHERE s.order_id = h.order_id);

 total_correct 
---------------
        300.00
(1 row)

The related trap: a filter on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN, placed in WHERE, removes the unmatched rows and silently turns it into an inner join:

SELECT 'filter in WHERE' AS variant, COUNT(*) AS orders_kept
FROM order_header h LEFT JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = h.order_id
WHERE s.carrier = 'DHL'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'filter in ON', COUNT(DISTINCT h.order_id)
FROM order_header h LEFT JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = h.order_id AND s.carrier = 'DHL';

     variant     | orders_kept 
-----------------+-------------
 filter in WHERE |           2
 filter in ON    |           3
(2 rows)

Put the condition in ON to keep every order.

83. Find employees who earn more than their manager.

Pattern: self-joins. The signal is a comparison between two rows of the same table: “more than their manager”, “pairs of”, “same city as”. The technique is the table twice, under two aliases, once as the employee and once as the manager:

SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM emp e
JOIN emp m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

 employee |  salary   | manager  | manager_salary 
----------+-----------+----------+----------------
 Manoj    | 190000.00 | Nishanth |      180000.00
(1 row)

The inner join drops the CEO, who has no manager, which is what the question wants. The comparison is strict (>), so an employee paid the same as their manager is not returned. Interviewers often state that rule explicitly; if they do not, ask. The follow-ups: “earn more than anyone above them in the chain” needs the recursive CTE from question 8, and “earn more than their department’s average” is a window function, salary > AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept).

84. LAST_VALUE() returns the current row instead of the last one. Why? 
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)  AS last_default_frame,
       LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
                              ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
                                       AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)       AS lowest_paid
FROM emp
WHERE dept = 'SALES'
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

 dept  |   name   |  salary   | last_default_frame | lowest_paid 
-------+----------+-----------+--------------------+-------------
 SALES | Raja     | 120000.00 | Raja               | Lakshmi
 SALES | Vasundra | 120000.00 | Raja               | Lakshmi
 SALES | Lakshmi  |  95000.00 | Lakshmi            | Lakshmi
(3 rows)

With an ORDER BY and no frame, the frame ends at the current row and its peers. So LAST_VALUE returns the last row of the frame, which is the current row or a tie of it, not the last row of the partition. Raja and Vasundra tie on salary, so both see Raja; Lakshmi sees herself.

Spell the frame out to the end of the partition, as in lowest_paid. Or avoid the problem with FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary ASC), which needs no frame. Question 4 is the same default-frame trap with SUM.

85. A 7-day rolling average per region, when some days have no sales.

Pattern: moving averages. The signal is “rolling”, “trailing” or “7-day average”. The technique is a window frame, and the whole question is which frame: the last 7 rows or the last 7 days.

-- 7-day rolling average per region, with missing days counted as zero
WITH cal AS (
  SELECT r.region, d::date AS sale_date
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT region FROM daily_sales) r
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(DATE '2026-10-01', DATE '2026-10-05', INTERVAL '1 day') d
),
filled AS (
  SELECT c.region, c.sale_date, COALESCE(s.amount, 0) AS amount
  FROM cal c LEFT JOIN daily_sales s USING (region, sale_date)
)
SELECT region, sale_date, amount,
       ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY sale_date
                               ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_7d
FROM filled
WHERE region = 'N'
ORDER BY sale_date;

 region | sale_date  | amount | avg_7d 
--------+------------+--------+--------
 N      | 2026-10-01 | 100.00 | 100.00
 N      | 2026-10-02 | 120.00 | 110.00
 N      | 2026-10-03 |      0 |  73.33
 N      | 2026-10-04 |  80.00 |  75.00
 N      | 2026-10-05 |  90.00 |  78.00
(5 rows)

ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts rows, so it is only “7 days” if every day has a row. The calendar join adds 3 October as 0, and the average on 4 October is (100 + 120 + 0 + 80) / 4 = 75.00. Without the calendar, 4 October would average three days and report 100.00.

A common version starts at the seventh available date. Amounts are summed per day first, and a row is returned only once a full window exists. Counting the rows in the frame does that. The visits table here has two visits on 8 October and none on 5 October (the shop was closed):

-- Average of the current and six previous AVAILABLE dates, from the 7th date on
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT visit_date, SUM(amount) AS daily_total FROM visits GROUP BY visit_date
),
win AS (
  SELECT visit_date, daily_total,
         AVG(daily_total) OVER w  AS avg_7_rows,
         COUNT(*) OVER w          AS rows_in_frame,
         MIN(visit_date) OVER w   AS frame_starts
  FROM daily
  WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY visit_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
)
SELECT visit_date, daily_total, ROUND(avg_7_rows, 2) AS avg_7_rows, frame_starts
FROM win
WHERE rows_in_frame = 7
ORDER BY visit_date;

 visit_date | daily_total | avg_7_rows | frame_starts 
------------+-------------+------------+--------------
 2026-10-08 |      105.00 |      75.71 | 2026-10-01
 2026-10-09 |       70.00 |      80.00 | 2026-10-02
(2 rows)

The first full window is 8 October, and its frame starts on 1 October: seven available dates, which span eight calendar days because 5 October is missing. If the business means seven calendar days, use a RANGE frame on the date:

-- Average over the 7 CALENDAR days ending on each date (RANGE frame)
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT visit_date, SUM(amount) AS daily_total FROM visits GROUP BY visit_date
),
win AS (
  SELECT visit_date, daily_total,
         AVG(daily_total) OVER w AS avg_days_present,
         SUM(daily_total) OVER w / 7.0 AS avg_7_calendar_days   -- a closed day counts as 0
  FROM daily
  WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY visit_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
)
SELECT visit_date, daily_total,
       ROUND(avg_days_present, 2) AS avg_days_present,
       ROUND(avg_7_calendar_days, 2) AS avg_7_calendar_days
FROM win
WHERE visit_date >= DATE '2026-10-07'      -- filter AFTER the window, or it sees only these rows
ORDER BY visit_date;

 visit_date | daily_total | avg_days_present | avg_7_calendar_days 
------------+-------------+------------------+---------------------
 2026-10-07 |      110.00 |            70.83 |               60.71
 2026-10-08 |      105.00 |            81.67 |               70.00
 2026-10-09 |       70.00 |            84.17 |               72.14
(3 rows)

On 7 October the two answers differ: 70.83 averages the six days that had visits, and 60.71 counts the closed day as zero. Neither is wrong. Ask which one the business means.

The trap in that query is the filter. The WHERE visit_date >= '2026-10-07' sits outside the window CTE. Written in the same SELECT as the window, it runs first, and each frame then sees only the filtered rows: the first draft of this query returned 110.00 for 7 October, the average of a single day.

SQL practice set

Eleven more problems in the style of a timed SQL screen. Five are answered by questions earlier in this post, and the other six are answered below, each with its own sample data (in the sample tables at the top) and the output from PostgreSQL 16.4. Try each one before opening the answer.

Problem Pattern Answered in
Events per calendar month, including months with none Aggregation by period Q86
Runs of consecutive completed days, numbered Gaps and islands Q5
How many people report directly to each manager Self-join and aggregation Q87
Distinct scores ranked with no gaps Ranking Q2
Daily cancellation rate when some users must be excluded Filtered aggregation Q88

86. Count shipments per month in YYYY-MM format, including months with none.

It is a GROUP BY on the formatted month:

-- Shipments per month, as YYYY-MM
SELECT TO_CHAR(shipped_on, 'YYYY-MM') AS ship_month, COUNT(*) AS num_shipments
FROM parcels
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

 ship_month | num_shipments 
------------+---------------
 2026-01    |             3
 2026-02    |             1
 2026-04    |             2
(3 rows)

Group by the formatted string or by DATE_TRUNC('month', ...), never by EXTRACT(MONTH ...) alone, which merges January 2026 with January 2027. TO_CHAR is PostgreSQL and Oracle; it is DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m') in MySQL, date_format(d, 'yyyy-MM') in Spark, and TO_CHAR again in Snowflake.

The follow-up: March is missing, because nothing shipped. A report usually wants it as 0, which takes a generated calendar and a LEFT JOIN:

-- The same, with months that had no shipments shown as 0
WITH months AS (
  SELECT generate_series(DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(shipped_on)),
                         DATE_TRUNC('month', MAX(shipped_on)),
                         INTERVAL '1 month')::date AS m
  FROM parcels
)
SELECT TO_CHAR(m.m, 'YYYY-MM') AS ship_month, COUNT(p.parcel_id) AS num_shipments
FROM months m
LEFT JOIN parcels p ON DATE_TRUNC('month', p.shipped_on) = m.m
GROUP BY m.m
ORDER BY m.m;

 ship_month | num_shipments 
------------+---------------
 2026-01    |             3
 2026-02    |             1
 2026-03    |             0
 2026-04    |             2
(4 rows)

COUNT(p.parcel_id) rather than COUNT(*): the calendar row for March has no matching parcel, and COUNT(*) would count that row as 1.

87. Count each manager's direct reports.

Pattern: self-joins, followed by an aggregation. Join each employee to the rows that name them as manager, and count:

-- Employees with at least one direct report, and how many
SELECT m.emp_id AS employee_id, m.name, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
FROM emp m
JOIN emp e ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.name
ORDER BY direct_reports DESC, employee_id;

 employee_id |   name   | direct_reports 
-------------+----------+----------------
           1 | Ranga    |              4
           2 | Nishanth |              2
           5 | Vasundra |              2
(3 rows)

Ranga manages Nishanth, Meena, Vasundra and Kavi. The inner join keeps only employees who manage someone, which is what the question asks. To list every employee with 0 for non-managers, use LEFT JOIN and COUNT(e.emp_id).

The follow-up is usually all reports, direct and indirect, which is the recursive CTE in question 8: there, Ranga’s total is 8.

88. Daily trip cancellation rate, excluding trips where the client or the driver is banned.

The answer joins the users table twice, once as the client and once as the driver, and puts the “not banned” rule in each join:

-- Daily cancellation rate, ignoring trips with a banned or unknown client or driver
SELECT t.request_date,
       COUNT(*)                                                     AS total_trips,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t.status LIKE 'cancelled%')           AS cancelled_trips,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t.status LIKE 'cancelled%')::numeric / COUNT(*), 2)
                                                                    AS cancellation_rate
FROM trips t
JOIN ride_users c ON c.user_id = t.client_id AND c.banned = 'No'
JOIN ride_users d ON d.user_id = t.driver_id AND d.banned = 'No'
GROUP BY t.request_date
ORDER BY t.request_date;

 request_date | total_trips | cancelled_trips | cancellation_rate 
--------------+-------------+-----------------+-------------------
 2026-10-05   |           3 |               1 |              0.33
 2026-10-06   |           1 |               0 |              0.00
(2 rows)

On 5 October, trip 2 is dropped because client 22 is banned, leaving three trips with one cancellation. On 6 October, trip 5 is dropped because driver 32 is banned. 7 October disappears entirely: its only trip has driver 34, who is not in the users table, and the inner join removes it. That matches the rule “exclude trips whose client or driver is unknown”; if unknown users should count, use LEFT JOIN and COALESCE(banned, 'No') instead.

Two details interviewers check: status LIKE 'cancelled%' catches both cancelled_by_client and cancelled_by_driver, and the ::numeric cast avoids integer division, which would make every rate 0 or 1.

89. Average session time per user from page_load and page_exit events.

The usual rule pairs each page_load with the earliest later page_exit for the same user on the same day. A LATERAL subquery expresses “the earliest later one” directly:

-- Each page_load pairs with the earliest later page_exit, same user, same day
WITH loads AS (SELECT user_id, event_time FROM web_log WHERE event_type = 'page_load'),
     exits AS (SELECT user_id, event_time FROM web_log WHERE event_type = 'page_exit'),
sessions AS (
  SELECT l.user_id, l.event_time AS load_time, x.exit_time
  FROM loads l
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT MIN(e.event_time) AS exit_time
    FROM exits e
    WHERE e.user_id = l.user_id
      AND e.event_time > l.event_time
      AND e.event_time::date = l.event_time::date      -- never across midnight
  ) x
  WHERE x.exit_time IS NOT NULL                        -- a load with no exit is not a session
)
SELECT user_id,
       ROUND(AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM exit_time - load_time) / 60)::numeric, 2) AS avg_session_minutes,
       COUNT(*) AS sessions
FROM sessions
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;

 user_id | avg_session_minutes | sessions 
---------+---------------------+----------
       1 |               18.00 |        3
       2 |               30.00 |        1
(2 rows)

User 1 has sessions of 12, 18 and 24 minutes, so the average is 18.00. User 2’s first session starts at 23:50 and ends after midnight; the same-day rule drops it, leaving one 30-minute session. User 3 loaded a page and never exited, so they have no session and no row.

Say the rules out loud, because each one changes the answer: a load with no exit is ignored rather than ended at midnight; two loads before one exit would both pair with that exit; and the same-day rule throws away the session that crossed midnight. A LEAD() version, pairing each event with the next one, is shorter but breaks as soon as two loads arrive in a row.

90. Subscription retention by start-month cohort: what share is still subscribed 1, 2 and 3 months later?

Pattern: retention cohorts, but measured from an end date rather than from activity. Here a subscription is retained at month N if it has no end date, or ends on or after the first day of the month N months after its cohort month. One row per cohort, with each month as a column, is a set of conditional counts:

-- Share of each start-month cohort still subscribed 1, 2 and 3 months later
WITH c AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', start_date)::date AS cohort, end_date FROM subscriptions
)
SELECT TO_CHAR(cohort, 'YYYY-MM') AS cohort_month,
       COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE end_date IS NULL OR end_date >= cohort + INTERVAL '1 month') / COUNT(*), 2) AS month1_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE end_date IS NULL OR end_date >= cohort + INTERVAL '2 months') / COUNT(*), 2) AS month2_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE end_date IS NULL OR end_date >= cohort + INTERVAL '3 months') / COUNT(*), 2) AS month3_pct
FROM c
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;

 cohort_month | cohort_size | month1_pct | month2_pct | month3_pct 
--------------+-------------+------------+------------+------------
 2026-01      |           4 |      75.00 |      50.00 |      25.00
 2026-02      |           2 |     100.00 |     100.00 |      50.00
(2 rows)

The January cohort has four subscriptions. Subscription 1 ended on 28 January, inside its first month, so month 1 is 3 of 4 (75%). Subscription 4 ended on exactly 1 February, the month-1 boundary, and still counts as retained because the rule says “on or after”; change it to “after” and month 1 drops to 50%. Subscription 3 ended on 3 March, so it is gone by month 3 (1 April).

Compare question 80, which measures retention by activity in each month. A subscriber who never logs in is retained here and lost there, so ask which definition the business uses.

91. Remove duplicate emails, keeping the row with the smallest id.

Pattern: deduplication, with the simplest possible “which one wins” rule. The usual version returns the result as a query:

-- One row per email, keeping the smallest id
SELECT MIN(id) AS id, email
FROM person
GROUP BY email
ORDER BY id;

 id |     email      
----+----------------
 11 | kavi@x.com
 12 | manoj@x.com
 19 | nishanth@x.com
 30 | Kavi@x.com
(4 rows)

When the rule is “keep the smallest id” and the output is only the key and the id, GROUP BY with MIN is enough; ROW_NUMBER (question 3) is needed only when you must keep the rest of the winning row’s columns.

As a delete in place, the classic self-join form removes every row that has a twin with a smaller id:

-- The same, as an in-place delete: remove any row that has a smaller-id twin
DELETE FROM person p
USING person q
WHERE p.email = q.email
  AND p.id > q.id;
SELECT id, email FROM person ORDER BY id;

 id |     email      
----+----------------
 11 | kavi@x.com
 12 | manoj@x.com
 19 | nishanth@x.com
 30 | Kavi@x.com
(4 rows)

Kavi@x.com (id 30) survives in both, because string comparison is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL. If the business treats emails case-insensitively, compare lower(email), and say so before you write the query; in MySQL, the default collation would have merged them without asking.

Python

92. Generators: what does yield do, and why does it matter for data pipelines?

A function containing yield returns a generator. Calling it runs nothing. Each next() resumes the function until the next yield, so values are produced one at a time and the function’s local state is kept between calls. Chained generators form a pipeline that holds one record at a time:

import csv

def read_records(path):
    with open(path, newline="") as fh:
        for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
            yield row

def valid(records):
    return (r for r in records if float(r["fare"]) > 10)

def chunked(iterable, size):
    batch = []
    for x in iterable:
        batch.append(x)
        if len(batch) == size:
            yield batch
            batch = []
    if batch:
        yield batch

batches = sum(1 for _ in chunked(valid(read_records(path)), 10_000))
print("batches of 10,000:", batches)

g = read_records(path)
print("first pass rows:", sum(1 for _ in g), "| second pass rows:", sum(1 for _ in g))

batches of 10,000: 18
first pass rows: 200000 | second pass rows: 0

Memory stays proportional to one batch, not to the 200,000-row file. That is the answer to “process a 20 GB file on a 4 GB machine” (question 17).

The trap is in the last line: a generator can be consumed only once. The second pass silently returns zero rows, with no error.

93. What is wrong with def add_tag(tag, tags=[])?

The default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, not on each call. Every call that omits tags shares the same list:

def add_tag_bad(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    tags = [] if tags is None else tags
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag_bad("a"), add_tag_bad("b"))
print(add_tag("a"), add_tag("b"))

['a', 'b'] ['a', 'b']
['a'] ['b']

The first line prints ['a', 'b'] twice: both calls returned the same list object, which was changed by the second call before the line was printed. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function. The same bug appears with a dict default used as a cache, which is sometimes deliberate, and should then be commented as such.

94. Shallow copy vs deep copy, and is vs ==. 
import copy

orig = {"ids": [1, 2]}
shallow, deep = copy.copy(orig), copy.deepcopy(orig)
shallow["ids"].append(3)
print("original after shallow-copy edit:", orig, "| deep copy:", deep)

a, b = [1, 2], [1, 2]
print("a == b:", a == b, "| a is b:", a is b)

x = int("1000"); y = int("1000")
print("1000 is 1000 (built at runtime):", x is y, "| 5 is 5:", int("5") is int("5"))

original after shallow-copy edit: {'ids': [1, 2, 3]} | deep copy: {'ids': [1, 2]}
a == b: True | a is b: False
1000 is 1000 (built at runtime): False | 5 is 5: True

copy.copy creates a new outer dict but shares the inner list, so appending through the copy changes the original. copy.deepcopy copies recursively. list(x), x[:] and dict(x) are all shallow.

== compares values; is compares identity. CPython caches small integers (-5 to 256), so 5 is 5 is true while 1000 is 1000 is false. Use is only for singletons such as None.

95. Write an idempotent extractor for a paginated REST API with rate limits.

The test runs against a local fake API that serves three pages and answers the second request with 429 Too Many Requests:

import random, time, requests

store, checkpoint = {}, {"cursor": None}

def fetch_all(url, max_retries=6):
    cursor = checkpoint["cursor"]                  # resume where the last run stopped
    while True:
        for attempt in range(max_retries):
            resp = requests.get(url, params={"cursor": cursor or ""}, timeout=30)
            if resp.status_code == 429 or resp.status_code >= 500:
                wait = float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt))
                time.sleep(wait + random.uniform(0, 0.01))   # backoff with jitter
                continue
            resp.raise_for_status()                # other 4xx: fail loudly
            break
        else:
            raise RuntimeError("retries exhausted")
        page = resp.json()
        for item in page["items"]:
            store[item] = {"id": item}             # upsert on a natural key
        cursor = page.get("next_cursor")
        checkpoint["cursor"] = cursor              # only after the page is stored
        if not cursor:
            return

fetch_all(URL)
print("records:", sorted(store), "| HTTP calls:", hits["n"], "(one was a 429)")
checkpoint["cursor"] = None
fetch_all(URL)                                     # a full rerun changes nothing
print("records after rerun:", len(store))

records: ['r1', 'r2', 'r3', 'r4', 'r5'] | HTTP calls: 4 (one was a 429)
records after rerun: 5

Three things make it idempotent: records are upserted on a key, the checkpoint moves only after a page is stored (a crash re-fetches at most one page), and re-applying a page changes nothing. In production, store is a MERGE into a table and checkpoint is a row in a state table.

The traps: retrying every 4xx (a 401 will never succeed), backing off without jitter (every worker retries at the same instant), and offset-based pagination over data that changes during the run, which skips or repeats rows.

96. A plain Python UDF makes a PySpark job ten times slower. Why, and what are the alternatives?

A Python UDF runs in a separate Python worker process next to each executor. Rows are serialized from the JVM to Python and back, and Catalyst cannot see inside the function. The plan shows the difference:

from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
import pandas as pd

@F.udf("double")
def plus_tax_py(x):
    return x * 1.18

@pandas_udf("double")
def plus_tax_pd(x: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return x * 1.18

nums.select(plus_tax_py("x").alias("py"), plus_tax_pd("x").alias("pd"),
            (F.col("x") * 1.18).alias("builtin")).show(3)
nums.select(plus_tax_py("x")).explain()
nums.select(plus_tax_pd("x")).explain()

+----+----+-------+
|  py|  pd|builtin|
+----+----+-------+
| 0.0| 0.0|    0.0|
|1.18|1.18|   1.18|
|2.36|2.36|   2.36|
+----+----+-------+
only showing top 3 rows

== Physical Plan ==
*(2) Project [pythonUDF0#624 AS plus_tax_py(x)#622]
+- BatchEvalPython [plus_tax_py(cast(id#593L as double))#621], [pythonUDF0#624]
   +- *(1) Range (0, 10, step=1, splits=4)


== Physical Plan ==
*(2) Project [pythonUDF0#628 AS plus_tax_pd(x)#626]
+- ArrowEvalPython [plus_tax_pd(cast(id#593L as double))#625], [pythonUDF0#628], 200
   +- *(1) Range (0, 10, step=1, splits=4)

BatchEvalPython is the row-at-a-time path (rows pickled in batches, the function called once per row). ArrowEvalPython moves Arrow column batches and calls the function once per batch with a pandas Series, which is vectorised. The built-in expression stays in the JVM and needs no Python at all.

The order of preference: built-in functions, then a pandas UDF, then a Scala or Java UDF registered in the JVM, and a plain Python UDF last.

97. Validate incoming records in Python before loading them.

Declare the schema once and validate at the boundary. A dataclass documents the shape but does not check it at runtime; Pydantic does:

from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class Order(BaseModel):
    order_id: str
    amount: Decimal
    ordered_at: datetime

records = [
    {"order_id": "o1", "amount": "19.99", "ordered_at": "2026-10-01T10:00:00Z"},
    {"order_id": "o2", "amount": "abc", "ordered_at": "2026-10-01T10:05:00Z"},
    {"order_id": "o3", "amount": "5", "ordered_at": "not a date"},
]
good, bad = [], []
for raw in records:
    try:
        good.append(Order(**raw))
    except ValidationError as e:
        bad.append({"raw": raw, "errors": [err["loc"][0] for err in e.errors()]})

print("good:", [(o.order_id, o.amount) for o in good])
print("quarantined:", [(b["raw"]["order_id"], b["errors"]) for b in bad])

good: [('o1', Decimal('19.99'))]
quarantined: [('o2', ['amount']), ('o3', ['ordered_at'])]

Bad records go to a quarantine table with their errors, so the load continues and someone can fix and replay them. Alert when the quarantine rate crosses a threshold. Dropping bad rows silently is how question 60’s 10,000 rows go missing. For Spark-scale validation, the same idea is question 129’s PERMISSIVE mode with a corrupt-record column.

98. Implement an LRU cache.

OrderedDict keeps insertion order and can move a key to the end in O(1), so the least recently used key is always first:

from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity, self.data = capacity, OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)            # mark as most recently used
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)     # evict the least recently used

c = LRUCache(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2); c.get("a"); c.put("c", 3)
print("keys after evicting LRU:", list(c.data))

keys after evicting LRU: ['a', 'c']

Reading a made b the least recently used, so adding c evicted b. Both operations are O(1). For caching a pure function’s results, the standard library already has functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...). Interviewers ask you to build one to see whether you know which structure gives O(1) on both sides: a hash map for lookup plus a linked list for order, which is what OrderedDict is.

99. Process many files in parallel, and make sure a failure in one is not lost. 
import os
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, as_completed

def count_rows(p):
    with open(p) as fh:
        return p, sum(1 for _ in fh) - 1           # minus the header

totals = {}
with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as ex:
    futures = [ex.submit(count_rows, p) for p in paths]
    for f in as_completed(futures):
        p, n = f.result()                          # re-raises a worker's exception here
        totals[os.path.basename(p)] = n
print("rows per file:", dict(sorted(totals.items())), "| total:", sum(totals.values()))

rows per file: {'part-0.csv': 1000, 'part-1.csv': 2000, 'part-2.csv': 3000, 'part-3.csv': 4000, 'part-4.csv': 5000, 'part-5.csv': 6000} | total: 21000

Use processes for CPU-bound parsing and threads for I/O-bound downloads (question 18). Two details interviewers look for: f.result() re-raises the worker’s exception in the parent, so a failure is not silently dropped, and the function must be defined at module level so it can be pickled and sent to the worker processes.
