], "shipment_id STRING, warehouse STRING, status STRING, scanned_at STRING, scanner_seq INT") \
    .withColumn("scanned_at", F.to_timestamp("scanned_at"))

def dedup_latest(df, keys, order_by):
    """One row per key, the first by `order_by`. Make order_by unique per key, or ties are arbitrary."""
    w = Window.partitionBy(*keys).orderBy(*order_by)
    return (df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w))
              .filter("_rn = 1").drop("_rn"))

current = dedup_latest(scans, ["shipment_id", "warehouse"],
                       [F.col("scanned_at").desc(), F.col("scanner_seq").desc()])
current.orderBy("shipment_id", "warehouse").show()
print("dropDuplicates on the same key also leaves", scans.dropDuplicates(["shipment_id", "warehouse"]).count(),
      "rows, with no rule for which one")

+-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+
|shipment_id|warehouse|    status|         scanned_at|scanner_seq|
+-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+
|       NULL|      BLR|    picked|2026-10-12 12:00:00|          5|
|     SHP-41|      BLR|    packed|2026-10-12 09:45:00|          8|
|     SHP-41|      HYD|in_transit|2026-10-12 21:00:00|          9|
|     SHP-52|      BLR|   on_hold|2026-10-12 11:30:00|          4|
+-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+

dropDuplicates on the same key also leaves 4 rows, with no rule for which one
  • SHP-41 has two scans at Bengaluru; the later one, packed, wins. Its Hyderabad scan is a different key, so it stays.
  • SHP-52’s two scans have the same timestamp; scanner_seq breaks the tie, so the result is the same on every run. Without a tiebreaker the winner is whichever row Spark happens to see first.
  • The scan with no shipment id forms its own group, because nulls are grouped together. Decide whether to keep it or send it to a rejects table.

dropDuplicates(["shipment_id", "warehouse"]) also returns 4 rows, but makes no promise about which row survives, so it can change between runs. It is fine for rows that are identical in every column, and wrong for “keep the latest”.

138. Write a meter-reading loader you could leave running overnight: settings, structured logs, a rejects table, retries and a safe write.

This one brings the earlier answers together, reusing upsert from question 130:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    source: str
    target: str
    rejects: str
    business_date: str
    statuses: tuple = ("ok", "estimated")
    reject_limit: float = 0.3
    write_attempts: int = 3

log = logging.getLogger("meter_loader")
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(message)s"))
log.addHandler(handler); log.setLevel(logging.INFO); log.propagate = False

def emit(step, **fields):                          # one JSON object per step: easy to query later
    log.info(json.dumps({"step": step, **fields}, sort_keys=True))

def retried(attempts, wait_s=0.2, on=(Exception,)):
    def deco(fn):
        @wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*a, **kw):
            for n in range(1, attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return fn(*a, **kw)
                except on as e:
                    emit("retry", fn=fn.__name__, attempt=n, error=type(e).__name__)
                    if n == attempts:
                        raise
                    time.sleep(wait_s * 2 ** (n - 1))
        return wrapper
    return deco

class Transient(Exception):
    pass

hiccups = {"left": 1}                              # the first write attempt fails, as if a node was lost

@retried(attempts=3, on=(Transient,))
def write_readings(df, s):
    if hiccups["left"]:
        hiccups["left"] -= 1
        raise Transient("storage timeout")
    upsert(df, s.target, key="meter_id", version_col="read_at")

def run(s):
    t0 = time.time()
    raw = spark.read.schema("meter_id STRING, kwh STRING, status STRING, read_at STRING, _bad_line STRING") \
               .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_bad_line").json(s.source).cache()
    emit("read", rows=raw.count(), business_date=s.business_date)

    typed = raw.withColumn("kwh_num", F.col("kwh").cast("double")).withColumn("read_at", F.to_timestamp("read_at"))
    why = (F.when(F.col("_bad_line").isNotNull(), "unparseable_line")
            .when(F.col("meter_id").isNull(), "no_meter_id")
            .when(F.col("kwh_num").isNull(), "kwh_not_numeric")
            .when(F.col("kwh_num") < 0, "negative_kwh")
            .when(~F.col("status").isin(*s.statuses), "unknown_status"))
    tagged = typed.withColumn("why", why)
    good = tagged.filter("why IS NULL").select("meter_id", F.col("kwh_num").alias("kwh"), "status", "read_at")
    bad = tagged.filter("why IS NOT NULL")
    n_good, n_bad = good.count(), bad.count()
    emit("validate", accepted=n_good, rejected=n_bad,
         by_reason={r["why"]: r["count"] for r in bad.groupBy("why").count().collect()})

    (bad.select(F.lit(s.business_date).alias("business_date"), "why",            # raw kept for replay
                F.to_json(F.struct(*[c for c in raw.columns if c != "_bad_line"])).alias("raw"), "_bad_line")
        .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite")
        .option("replaceWhere", f"business_date = '{s.business_date}'").save(s.rejects))

    if n_bad / max(n_good + n_bad, 1) > s.reject_limit:
        emit("stop", reject_share=round(n_bad / (n_good + n_bad), 3))
        raise RuntimeError("reject share above the limit; target left untouched")

    write_readings(good, s)
    emit("finished", seconds=round(time.time() - t0, 1),
         target_rows=spark.read.format("delta").load(s.target).count())

readings_file = f"{BASE}/meters.json"
with open(readings_file, "w") as fh:
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-1", "kwh": "14.2", "status": "ok", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n')
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-2", "kwh": "n/a", "status": "ok", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n')
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-3", "kwh": "9.8", "status": "tampered", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n')
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-4", "kwh": "3.1", "status": "ok"\n')
    for i in range(5, 13):
        fh.write(json.dumps({"meter_id": f"M-{i}", "kwh": f"{i * 1.5:.1f}", "status": "estimated",
                             "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}) + "\n")

meter_table = f"file://{BASE}/meter_readings"
spark.createDataFrame([("M-1", 13.9, "ok", "2026-10-27 06:00:00")],
                      "meter_id STRING, kwh DOUBLE, status STRING, read_at STRING") \
     .withColumn("read_at", F.to_timestamp("read_at")).write.format("delta").save(meter_table)

s = Settings(source=f"file://{readings_file}", target=meter_table,
             rejects=f"file://{BASE}/meter_rejects", business_date="2026-10-28")
run(s)
try:
    run(Settings(**{**s.__dict__, "reject_limit": 0.1}))      # a feed that is normally clean
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("strict run:", e)
spark.read.format("delta").load(s.rejects).select("why", "raw", "_bad_line").orderBy("why").show(truncate=60)

spark.stop()

{"business_date": "2026-10-28", "rows": 12, "step": "read"}
{"accepted": 9, "by_reason": {"kwh_not_numeric": 1, "unknown_status": 1, "unparseable_line": 1}, "rejected": 3, "step": "validate"}
{"attempt": 1, "error": "Transient", "fn": "write_readings", "step": "retry"}
{"seconds": 5.4, "step": "finished", "target_rows": 9}
{"business_date": "2026-10-28", "rows": 12, "step": "read"}
{"accepted": 9, "by_reason": {"kwh_not_numeric": 1, "unknown_status": 1, "unparseable_line": 1}, "rejected": 3, "step": "validate"}
{"reject_share": 0.25, "step": "stop"}
strict run: reject share above the limit; target left untouched
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
|             why|                                                         raw|                                       _bad_line|
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
| kwh_not_numeric|{"meter_id":"M-2","kwh":"n/a","status":"ok","read_at":"20...|                                            NULL|
|  unknown_status|{"meter_id":"M-3","kwh":"9.8","status":"tampered","read_a...|                                            NULL|
|unparseable_line|                                                          {}|{"meter_id": "M-4", "kwh": "3.1", "status": "ok"|
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+

Walk the interviewer through it in this order:

  • Settings in a frozen dataclass. Nothing is hard-coded in the logic, and the business date is passed in, so a backfill is the same call with an older date.
  • One JSON log line per step, with counts. Last night’s rejects become a log query.
  • Rejected rows go to a table, with the reason and the raw input (the truncated line survives intact in _bad_line). It is overwritten per business date, so a rerun replaces rather than duplicates it, and rows can be replayed after a fix.
  • A limit on the reject share. Three bad rows out of twelve (25%) is tolerated at a 30% limit; at 10% the run stops before touching the target, because a sudden jump usually means the source changed.
  • Retry only what can succeed on retry. The storage timeout on the first write was retried with backoff and succeeded; a bad row is never retried.
  • A write that tolerates repetition. The upsert updated M-1 with its newer reading and added eight meters: 9 rows, however many times the job runs.

Streaming and Kafka

139. Kafka partitions, consumer groups and ordering: how many consumers can read a topic in parallel, and what is ordered?
  • A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log; each message gets an increasing offset within its partition.
  • Ordering is per partition only. Messages with the same key go to the same partition (the default partitioner hashes the key), so per-key order holds and global order does not.
  • A consumer group shares a topic’s partitions: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group. Parallelism is capped by the partition count, so 12 partitions and 20 consumers leave 8 idle.
  • Adding or removing a consumer triggers a rebalance, which reassigns partitions.
kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --create --topic payments \
  --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2

kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --describe --group fraud-scorer
# shows CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG for each partition

Durability: with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write succeeds only when two replicas have it, so losing one broker loses no acknowledged data. Choosing the key is the design decision: key payments by account_id for per-account order, and watch for a hot key that overloads one partition (question 30’s skew, one layer earlier).

Question 38’s run showed the hashing: with 3 partitions and keys A1, A2, A3, the final offsets were {'0': 4, '1': 2, '2': 0}. Partition 2 received nothing, because three keys do not spread evenly over three partitions.

140. Join two streams (ad impressions and clicks). What stops the join state from growing forever?

A stream-stream join keeps both sides in state, waiting for a match. Bound it with a watermark on each side and a time-range condition in the join:

imps = (spark.readStream.schema("ad_id STRING, imp_ts TIMESTAMP").json(f"{src}/impressions")
        .withWatermark("imp_ts", "2 hours"))
clks = (spark.readStream.schema("click_ad_id STRING, click_ts TIMESTAMP").json(f"{src}/clicks")
        .withWatermark("click_ts", "3 hours"))

joined = imps.join(clks, F.expr("""
    click_ad_id = ad_id AND
    click_ts >= imp_ts AND click_ts <= imp_ts + interval 1 hour"""))

q = (joined.writeStream.format("memory").queryName("ad_clicks")
     .option("checkpointLocation", chk).trigger(availableNow=True).start())

Three impressions at 10:00, 10:01 and 10:02; a click on a1 five minutes later, and a click on a2 89 minutes later:

+-----+-------------------+-------------------+
|ad_id|             imp_ts|           click_ts|
+-----+-------------------+-------------------+
|   a1|2026-10-01 10:00:00|2026-10-01 10:05:00|
+-----+-------------------+-------------------+

Only a1 matched: the a2 click is outside the one-hour range. The range condition plus the watermarks tell Spark when an impression can no longer match, so it can drop it from state. Without them the query still runs, but the state of an inner join grows forever. For outer joins, the watermark and range condition are mandatory, because Spark must know when to emit the unmatched row with nulls.

Data modeling

These build on questions 51 to 55. The data modeling guide covers each topic in depth with runnable examples.

141. Model a sales fact for five sales channels and three product hierarchies. What is the grain?

Declare the grain first: one row per order line, the lowest level the sources record. Channel becomes a dimension, not five separate fact tables, so cross-channel totals are a plain GROUP BY:

CREATE TABLE dim_channel (
  channel_sk   INT,
  channel_code STRING,           -- web, app, store, marketplace, wholesale
  channel_type STRING            -- direct / partner
);

CREATE TABLE fact_order_line (
  order_id        STRING,        -- degenerate dimension
  line_number     INT,
  order_date_key  INT,
  channel_sk      INT,
  product_sk      BIGINT,        -- hierarchies live on dim_product
  customer_sk     BIGINT,
  quantity        INT,
  net_amount      DECIMAL(12, 2)
);

SELECT c.channel_code, p.category, SUM(f.net_amount)
FROM fact_order_line f
JOIN dim_channel c ON c.channel_sk = f.channel_sk
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_sk = f.product_sk
GROUP BY c.channel_code, p.category;

The three product hierarchies (category, brand, merchandising group) are attributes of dim_product, or separate hierarchy tables if they are ragged or change on their own schedule. A hierarchy describes the product, not the sale, so the fact holds only product_sk.

If one channel reports at a coarser level (wholesale sends daily totals, not lines), do not mix it into the line fact. Build a second fact at the daily grain and conform the shared dimensions so the two can be compared.

142. Role-playing, junk and degenerate dimensions.

Role-playing: one physical dimension used in several roles, exposed as views named for the role:

CREATE VIEW dim_order_date    AS SELECT date_key AS order_date_key,    full_date AS order_date    FROM dim_date;
CREATE VIEW dim_ship_date     AS SELECT date_key AS ship_date_key,     full_date AS ship_date     FROM dim_date;
CREATE VIEW dim_delivery_date AS SELECT date_key AS delivery_date_key, full_date AS delivery_date FROM dim_date;

Junk dimension: low-cardinality flags combined into one small dimension, one row per combination, so the fact holds one key instead of many flag columns:

CREATE TABLE dim_order_flags AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY is_gift, payment_type, has_promo) AS order_flags_sk,
       is_gift, payment_type, has_promo
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT is_gift, payment_type, has_promo FROM staging.orders) t;

Degenerate dimension: a key with no dimension table, such as order_id on the fact. It groups lines into an order and traces back to the source, and has no attributes of its own to store.

143. What are conformed dimensions, and what is a bus matrix?

A conformed dimension has the same keys, attribute names and meanings in every fact that uses it. Then “drilling across” two facts is valid:

-- Sales and support tickets by the same customer segment
WITH s AS (SELECT c.segment, SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue
           FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer c USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY c.segment),
     t AS (SELECT c.segment, COUNT(*) AS tickets
           FROM fact_support_ticket f JOIN dim_customer c USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY c.segment)
SELECT s.segment, s.revenue, t.tickets, t.tickets / (s.revenue / 1000) AS tickets_per_1k_revenue
FROM s JOIN t USING (segment);

Aggregate each fact separately, then join the results on the conformed attribute. Joining the two facts directly would fan out (question 82).

The bus matrix is the planning grid: business processes as rows, dimensions as columns, and a mark where a process uses a dimension:

                   date  customer  product  store  channel
 orders             X       X        X        X       X
 shipments          X       X        X        X
 returns            X       X        X        X       X
 support tickets    X       X        X

It shows which dimensions must be conformed before teams build facts on their own. Without it, each team builds its own customer dimension and the numbers stop agreeing.

144. SCD Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 6: how do you choose?

Ask how the business reports history, per attribute:

  • Type 1 when only the current value matters, or the change is a correction. History is restated.
  • Type 2 when facts must report under the value valid at the time: sales by the region the customer was in when they bought.
  • Type 6 when users need both “as was” and “as is” on the same row: Type 2 rows, plus a current_ column overwritten on every version.
-- Type 6: after Ranga moves Pune -> Mumbai, both versions carry the current city
customer_sk | customer_id | city   | current_city | valid_from | valid_to   | is_current
101         | C01         | Pune   | Mumbai       | 2026-01-01 | 2026-03-01 | false
102         | C01         | Mumbai | Mumbai       | 2026-03-01 | NULL       | true

-- "as was": revenue by the city at purchase time
SELECT d.city, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer d USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY d.city;
-- "as is": the same facts by today's city, with no extra join
SELECT d.current_city, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer d USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY d.current_city;

The choice is per attribute, not per table: email can be Type 1 while loyalty_tier is Type 2 in the same dimension. Question 51 has the Type 2 MERGE.

145. A fact arrives before its dimension row (an early-arriving fact). What do you load?

Never drop the fact and never load a NULL key. The standard answer is an inferred member: insert a placeholder dimension row with the business key, then overwrite it in place when the real row arrives:

-- 1. Before loading facts: create placeholders for unknown business keys
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_sk, customer_id, city, is_inferred, valid_from, is_current)
SELECT next_sk(), s.customer_id, 'Unknown', true, s.order_date, true
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS order_date
      FROM staging.orders GROUP BY customer_id) s
LEFT ANTI JOIN dim_customer d ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id;

-- 2. When the real customer row arrives: a Type 1 overwrite of the placeholder,
--    even in a Type 2 dimension, so the facts' keys stay valid
MERGE INTO dim_customer t
USING staging.customers s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id AND t.is_inferred
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET city = s.city, is_inferred = false;

(next_sk() stands for your surrogate-key generator, such as an identity column.) The alternative is pointing the fact at a reserved unknown member (-1) and reprocessing the fact later. The inferred member avoids that reprocessing. Monitor how many inferred rows are never completed.

146. One big table (OBT) vs a star schema in a lakehouse.

An OBT pre-joins the fact with its dimension attributes:

CREATE TABLE gold.sales_obt USING delta AS
SELECT f.order_id, f.order_date_key, f.quantity, f.net_amount,
       c.segment, c.city, p.category, p.brand, ch.channel_code
FROM fact_order_line f
JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_sk = f.customer_sk
JOIN dim_product  p ON p.product_sk  = f.product_sk
JOIN dim_channel ch ON ch.channel_sk = f.channel_sk;

Columnar formats read only the columns a query needs and compress repeated values well, so wide tables are much cheaper than they were in a row store, and dashboards get join-free SQL.

What an OBT costs: a Type 1 dimension change means rewriting every fact row that carries the attribute; the history semantics are frozen when the table is built; and every new attribute is a backfill.

A defensible answer keeps the star as the source of truth and derives OBTs for specific dashboards, rebuilt from the star whenever needed.

System design

Expect one system design round at most product companies. The 2026 guides describe it as the round that carries the most weight. The follow-ups are predictable: why this storage layer, what you ruled out, how backfill works, what breaks when a source changes, and what it costs over time.

147. Design a pipeline that ingests 1 TB of clickstream a day and serves dashboards at under 2 seconds P95.

Start with the numbers: 1 TB a day is about 12 MB/s on average, so plan for 3 to 5 times that at peak. Then the layers:

 SDK / web ──► Kafka (partition by user_id) ──► stream job ──► bronze table
                                                     │          (append, raw)
                                                     ▼
                                    silver: deduplicated, sessionized events
                                                     │
                                                     ▼
              gold: pre-aggregated by minute/hour × dimension ──► serving store
                                                                  (OLAP engine)

The key decision is that dashboards never scan raw events. Two seconds at P95 comes from pre-aggregated gold tables, or from a real-time OLAP store (Druid, Pinot, ClickHouse), not from a lake query over a terabyte. The gold step is a windowed aggregate:

events = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.clicks")
          .withWatermark("event_ts", "15 minutes")
          .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))

per_minute = (events
    .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "1 minute"), "page", "country")
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("views"), F.approx_count_distinct("user_id").alias("users")))

(per_minute.writeStream.outputMode("append")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://lake/_chk/clicks_per_minute")
   .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
   .toTable("gold.clicks_per_minute"))

Cover deduplication by event ID, late events with a watermark, a schema registry for the event contract, partitioning by event date, and compaction of the small files that streaming writes (question 36).

The follow-ups: the Kafka partition count comes from peak throughput per partition and consumer parallelism; and a day is replayed from bronze, not from Kafka, once Kafka’s retention has passed.

148. Backfill nine months of history after a logic fix, without double counting and without stopping the daily job.

Make every run partition-scoped and overwrite-based, so a backfill is just the normal job run with old dates:

from datetime import date, timedelta
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def run_day(d):
    df = transform(spark.read.table("silver.orders").filter(F.col("order_date") == d))
    (df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite")
       .option("replaceWhere", f"order_date = '{d}'")       # replaces exactly one day
       .saveAsTable("gold_shadow.daily_sales"))             # a copy, not the live table
    return d

days = [date(2026, 1, 1) + timedelta(n) for n in range(273)]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:              # throttle: the daily job still runs
    for d in pool.map(run_day, reversed(days)):              # newest months first
        print("done", d)
  • Write to a shadow table first, reconcile its counts and totals against the live table, then swap.
  • Throttle with a small worker pool so the backfill does not starve the daily SLA.
  • Freeze the inputs: read a fixed snapshot of silver (VERSION AS OF), not a table that is still changing.

The trap: appending recomputed data on top of the old output. That is the double count. Overwrite-by-partition makes reruns safe, including a rerun of the backfill itself.

149. An upstream API changes a field from a string to an object, and the pipeline starts failing. What do you do in the next hour?

In order:

  1. Stop the damage. Pause the job, or let it fail closed. Do not let it write partial or mis-parsed data into tables consumers read.
  2. Keep the raw data. Make sure bronze still lands raw payloads, so nothing is lost while you fix the parser.
  3. Tell people: which tables are stale, since when, and when you will update them next.
  4. Fix forward: parse both shapes, and route anything unparseable to quarantine.
  5. Replay from bronze for the affected window, then reconcile the counts.

Step 4 in PySpark, when customer changed from "C01" to {"id": "C01", "tier": "gold"}:

raw = spark.read.table("bronze.orders_raw")                  # payload kept as a string

parsed = raw.select(
    F.get_json_object("payload", "$.order_id").alias("order_id"),
    F.coalesce(
        F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer.id"),       # new shape: object
        F.when(~F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer").startswith("{"),
               F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer"))   # old shape: plain string
    ).alias("customer_id"),
    "payload")

parsed.filter("customer_id IS NULL").write.mode("append").saveAsTable("quarantine.orders")
parsed.filter("customer_id IS NOT NULL").drop("payload").createOrReplaceTempView("fixed")

One payload of each shape, plus one with no customer:

+--------+-----------+
|order_id|customer_id|
+--------+-----------+
|      o1|        C01|
|      o2|        C02|
|      o3|       NULL|
+--------+-----------+

Afterwards: a schema contract with the producer, a schema check at ingestion that alerts before the transform fails, and a test with the new payload.

150. Design CDC replication from a PostgreSQL OLTP database into a lakehouse table. 
 PostgreSQL WAL ──► Debezium (logical replication slot) ──► Kafka topic per table
                                                                 │
          initial snapshot ─────────────────────────────────────┤
                                                                 ▼
                         Spark: latest change per key by LSN, then MERGE

The Debezium connector, registered with Kafka Connect:

{
  "name": "orders-cdc",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
    "database.hostname": "orders-db", "database.port": "5432",
    "database.user": "debezium", "database.password": "${file:/secrets/db.properties:password}",
    "database.dbname": "shop",
    "topic.prefix": "shop",
    "table.include.list": "public.orders",
    "slot.name": "orders_cdc",
    "snapshot.mode": "initial"
  }
}

The apply step keeps the newest change per key and ignores anything older than what the target already has:

w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("lsn"))
latest = (changes.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))

(DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders").alias("t")
   .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id")
   .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn")
   .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="s.op <> 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn",
                      set={"status": "s.status", "lsn": "s.lsn"})
   .whenNotMatchedInsert(condition="s.op <> 'd'",
                         values={"order_id": "s.order_id", "status": "s.status", "lsn": "s.lsn"})
   .execute())

The target starts with orders 1 and 2 at LSN 100. Five changes arrive out of order: two updates to order 1 (LSN 103 and 105), a delete of order 2 at 104, a stale update of order 2 at 99, and a new order 3:

+--------+-------+---+
|order_id| status|lsn|
+--------+-------+---+
|       1|shipped|105|
|       3| placed|106|
+--------+-------+---+

Order 1 took the LSN 105 update, not 103. Order 2 was deleted, because the newest change for it (104) is the delete, and the stale LSN 99 update lost the ROW_NUMBER. Order 3 was inserted.

The operational risk to name: a replication slot that nobody consumes keeps WAL on the primary until its disk fills. Monitor slot lag:

SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots;

The data modeling guide runs an idempotent CDC apply end to end, including what a late event does after a hard delete.

151. Estimate storage and cost at one, three and ten years for a 500 GB-a-day source.

Interviewers want arithmetic, stated assumptions and the levers that change the result:

raw_gb_per_day = 500
compression = 5          # assumption: measure it on a sample
layers = 2.2             # bronze + silver + a smaller gold
retained_versions = 1.1  # time travel keeps some old files alive
usd_per_gb_month = 0.023 # object storage, standard class

for years in (1, 3, 10):
    tb = raw_gb_per_day * 365 * years / compression * layers * retained_versions / 1024
    print(f"{years:>2} years: {tb:6.0f} TB stored, about ${tb * 1024 * usd_per_gb_month:,.0f} a month")

 1 years:     86 TB stored, about $2,032 a month
 3 years:    259 TB stored, about $6,095 a month
10 years:    863 TB stored, about $20,316 a month

Then the levers: lifecycle rules that move old bronze to colder storage classes (question 75), a retention policy per layer, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup, and aggregating old detail nobody queries. Compute usually costs more than storage, so mention incremental processing, which avoids recomputing history every day.

152. Design an event deduplication layer for at-least-once delivery at billions of events a day.

At-least-once delivery makes duplicates normal, so deduplication is a design component, not a cleanup job. Two layers:

deduped = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.events")
           .withWatermark("event_ts", "2 hours")              # longest realistic redelivery
           .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))      # layer 1: bounded state

def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):                                # layer 2: idempotent sink
    (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.events").alias("t")
       .merge(batch_df.alias("s"), "t.event_date = s.event_date AND t.event_id = s.event_id")
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
       .execute())

deduped.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert).option("checkpointLocation", chk).start()
  • Key: a producer-assigned event ID. Without one, hash the business fields, and accept that two identical genuine events will merge.
  • Window: state with a watermark, sized to the longest redelivery delay. Question 38 showed it catching a producer retry inside one batch and resent events across runs.
  • Sink: the MERGE catches duplicates that arrive after the state has expired.
  • Measure: track the duplicate rate. A sudden rise usually means a producer retry storm, not more traffic.

Airflow

These DAGs were loaded with DagBag and the fan-out DAG was test-run with airflow dags test on Airflow 3.1.0.

153. How do you make an Airflow DAG idempotent?

Each task run must process a fixed slice of data and produce the same output however many times it runs. Question 74’s DAG shows all three rules:

  • Use the data interval, not the clock. The task takes data_interval_start and data_interval_end from the run context instead of calling datetime.now(). Rerunning last Tuesday then processes last Tuesday.
  • Overwrite the slice the task owns (INSERT OVERWRITE ... PARTITION), or MERGE on a key. Never append.
  • Keep tasks atomic. Write to staging and swap, so a failed attempt leaves nothing for the retry to trip over.
@task
def load_partition(data_interval_start=None, data_interval_end=None):
    # Airflow fills these from the run being executed
    run_sql(f"""
        INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE sales.orders PARTITION (order_date = '{data_interval_start:%Y-%m-%d}')
        SELECT * FROM staging.orders
        WHERE event_ts >= '{data_interval_start}' AND event_ts < '{data_interval_end}'
    """)

The trap: a task that “loads everything since the last run” using a watermark stored outside Airflow. A manual rerun of an old interval then loads whatever is new today, not that interval’s data.

154. catchup, backfill, and what happens when you deploy a DAG with a start_date in the past.

With catchup=True, the scheduler creates a run for every interval between start_date and now that has not run. Deploying a daily DAG with a start_date a year ago creates 365 runs at once. With catchup=False, only the latest interval runs.

Set it on every DAG. The default comes from catchup_by_default, which Airflow 3 changed from True to False, so the same DAG file behaves differently after an upgrade. The loaded DAGs confirm the setting:

from airflow.models.dagbag import DagBag

bag = DagBag("/opt/airflow/dags", include_examples=False)
print("import errors:", bag.import_errors)
for dag_id, dag in sorted(bag.dags.items()):
    print(dag_id, "catchup=", dag.catchup, "tasks=", [t.task_id for t in dag.tasks])

import errors: {}
daily_orders catchup= False tasks= ['wait_for_file', 'load_partition']
file_fanout catchup= False tasks= ['list_files', 'process', 'publish']
orders_report catchup= False tasks= ['build_report']

Run deliberate backfills with the CLI, throttled:

airflow backfill create --dag-id daily_orders \
  --from-date 2026-01-01 --to-date 2026-09-30 --max-active-runs 3

Airflow 3 runs backfills inside the scheduler; earlier versions ran them in a separate CLI process that died with your terminal. The DagBag check above is also worth putting in CI, so a DAG that fails to import never reaches production.

155. Sensors: poke vs reschedule vs deferrable, and why sensors can deadlock a cluster. 
from airflow.providers.standard.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor

FileSensor(task_id="poke", filepath=path, mode="poke", poke_interval=60)            # holds a slot
FileSensor(task_id="reschedule", filepath=path, mode="reschedule", poke_interval=300)  # frees it between checks
FileSensor(task_id="deferred", filepath=path, deferrable=True, timeout=6 * 3600)    # hands the wait to the triggerer
  • Poke holds a worker slot for the whole wait.
  • Reschedule releases the slot between checks.
  • Deferrable hands the wait to the triggerer process, which watches thousands of waits asynchronously, and uses no worker slot until the condition fires. FileSensor in Airflow 3.1 accepts deferrable=True.

If many poke-mode sensors wait on late files, they can occupy every worker slot, and the tasks that would produce those files can never start. Use deferrable or reschedule mode for long waits, always set a timeout, and decide what a timeout means: fail and alert, or soft_fail=True to skip.

156. What is XCom for, and what should you never put in it? Show dynamic task mapping.

XCom passes small values between tasks: a path, a row count, a batch ID. The TaskFlow API pushes a task’s return value automatically. Dynamic task mapping creates one task instance per input at runtime:

from airflow.sdk import DAG, Asset, task

orders_clean = Asset("s3://lake/silver/orders")

with DAG(dag_id="file_fanout", schedule=None, start_date=datetime(2026, 10, 1)) as dag:

    @task
    def list_files() -> list[str]:
        # Return paths, never the data: XComs live in the metadata database.
        return [f"s3://landing/orders/part-{i}.json" for i in range(3)]

    @task
    def process(path: str) -> int:
        print(f"processing {path}")
        return 100                        # a row count is a fine XCom

    @task(outlets=[orders_clean])
    def publish(counts: list[int]) -> int:
        return sum(counts)

    publish(process.expand(path=list_files()))     # one mapped task per file

airflow dags test file_fanout ran three mapped process instances (map_index 0, 1 and 2), one per path, and publish received the list of their counts.

Never pass datasets through XCom. Values are stored in the metadata database by default, so large ones bloat it and slow the scheduler and UI. Write data to storage and pass its location. A custom XCom backend can store large values in object storage if you truly need them.

157. What changed in Airflow 3, and what does an interviewer expect you to know about it?

Airflow 3.0 was released in April 2025. The changes that come up:

  • Assets replace Datasets for data-aware scheduling. In question 156, publish declares outlets=[orders_clean], and this DAG runs whenever that asset is updated, with no timetable:
with DAG(dag_id="orders_report", schedule=[orders_clean], start_date=datetime(2026, 10, 1)):
    @task
    def build_report():
        print("runs whenever s3://lake/silver/orders is updated")
    build_report()
  • A new authoring import: from airflow.sdk import DAG, task, Asset.
  • DAG versioning: the UI shows which version of the DAG code each run used.
  • Task SDK and execution API: tasks talk to the API server instead of connecting to the metadata database directly, which is what makes remote and multi-language execution possible.
  • Scheduler-managed backfills (question 154).
  • Removals: SubDAGs (use TaskGroups), SLA callbacks (deadline alerts arrived in later 3.x releases), and the execution_date context key (use logical_date). catchup_by_default is now False.

Databricks

Most Databricks features run only on Databricks, so the code here was checked against the Databricks documentation rather than run. The exception is liquid clustering, which open-source Delta Lake 3.3 also supports, and which ran on Spark 3.5.9.

158. Liquid clustering vs partitioning vs Z-order. When do you use which?
  • Partitioning fixes a directory layout at creation. Good for one low-cardinality filter column (date) on a very large table; bad for anything else, and changing it means rewriting the table.
  • Z-order (OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY) co-locates values inside partitions, but every run rewrites everything again, and the columns are not recorded on the table.
  • Liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY) records the clustering columns on the table, clusters data incrementally on OPTIMIZE, and lets you change the columns without rewriting existing data.
spark.sql(f"""CREATE TABLE delta.`{lc}` (event_id BIGINT, user_id BIGINT, event_date DATE)
              USING delta CLUSTER BY (user_id, event_date)""")
# ... 8 appends ...
spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE delta.`{lc}`").select("metrics.numFilesAdded", "metrics.numFilesRemoved").show()
print(spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`{lc}`").select("clusteringColumns").first())

+-------------+---------------+
|numFilesAdded|numFilesRemoved|
+-------------+---------------+
|            1|              8|
+-------------+---------------+

Row(clusteringColumns=['user_id', 'event_date'])

Changing the clustering key is a metadata operation:

spark.sql("CREATE TABLE gold_cpd USING delta CLUSTER BY (customer_id) AS SELECT ...")
spark.sql("ALTER TABLE gold_cpd CLUSTER BY (orders)")

Row(clusteringColumns=['customer_id'])
after ALTER: Row(clusteringColumns=['orders'])

New writes and the next OPTIMIZE use the new key; old files are reclustered gradually. On Databricks, CLUSTER BY AUTO lets the platform choose the columns from the query history. Liquid clustering cannot be combined with PARTITIONED BY or ZORDER BY on the same table. Use it for new tables by default, and keep partitioning only for very large tables with one dominant date filter and a retention policy that drops whole partitions.

159. Build a bronze-silver-gold pipeline with data-quality rules in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables).

You declare the tables and their rules; the platform works out the order, creates the tables, manages checkpoints and retries, and records every expectation’s pass and fail counts in the pipeline event log.

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

@dp.table(comment="Raw orders, as delivered")
def bronze_orders():
    return (spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
            .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
            .load("/Volumes/prod/landing/orders/"))

@dp.table(comment="Typed, valid orders")
@dp.expect("has_customer", "customer_id IS NOT NULL")            # keep, but count failures
@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_amount", "amount >= 0")                # drop failing rows
@dp.expect_or_fail("has_order_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL")       # stop the update
def silver_orders():
    return (spark.readStream.table("bronze_orders")
            .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(12,2)"))
            .withColumn("order_date", F.to_date("order_ts")))

@dp.materialized_view(comment="Revenue per day")
def gold_daily_revenue():
    return (spark.read.table("silver_orders")
            .groupBy("order_date").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))
  • @dp.table over a streaming read is a streaming table: it processes each input row once, incrementally.
  • @dp.materialized_view over a batch read is recomputed, incrementally where the platform can, to always match its query.
  • Expectations: expect records failures and keeps the row, expect_or_drop removes the row, expect_or_fail fails the update. Group several with @dp.expect_all({...}).

from pyspark import pipelines as dp is the current import. Older code uses import dlt with the same decorators (@dlt.table, @dlt.expect_or_drop), which still works.

160. Apply a CDC feed as SCD Type 2 in a Databricks pipeline, without writing the MERGE yourself.

create_auto_cdc_flow (formerly apply_changes) handles ordering, deletes and history:

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, expr

dp.create_streaming_table("customers_history")

dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="customers_history",
    source="customers_cdc",                       # a streaming source of change rows
    keys=["customer_id"],
    sequence_by=col("lsn"),                       # resolves out-of-order changes
    apply_as_deletes=expr("op = 'DELETE'"),
    except_column_list=["op", "lsn"],
    stored_as_scd_type="2",                       # or 1 for latest-only
)

sequence_by does what the ROW_NUMBER by LSN did in question 150: a change with a lower sequence than the stored one cannot overwrite it. With stored_as_scd_type="2", the target gets __START_AT and __END_AT columns, which are question 51’s effective_date and end_date.

Interviewers ask this to see whether you know what it replaces. Be able to write the MERGE by hand as well (question 51), because that is what AUTO CDC does, and it is what you need on any engine without it.

161. Unity Catalog: grant analysts read access, restrict rows by region, and mask emails.

Unity Catalog has a three-level namespace, catalog.schema.table, and a grant at each level. Reading a table needs all three:

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod TO `analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA  ON SCHEMA  prod.sales TO `analysts`;
GRANT SELECT      ON TABLE   prod.sales.orders TO `analysts`;

Row filter: a SQL function returning a boolean, attached to the table:

CREATE FUNCTION prod.sales.region_filter(region STRING)
RETURN IF(is_account_group_member('sales_admins'), true, region = 'IN');

ALTER TABLE prod.sales.orders SET ROW FILTER prod.sales.region_filter ON (region);

Column mask: a function that returns the value to show:

CREATE FUNCTION prod.sales.mask_email(email STRING)
RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('pii_readers') THEN email
            ELSE regexp_replace(email, '^[^@]+', '***') END;

ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK prod.sales.mask_email;

Both apply to every query from every engine that goes through Unity Catalog, so there is no view to keep in sync and no way around them from a notebook. Grant to groups, never to individuals, and audit access through system.access.audit.

162. All-purpose compute vs job compute vs serverless vs SQL warehouses, and what Photon changes.
  • All-purpose compute: interactive clusters for notebooks, shared by people. The most expensive DBU rate. Never run scheduled production jobs on it.
  • Job compute: a cluster created for one job run and terminated after it. A cheaper rate, isolated from other work, and the right default for scheduled pipelines.
  • Serverless (jobs, notebooks, pipelines): no cluster to configure, and start-up in seconds. You trade control over instance types and Spark configuration for zero idle cost and no tuning.
  • SQL warehouses: compute for SQL and BI tools, with auto-stop and scaling by concurrency.

A job definition that uses job compute, from an Asset Bundle (question 164):

job_clusters:
  - job_cluster_key: main
    new_cluster:
      spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12      # an LTS runtime
      node_type_id: i3.xlarge
      autoscale: {min_workers: 2, max_workers: 8}
      runtime_engine: PHOTON

Photon is Databricks’ native, vectorized C++ engine for Spark SQL and DataFrame operations. It speeds up scans, joins and aggregations over Delta and Parquet, and costs a higher DBU rate. It does not accelerate Python UDFs or RDD code, so check a job’s plan for operators that fall back before paying for it.

163. Databricks spend doubled this month. How do you find out why?

Billable usage is in the system.billing.usage system table, one row per usage record, with the job or warehouse that caused it:

-- DBUs by product and SKU, this month vs last
SELECT date_trunc('month', usage_date) AS month,
       billing_origin_product,
       sku_name,
       SUM(usage_quantity)              AS dbus
FROM system.billing.usage
WHERE usage_date >= date_trunc('month', add_months(current_date(), -1))
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY month, dbus DESC;

-- The jobs that grew the most
SELECT usage_metadata.job_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN usage_date >= date_trunc('month', current_date()) THEN usage_quantity END) AS this_month,
       SUM(CASE WHEN usage_date <  date_trunc('month', current_date()) THEN usage_quantity END) AS last_month
FROM system.billing.usage
WHERE usage_metadata.job_id IS NOT NULL
  AND usage_date >= date_trunc('month', add_months(current_date(), -1))
GROUP BY usage_metadata.job_id
ORDER BY this_month - COALESCE(last_month, 0) DESC
LIMIT 20;

The usual causes are: production jobs moved onto all-purpose clusters, clusters with no auto-termination, a job whose input grew (check its run duration), and Photon or serverless switched on without comparing the cost. Prevent a repeat with cluster policies (enforce auto-termination, allowed node types and tags) and budgets with alerts. Tag every job with a team, so custom_tags can attribute the cost.

164. How do you deploy Databricks jobs through CI/CD?

Databricks Asset Bundles describe jobs, pipelines and their code as YAML in the repository, deployed per environment with the Databricks CLI:

# databricks.yml
bundle:
  name: orders

resources:
  jobs:
    orders_daily:
      name: orders-daily
      schedule:
        quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 2 * * ?"
        timezone_id: Asia/Kolkata
      tasks:
        - task_key: load
          job_cluster_key: main
          python_wheel_task:
            package_name: orders
            entry_point: load
          libraries:
            - whl: ./dist/*.whl
      job_clusters:
        - job_cluster_key: main
          new_cluster:
            spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12
            node_type_id: i3.xlarge
            num_workers: 2

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development          # prefixes names, pauses schedules
    default: true
  prod:
    mode: production
    workspace:
      host: https://prod.cloud.databricks.com

databricks bundle validate
databricks bundle deploy -t dev        # every pull request
databricks bundle run -t dev orders_daily
databricks bundle deploy -t prod       # on merge to main, from CI with a service principal

The points to make: code and job definitions are reviewed together, dev deployments are isolated per developer, production deploys only from CI with a service principal (not a person’s token), and unit tests run on the wheel before deploy.

Snowflake

Snowflake SQL cannot run outside Snowflake, so this code was checked against the Snowflake documentation rather than executed.

165. What is a Snowflake micro-partition, and how does clustering affect query performance?

Snowflake stores every table as micro-partitions: immutable, columnar units of 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, created automatically in load order. For each one it keeps metadata, including every column’s min and max.

A filter skips micro-partitions whose range cannot match. That is pruning, the main performance lever, and it works only when ranges do not overlap much. Data loaded in date order prunes well on date and badly on customer_id.

-- How well is the table clustered on the column queries filter by?
SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('sales.orders', '(customer_id)');

-- Is pruning working? Compare partitions scanned with partitions total.
SELECT query_id, partitions_scanned, partitions_total,
       ROUND(100 * partitions_scanned / NULLIF(partitions_total, 0), 1) AS pct_scanned
FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history
WHERE query_text ILIKE '%sales.orders%' AND start_time > DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY partitions_scanned DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Define a clustering key: Automatic Clustering reorganizes in the background
ALTER TABLE sales.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id, order_date);

Automatic Clustering costs credits, so use a clustering key only on large tables (multi-terabyte) with a dominant filter that pruning currently misses. For point lookups on high-cardinality columns, the search optimization service (ALTER TABLE ... ADD SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON EQUALITY(customer_id)) is the alternative.

166. Permanent vs transient vs temporary tables in Snowflake. 
CREATE TABLE        sales.orders      (...);   -- Time Travel 1 day (up to 90 on Enterprise) + 7-day Fail-safe
CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE staging.orders (...);   -- Time Travel 0 or 1 day, no Fail-safe
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_orders     (...);   -- this session only, 0 or 1 day, no Fail-safe

ALTER TABLE sales.orders SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 30;

Use transient tables for staging and intermediate data that can be rebuilt. Fail-safe storage is billed, so a staging table that is rewritten every hour as a permanent table pays for seven days of old versions that nobody will ever restore. A transient database or schema makes every table in it transient by default.

167. Snowflake streams vs tasks: build incremental ELT inside Snowflake.

A stream tracks the changes to a table since its offset. A task runs SQL on a schedule. Together they give incremental ELT:

CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM raw.orders_stream ON TABLE raw.orders;

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK etl.merge_orders
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('raw.orders_stream')     -- skip runs with nothing to do
AS
  MERGE INTO core.orders t
  USING (SELECT * FROM raw.orders_stream WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT') s
  ON t.order_id = s.order_id
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET status = s.status, amount = s.amount, updated_at = s.updated_at
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, status, amount, updated_at)
                        VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.amount, s.updated_at);

ALTER TASK etl.merge_orders RESUME;                    -- tasks are created suspended

The stream exposes METADATA$ACTION and METADATA$ISUPDATE. An update appears as a DELETE row plus an INSERT row, both with METADATA$ISUPDATE = TRUE, which is why the MERGE reads only the INSERT side. Consuming the stream in a DML statement advances its offset when the transaction commits, so a failed MERGE leaves the changes for the next run.

The WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA clause means a run with no changes does not start the warehouse, which is the cost point interviewers look for. Dynamic tables (question 172) are the declarative alternative.

168. A Snowflake virtual warehouse is expensive. How do you tell whether it is the right size?

Read the evidence before changing the size:

SELECT warehouse_name,
       COUNT(*)                                             AS queries,
       ROUND(AVG(total_elapsed_time) / 1000, 1)             AS avg_s,
       SUM(IFF(bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage > 0, 1, 0))  AS remote_spills,
       SUM(IFF(bytes_spilled_to_local_storage  > 0, 1, 0))  AS local_spills,
       ROUND(AVG(queued_overload_time) / 1000, 1)           AS avg_queued_s
FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history
WHERE start_time > DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY warehouse_name
ORDER BY queries DESC;
  • Spilling (local, and worse, remote) means queries do not fit in memory: scale up a size.
  • Queuing with short queries means too much concurrency: scale out with a multi-cluster warehouse, not up.
  • Long idle time between sparse queries means auto-suspend is too long. Billing is per second with a 60-second minimum each time the warehouse resumes.
  • Poor pruning (question 165) means the query or the layout is the problem, and no size fixes it.
ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1 MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3 SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD';

CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR bi_monthly WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 500
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;
ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = bi_monthly;

Put ELT, BI and ad hoc work on separate warehouses, so each can be sized and attributed on its own.

169. COPY INTO vs Snowpipe vs Snowpipe Streaming: how do files get into Snowflake?

COPY INTO is a batch load you run on a warehouse. It remembers which files it loaded for 64 days and skips them, so rerunning it is safe:

CREATE STAGE raw.orders_stage
  URL = 's3://landing/orders/' STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_landing
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON);

COPY INTO raw.orders (payload, file_name, loaded_at)
FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM @raw.orders_stage)
ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';            -- skip bad rows, keep going

-- What failed, and why
SELECT * FROM TABLE(VALIDATE(raw.orders, JOB_ID => '_last'));

Snowpipe runs the same COPY automatically when a file lands, triggered by cloud storage event notifications, on Snowflake-managed serverless compute rather than your warehouse:

CREATE PIPE raw.orders_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS
  COPY INTO raw.orders (payload, file_name, loaded_at)
  FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM @raw.orders_stage);

SELECT SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS('raw.orders_pipe');

Snowpipe Streaming writes rows directly through an SDK or the Kafka connector, with no files at all, for latency in seconds.

Choose by arrival pattern: scheduled batches use COPY INTO, files trickling in all day use Snowpipe, and event streams use Snowpipe Streaming. Thousands of tiny files load inefficiently with either file-based path; Snowflake’s guidance is files of roughly 100 to 250 MB compressed.

170. Query nested JSON in Snowflake with VARIANT and FLATTEN.

Land JSON in a VARIANT column, then query it with path notation and casts:

CREATE TABLE raw.orders (payload VARIANT);

SELECT payload:order_id::STRING             AS order_id,
       payload:customer.city::STRING        AS city,       -- nested object
       payload:items[0].sku::STRING         AS first_sku,  -- array index
       ARRAY_SIZE(payload:items)            AS item_count
FROM raw.orders;

LATERAL FLATTEN turns an array into rows, one per element:

SELECT o.payload:order_id::STRING AS order_id,
       i.index                    AS line_number,
       i.value:sku::STRING        AS sku,
       i.value:qty::INT           AS qty
FROM raw.orders o,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => o.payload:items) i;

Two traps: a path that does not exist returns NULL, not an error, so a typo in a field name silently produces empty columns; and without the ::STRING cast, strings come back as JSON with quotes. Flatten into typed silver tables once, rather than parsing the VARIANT in every dashboard query.

171. Zero-copy cloning, Time Travel and UNDROP: someone ran a bad UPDATE an hour ago. Recover it.

Time Travel reads a table as it was:

-- What did the table look like before the bad statement?
SELECT * FROM core.orders BEFORE (STATEMENT => '01b2c3d4-0000-1234-0000-000000000abc');
SELECT * FROM core.orders AT (OFFSET => -3600);               -- one hour ago

Recover by cloning the old version and swapping it in. A clone shares the original’s micro-partitions, so it is created instantly and costs no storage until either side changes:

CREATE TABLE core.orders_restored CLONE core.orders AT (OFFSET => -3600);
ALTER TABLE core.orders SWAP WITH core.orders_restored;       -- atomic

UNDROP brings back a dropped table, schema or database within its Time Travel retention:

DROP TABLE core.orders;
UNDROP TABLE core.orders;

Cloning a whole database is also how teams give every developer a full-size test environment in seconds: CREATE DATABASE dev_asha CLONE prod;. After the retention period ends, Fail-safe keeps the data for another 7 days, but only Snowflake support can recover from it.

172. Dynamic tables vs streams and tasks vs materialized views.

A dynamic table is a query plus a freshness target. Snowflake refreshes it, incrementally when it can:

CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE core.daily_revenue
  TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = AUTO
AS
  SELECT order_date, region, SUM(amount) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM core.orders
  GROUP BY order_date, region;
  • Dynamic tables: declarative pipelines. You state the result and the maximum lag; Snowflake schedules refreshes and chains dependent dynamic tables. TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM refreshes a table only when a table that depends on it needs fresh data.
  • Streams and tasks (question 167): imperative. Use them when you need procedural logic, side effects, or control over exactly what happens to each change.
  • Materialized views: a single table, with restrictions (no joins), maintained automatically. Best for speeding up a repeated query on one large table.

REFRESH_MODE = AUTO falls back to a full refresh when the query cannot be maintained incrementally. Check the refresh mode Snowflake chose with SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES, because a “dynamic” table that fully refreshes every 15 minutes over a large table is an expensive surprise.

173. Snowflake's three caches: why did the same query run in 50 ms and then in 40 seconds?
  1. Result cache (cloud services layer): an identical query returns the stored result with no warehouse at all, for 24 hours (each reuse extends it, up to 31 days), as long as the underlying data has not changed and the query has no non-deterministic functions such as CURRENT_TIMESTAMP().
  2. Warehouse (local disk) cache: micro-partitions read by recent queries stay on the warehouse’s SSDs while it runs. It is lost when the warehouse suspends.
  3. Metadata: COUNT(*), MIN and MAX on a column can be answered from micro-partition metadata without scanning.
ALTER SESSION SET USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE;   -- turn the result cache off to benchmark honestly

The 50 ms run hit the result cache. The 40-second run came after new data landed (invalidating the result cache) on a warehouse that had just resumed (an empty local cache). Benchmarks that do not account for this measure the caches, not the query. There is a cost angle too: a very short AUTO_SUSPEND saves credits but throws away the local cache every time.

174. Role-based access, masking policies and row access policies in Snowflake.

Privileges go to roles, roles go to users, and roles can be granted to other roles to form a hierarchy:

CREATE ROLE analyst;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE prod TO ROLE analyst;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA prod.sales TO ROLE analyst;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA prod.sales TO ROLE analyst;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA prod.sales TO ROLE analyst;   -- tables created later
GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE sysadmin;                                  -- keep the hierarchy connected
GRANT ROLE analyst TO USER ranga;

Masking policy for a column:

CREATE MASKING POLICY pii.email_mask AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING ->
  CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val
       ELSE REGEXP_REPLACE(val, '^[^@]+', '***') END;

ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET MASKING POLICY pii.email_mask;

Row access policy, driven by a mapping table so access is data, not code:

CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY sec.region_policy AS (region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sec.role_regions m
          WHERE m.role_name = CURRENT_ROLE() AND m.region = region);

ALTER TABLE prod.sales.orders ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY sec.region_policy ON (region);

FUTURE grants are the detail people miss: without them, every new table needs a new grant. IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION also covers roles inherited through the hierarchy, which CURRENT_ROLE() does not.

dbt

The dbt answers ran on dbt-core 1.10 with the DuckDB adapter, the same way they would on Snowflake or Databricks, with one adapter difference noted in the first answer.

175. dbt incremental models: how do they work, and what goes wrong?

An incremental model builds the full table on the first run. On later runs is_incremental() is true, and the model selects only new or changed rows:

-- models/fct_orders.sql
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='order_id',
    incremental_strategy='delete+insert',
    on_schema_change='fail'
) }}

select order_id, customer_id, status, amount, updated_at
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

{% if is_incremental() %}
-- Look back one day so a late row with an older updated_at is not skipped.
where updated_at > (select max(updated_at) - interval 1 day from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

The second run brings an update to order 1, a new order 4, and a late order 5 whose updated_at (08:00 on 1 October) is older than the table’s latest (10:00). The same run with and without the lookback:

with 1-day lookback -> order ids: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
without lookback    -> order ids: [1, 2, 3, 4]

Without the lookback, order 5 is skipped, and nothing reports it. With a unique_key, the overlap the lookback creates re-processes some rows harmlessly, and order 1 is updated in place instead of duplicated.

Three things the run itself taught:

  • Strategies depend on the adapter. DuckDB rejected merge with “The incremental strategy ‘merge’ is not valid for this adapter”, so this ran with delete+insert. Snowflake and Databricks support merge, and use it by default.
  • Contracts constrain incremental models. With contract: {enforced: true}, dbt refused to parse the project until on_schema_change was append_new_columns or fail.
  • A logic change does not fix history until you run dbt run --full-refresh -s fct_orders.
176. dbt snapshots and dbt tests.

A snapshot implements SCD Type 2 on a source. In dbt 1.9 and later it is configured in YAML:

# snapshots/customers.yml
snapshots:
  - name: customers_snapshot
    relation: ref('raw_customers')
    config:
      unique_key: customer_id
      strategy: timestamp
      updated_at: updated_at

After customer 10 moved from Pune to Mumbai and dbt snapshot ran again:

customers_snapshot:
(10, 'Pune', datetime(2026, 9, 1, 0, 0), datetime(2026, 10, 2, 0, 0))
(10, 'Mumbai', datetime(2026, 10, 2, 0, 0), None)
(11, 'Delhi', datetime(2026, 9, 1, 0, 0), None)
(12, 'Chennai', datetime(2026, 9, 15, 0, 0), None)

dbt_valid_to closed the Pune row and the Mumbai row is current. A snapshot sees only the state at each run, so two changes between runs record only the last one. CDC catches every change; a snapshot does not.

Tests are queries that must return zero rows. Generic tests are declared in YAML, alongside a model contract:

# models/schema.yml
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    config:
      contract:
        enforced: true
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        data_type: integer
        constraints: [{type: not_null}]
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: integer
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              arguments: {to: ref('raw_customers'), field: customer_id}
      - name: status
        data_type: varchar
        data_tests:
          - accepted_values:
              arguments: {values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'cancelled']}

A singular test is a SQL file:

-- tests/assert_no_negative_amounts.sql
select * from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} where amount < 0

Done. PASS=6 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 TOTAL=6

Put unique and not_null on every model’s grain key: it is the cheapest protection against the fan-out in question 82.

177. ref vs source, materializations, and how you structure a dbt project.
  • source() points at a raw table that dbt does not build, declared in YAML so dbt can test it and check its freshness.
  • ref() points at another model. dbt builds the dependency graph from the ref calls, runs models in order, and swaps in the right schema per environment.
# models/staging/sources.yml
sources:
  - name: shop
    schema: raw
    loaded_at_field: _loaded_at
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
    tables:
      - name: orders

-- models/staging/stg_orders.sql   (view: cheap, always current)
select order_id, customer_id, lower(status) as status,
       cast(amount as decimal(10, 2)) as amount, cast(updated_at as timestamp) as updated_at
from {{ source('shop', 'orders') }}

Materializations: view for light staging models, table for small marts rebuilt each run, incremental for large facts (question 175), and ephemeral for a CTE inlined into its consumers.

The usual layout: staging (one model per source table: rename, cast, nothing else), intermediate (joins and business logic), and marts (facts and dimensions for consumers). Run dbt source freshness before dbt build, so a stale source fails the run instead of publishing stale numbers.

178. Run dbt in CI without rebuilding the whole project on every pull request.

“Slim CI” builds only the models a pull request changed, plus everything downstream of them, and reads unchanged parents from production:

# Production's manifest.json, saved by the last prod deploy
dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci
  • state:modified+: models whose code or config changed, and the + adds their children.
  • --defer --state: any parent that was not rebuilt is read from production instead of the empty CI schema.
  • dbt build: runs models, tests, snapshots and seeds in dependency order, so a failing test stops its children.

Write CI into its own schema per pull request, drop it when the pull request closes, and run dbt build --select state:modified+ with --fail-fast so the first broken test fails the check quickly.

Data quality and observability

179. What do you monitor on a production table, and where do the alerts go?

Five signals cover most incidents: freshness, volume, schema, distribution and lineage. The first four are a query each:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

def table_health(table, ts_col, key_col, expected_cols):
    df = spark.read.table(table)
    today = df.filter(F.col(ts_col) >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), 0))
    stats = df.agg(F.max(ts_col).alias("latest"),
                   F.avg(F.col(key_col).isNull().cast("int")).alias("null_rate")).first()
    history = (df.filter(F.col(ts_col) >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), 28))
               .groupBy(F.to_date(ts_col).alias("d")).count())
    usual = history.agg(F.percentile_approx("count", 0.5).alias("median")).first()["median"]
    return {
        "fresh":   stats["latest"] >= datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=6),
        "volume":  today.count() >= 0.5 * (usual or 0),          # half the usual day is suspicious
        "schema":  set(df.columns) == set(expected_cols),
        "nulls":   (stats["null_rate"] or 0) < 0.01,
    }

print(table_health("orders_t", "order_ts", "customer_id", ["order_id", "customer_id", "order_ts"]))

On a test table with 100 orders a day for four weeks, 30 so far today, and a missing customer_id on every fiftieth row:

{'fresh': True, 'volume': False, 'schema': True, 'nulls': False}

Fresh and schema pass. Volume fails because 30 is below half of the usual 100, and nulls fail because 2% of keys are missing against a 1% threshold. Run the volume check after the day’s expected load time, or it fires every morning.

Lineage answers “who is affected” when a check fails (question 62).

Alerts go to the team that owns the table, with the table name, the failed check, expected and actual values, and a runbook link. Page only for broken SLAs on critical tables; send a channel message for the rest. An alert that nobody acts on should be fixed or deleted, because alert fatigue hides the real one.

180. What is the write-audit-publish (WAP) pattern? Show it on Iceberg.

Write new data where consumers cannot see it, audit it, and publish it atomically only if the checks pass. Iceberg branches make this a few lines. This ran on Iceberg 1.11 with Spark 3.5.9:

spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.db.orders (order_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE) USING iceberg "
          "TBLPROPERTIES ('write.wap.enabled' = 'true')")

def write_audit_publish(batch, branch):
    spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lake.db.orders CREATE BRANCH IF NOT EXISTS {branch}")
    spark.conf.set("spark.wap.branch", branch)               # writes go to the branch
    batch.writeTo("lake.db.orders").append()
    spark.conf.unset("spark.wap.branch")

    staged = spark.read.option("branch", branch).table("lake.db.orders")
    bad = staged.filter("amount < 0 OR order_id IS NULL").count()
    print(f"{branch}: main rows={spark.table('lake.db.orders').count()}, "
          f"branch rows={staged.count()}, failed checks={bad}")
    if bad:
        spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lake.db.orders DROP BRANCH {branch}")   # discard
        return "rejected"
    spark.sql(f"CALL lake.system.fast_forward('db.orders', 'main', '{branch}')")
    spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lake.db.orders DROP BRANCH {branch}")
    return "published"

audit_1: main rows=2, branch rows=4, failed checks=0
published
audit_2: main rows=4, branch rows=5, failed checks=1
rejected
main rows now: [1, 2, 3, 4]

While the first batch sat on audit_1, readers of main still saw 2 rows. It passed and was fast-forwarded in one commit. The second batch failed its check, so its branch was dropped and main never saw order 5.

On Delta there are no branches, so write to a staging table, check it, and MERGE or INSERT into the target in one commit. In dbt, build into a separate schema and swap. The cost is the extra latency and the storage for the staged data.

181. A producer team wants to rename a column you consume. How does a data contract handle it?

A data contract is a versioned specification of a dataset (schema, meaning, quality guarantees, SLA, owner) that is checked automatically in the producer’s CI, so a breaking change fails their build before it reaches you:

# contracts/orders.yml, owned by the orders team
dataset: sales.orders
version: 2.1.0
owner: orders-team@company.com
sla: {freshness_hours: 2}
columns:
  - {name: order_id,    type: string,        nullable: false, unique: true}
  - {name: customer_id, type: string,        nullable: false}
  - {name: amount,      type: decimal(12,2), nullable: false, checks: ["amount >= 0"]}
  - {name: cust_id,     type: string,        deprecated: true, replaced_by: customer_id, remove_after: 2026-12-31}

import yaml

def breaking_changes(old_path, new_path):
    old = {c["name"]: c for c in yaml.safe_load(open(old_path))["columns"]}
    new = {c["name"]: c for c in yaml.safe_load(open(new_path))["columns"]}
    removed = [n for n in old if n not in new]
    retyped = [n for n in old if n in new and old[n]["type"] != new[n]["type"]]
    return removed + retyped      # CI fails the producer's PR if this is not empty

print("breaking:", breaking_changes("contracts/v1.yml", "contracts/v2.yml"))

Version 2 of a test contract renamed cust_id to customer_id and changed amount from decimal(12,2) to double:

breaking: ['cust_id', 'amount']

A rename is a breaking change, so the process is: add the new column, keep publishing the old one marked deprecated for an agreed period (cust_id above), tell consumers, and remove it in a new major version. Question 59 covers the consumer side.

LLM and AI data pipelines

These are newer. They appear in 2026 interview guides for teams that feed models or call LLMs inside pipelines.

182. Design a pipeline that processes 10,000 documents a day through an LLM, within rate limits, retries and a cost budget.

Treat the model as a slow, rate-limited, metered external API. The core loop, run against a fake model that rate-limits every fourth call:

import hashlib, random, time

PROMPT_VERSION = "summarize-v3"
MODEL = "small-model"
cache = {}                       # in production: a table keyed by the same hash
dead_letter, spent_tokens = [], 0
DAILY_TOKEN_BUDGET = 1_000

def cache_key(doc_id, text):
    content = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()
    return f"{doc_id}:{content}:{PROMPT_VERSION}:{MODEL}"

def process(doc_id, text, max_retries=5):
    global spent_tokens
    key = cache_key(doc_id, text)
    if key in cache:
        return "cached"
    if spent_tokens >= DAILY_TOKEN_BUDGET:
        return "deferred (budget)"
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            out = llm.summarize(text, MODEL)
            break
        except RateLimited:
            time.sleep(min(0.01 * 2 ** attempt, 0.1) + random.uniform(0, 0.005))
    else:
        dead_letter.append(doc_id)
        return "dead-lettered"
    if not isinstance(out.get("summary"), str):          # validate before storing
        dead_letter.append(doc_id)
        return "invalid output"
    spent_tokens += out["tokens"]
    cache[key] = {**out, "prompt_version": PROMPT_VERSION, "model": MODEL}
    return "processed"

first = [process(d, t) for d, t in docs.items()]          # 12 documents
docs["d1"] += " restated"                                 # one document changed
second = [process(d, t) for d, t in docs.items()]

run 1: {'deferred (budget)': 2, 'processed': 10}
run 2: {'cached': 9, 'deferred (budget)': 3}
model calls: 13 | tokens spent: 1042
  • Idempotent and cached: the key is document ID + content hash + prompt version + model, so the second run re-used 9 results and paid only for what changed. Changing the prompt or the model invalidates exactly the right entries.
  • Rate limits: retries with backoff and jitter absorbed the 429s. In production, size a worker pool to the provider’s request and token limits, not to the document count, and send repeat failures to a dead-letter queue.
  • Budget: the run stopped calling the model at the budget and deferred the rest to tomorrow.

The flaw the run exposed: 1,042 tokens were spent against a budget of 1,000, because the check happens before a call whose cost is only known after it. Reserve an estimate before the call (prompt tokens plus the output limit) and settle the difference afterwards, and the overshoot goes away.

183. Keep a vector index in sync with a source table of documents.

This is CDC again, with an embedding step:

import hashlib

def chunks(doc_id, text, size=800, overlap=100):
    step = size - overlap
    for i, start in enumerate(range(0, max(len(text) - overlap, 1), step)):
        yield {"chunk_id": f"{doc_id}:{i}",                # deterministic: same doc, same ids
               "doc_id": doc_id, "text": text[start:start + size]}

def sync(changes, index, embed, model_version):
    for c in changes:                                       # from a change feed or a hash diff
        if c["op"] == "delete":
            index.delete(filter={"doc_id": c["doc_id"]})    # the step most often forgotten
            continue
        new_hash = hashlib.sha256(c["text"].encode()).hexdigest()
        if index.get_doc_hash(c["doc_id"]) == new_hash:
            continue                                        # unchanged: no embedding cost
        index.delete(filter={"doc_id": c["doc_id"]})        # replace, do not add
        for ch in chunks(c["doc_id"], c["text"]):
            index.upsert(id=ch["chunk_id"], vector=embed(ch["text"]),
                         metadata={**ch, "doc_hash": new_hash, "model": model_version})
  • Detect changes with a change feed or a content hash, and re-embed only new or changed documents.
  • Chunk deterministically, so a re-embed replaces a document’s chunks instead of adding to them. Delete first: a shorter new version has fewer chunks, and the old extra ones would linger.
  • Propagate deletes. A document deleted at the source must leave the index, or retrieval keeps returning it.
  • Version the embedding model. A new model needs a full re-embed into a new index, then a cutover, because vectors from two models cannot be compared.

(index and embed stand for your vector store client and embedding call.)

How to prepare from this list

Start with the frequency table. Window functions, skew, idempotency, late data and incremental loads appear at most companies. Being solid on those five covers most rounds.

Prepare by company type. For product companies, practise designing systems out loud and coding without an IDE. For services and consulting firms, know Azure Data Factory and Databricks operationally, implement SCD Type 2 from memory, and prepare the managerial stories.

Answer scenarios with evidence. For every “it became slow” or “the numbers are wrong” question, the structure is the same: what changed, where you look, what you found, what you fixed, and how you verified it. That structure is what these interviews reward.

Then drill by component. Once the company-tagged questions are solid, use the component section to cover the rounds your target companies run: Java or Scala for JVM-heavy teams, Snowflake and dbt for analytics-engineering roles, and system design for every senior role.

Run the code, then change one thing. Every answer has the code and the output it produced. Load the sample tables, run the query, then break it on purpose: remove the tiebreaker, drop the calendar join, delete the checkpoint. Seeing the wrong answer appear is what makes the trap stick.

Do not memorise answers. Interviewers change one condition (“now the key is null”, “now there is no timestamp”) and watch whether the answer adapts. Every outline above names the mechanism so you can reason from it.
