Two of three survived here, and nothing says so. FAILFAST throws SparkException: [MALFORMED_RECORD_IN_PARSING.WITHOUT_SUGGESTION] on the first bad record. For a pipeline, use PERMISSIVE with the corrupt-record column, write rows where it is not null to a quarantine table, and alert on the count. One trap: since Spark 2.3, a query that references only the corrupt-record column of a raw JSON or CSV file is rejected. Cache or save the parsed DataFrame first, then filter on it. PySpark practice set Coding rounds for Spark-heavy teams tend to draw from the same pool: write a MERGE that survives retries, sessionize clicks, flatten JSON, beat skew, check data quality. One problem below points to answers earlier in the post; the rest are answered here. Each one ran on Spark 3.5.9 with Delta Lake 3.3.2, and the code shown is what produced the output under it. Problem Skills it exercises Answered in Upsert customer profiles so a retry is harmless MERGE, a version guard, in-batch dedup Q130 Turn reading-app screens into sessions lag, a running sum, session_window Q131 Flatten trip events with nested lists explode_outer, struct paths, from_json Q132 One tenant sends 90% of the traffic Two-step salted aggregation Q133 (salted joins: Q31) Speed up a job that misses its SLA Reading the Spark UI, joins, UDFs, file sizes Q34, Q26, Q31, Q36, Q96 Validate invoices against configurable rules A rule registry, a report, a release gate Q134 Keep history for a product dimension SCD Type 2 with plain DataFrames Q135 (with MERGE: Q51) Live page views per country Event-time windows, a watermark, a Delta sink Q136 The latest scan per shipment and warehouse row_number over a window Q137 A meter-reading loader that runs unattended Settings, JSON logs, rejects table, retries Q138 130. Write an upsert for customer profiles that is safe to retry: repeated keys in a batch, stale changes, and replays. A Delta MERGE keyed on the customer does the inserting and updating. Three additions make it safe to run again and again: profiles = f"file://{BASE}/profiles" spark.createDataFrame([ ("CU-9", "vinod@x.com", "free", "2026-10-20 08:00:00"), ("CU-7", "yashu@x.com", "pro", "2026-10-21 12:00:00"), ], "customer_id STRING, email STRING, plan STRING, updated_at STRING") \ .withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at")).write.format("delta").save(profiles) def upsert(batch, path, key="customer_id", version_col="updated_at"): """Safe to retry: a replayed batch, or an older version of a row, changes nothing.""" newest = dedup_latest(batch, [key], [F.col(version_col).desc()]) # one row per key (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("t") .merge(newest.alias("s"), f"t.{key} = s.{key}") .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition=f"s.{version_col} > t.{version_col}") # newer only .whenNotMatchedInsertAll() .execute()) changes = spark.createDataFrame([ ("CU-9", "vinod@x.com", "pro", "2026-10-22 09:00:00"), ("CU-9", "vinod.k@x.com", "pro", "2026-10-22 18:00:00"), # the same customer twice ("CU-7", "yashu@x.com", "free", "2026-10-19 10:00:00"), # older than what we hold ("CU-3", "lakshmi@x.com", "team", "2026-10-22 11:00:00"), # new ], "customer_id STRING, email STRING, plan STRING, updated_at STRING") \ .withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at")) upsert(changes, profiles) first = spark.read.format("delta").load(profiles).orderBy("customer_id").collect() upsert(changes, profiles) # the retry second = spark.read.format("delta").load(profiles).orderBy("customer_id").collect() spark.read.format("delta").load(profiles).orderBy("customer_id").show() print("same table after applying the batch twice:", first == second) try: (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, profiles).alias("t").merge(changes.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id") .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()) except Exception as e: print("MERGE straight from the raw batch:", type(e).__name__, "-", str(e).splitlines()[0][:110]) +-----------+-------------+----+-------------------+ |customer_id| email|plan| updated_at| +-----------+-------------+----+-------------------+ | CU-3|lakshmi@x.com|team|2026-10-22 11:00:00| | CU-7| yashu@x.com| pro|2026-10-21 12:00:00| | CU-9|vinod.k@x.com| pro|2026-10-22 18:00:00| +-----------+-------------+----+-------------------+ same table after applying the batch twice: True MERGE straight from the raw batch: UnsupportedOperationException - [DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE] Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched A key repeated within the batch. CU-9 changed twice. Delta refuses to apply two source rows to one target row, and the last line shows the error you get (DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE). Reducing the batch to the newest row per key first (dedup_latest, question 137) keeps the 18:00 change. A change older than the table. CU-7’s incoming row is from 19 October, but the table already holds the 21 October version. The s.updated_at > t.updated_at guard ignores it, so a delayed message cannot undo a newer one. A replay. Applying the same batch a second time leaves the table identical. On a large partitioned table, add the partition column to the join condition so the MERGE reads only the partitions the batch touches. 131. Turn a reading app's screen views into sessions: a new session after more than 30 idle minutes. Same logic as the SQL answer (question 76): minutes since the previous view with lag, a 1 where a session starts, and a running sum of those 1s as the session number. Spark also offers session_window: reads = spark.createDataFrame([ ("anada", "2026-10-03 08:15:00", "home"), ("anada", "2026-10-03 08:20:00", "chapter-1"), ("anada", "2026-10-03 08:44:00", "chapter-2"), ("anada", "2026-10-03 09:20:00", "home"), ("anada", "2026-10-03 09:21:00", "chapter-3"), ("lakshmi", "2026-10-03 21:00:00", "home"), ("lakshmi", "2026-10-03 21:30:00", "chapter-9"), # 30 min exactly ], "user_id STRING, ts STRING, screen STRING").withColumn("ts", F.to_timestamp("ts")) by_user = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("ts") minutes_idle = (F.col("ts").cast("long") - F.lag("ts").over(by_user).cast("long")) / 60 sessions = (reads .withColumn("idle_min", minutes_idle) .withColumn("starts", F.when(F.col("idle_min").isNull() | (F.col("idle_min") > 30), 1).otherwise(0)) .withColumn("session_no", F.sum("starts").over(by_user.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, 0))) .withColumn("session_id", F.concat_ws("#", "user_id", "session_no"))) sessions.orderBy("user_id", "ts").show() print("the same with session_window:") (reads.groupBy("user_id", F.session_window("ts", "30 minutes")) .agg(F.count("*").alias("screens")) .select("user_id", "session_window.start", "session_window.end", "screens") .orderBy("user_id", "start").show(truncate=False)) +-------+-------------------+---------+--------+------+----------+----------+ |user_id| ts| screen|idle_min|starts|session_no|session_id| +-------+-------------------+---------+--------+------+----------+----------+ | anada|2026-10-03 08:15:00| home| NULL| 1| 1| anada#1| | anada|2026-10-03 08:20:00|chapter-1| 5.0| 0| 1| anada#1| | anada|2026-10-03 08:44:00|chapter-2| 24.0| 0| 1| anada#1| | anada|2026-10-03 09:20:00| home| 36.0| 1| 2| anada#2| | anada|2026-10-03 09:21:00|chapter-3| 1.0| 0| 2| anada#2| |lakshmi|2026-10-03 21:00:00| home| NULL| 1| 1| lakshmi#1| |lakshmi|2026-10-03 21:30:00|chapter-9| 30.0| 0| 1| lakshmi#1| +-------+-------------------+---------+--------+------+----------+----------+ the same with session_window: +-------+-------------------+-------------------+-------+ |user_id|start |end |screens| +-------+-------------------+-------------------+-------+ |anada |2026-10-03 08:15:00|2026-10-03 09:14:00|3 | |anada |2026-10-03 09:20:00|2026-10-03 09:51:00|2 | |lakshmi|2026-10-03 21:00:00|2026-10-03 22:00:00|2 | +-------+-------------------+-------------------+-------+ Anada was idle for 36 minutes before 09:20, so session 2 begins there. Lakshmi’s second screen is exactly 30 minutes after her first, and the rule is “more than 30”, so it stays in session 1. Notice the end column from session_window: it is the last event plus the 30-minute gap (08:44 becomes 09:14), not the last event itself. Window functions are the choice when every row needs its session id; session_window is the choice for per-session totals, and it also runs in Structured Streaming with a watermark. 132. Flatten trip events: a nested rider object, a list of stops that each carry a list of tags, and fare details stored as a JSON string. Nested objects and lists need different tools. A nested object is just a path (rider.home.city) and never changes how many rows you have. A list needs explode, which adds a row per element. A JSON string needs from_json with a schema before either applies. The three trips cover the awkward cases: an empty stop list, a missing stop list, a missing home address and an unparseable fare: trips_json = f"{BASE}/trips.json" with open(trips_json, "w") as fh: for t in [ {"trip_id": "T1", "rider": {"name": "Anada", "home": {"city": "Mysuru"}}, "stops": [{"seq": 1, "place": "Airport", "tags": ["pickup", "toll"]}, {"seq": 2, "place": "Palace", "tags": []}], "fare": '{"currency": "INR", "total": 640.0}'}, {"trip_id": "T2", "rider": {"name": "Lakshmi", "home": None}, "stops": [], "fare": '{"currency": "INR", "total": 85.0}'}, # empty list {"trip_id": "T3", "rider": {"name": "Manoj", "home": {"city": "Kochi"}}, "stops": None, "fare": "{broken"}, # null list, bad JSON ]: fh.write(json.dumps(t) + "\n") raw = spark.read.json(trips_json) raw.printSchema() fare_schema = StructType([StructField("currency", StringType()), StructField("total", DoubleType())]) flat = (raw .withColumn("stop", F.explode_outer("stops")) # a row per stop; keeps T2 and T3 .withColumn("tag", F.explode_outer("stop.tags")) # a list inside a list: explode again .withColumn("fare", F.from_json("fare", fare_schema)) # unparseable text becomes null .select("trip_id", F.col("rider.name").alias("rider"), # nested objects: just a path F.col("rider.home.city").alias("home_city"), F.col("stop.seq").alias("stop_seq"), F.col("stop.place").alias("place"), "tag", F.col("fare.total").alias("fare_total"))) flat.orderBy("trip_id", "stop_seq", "tag").show() print("stop rows with explode:", raw.select(F.explode("stops")).count(), "| with explode_outer:", raw.select(F.explode_outer("stops")).count()) root |-- fare: string (nullable = true) |-- rider: struct (nullable = true) | |-- home: struct (nullable = true) | | |-- city: string (nullable = true) | |-- name: string (nullable = true) |-- stops: array (nullable = true) | |-- element: struct (containsNull = true) | | |-- place: string (nullable = true) | | |-- seq: long (nullable = true) | | |-- tags: array (nullable = true) | | | |-- element: string (containsNull = true) |-- trip_id: string (nullable = true) +-------+-------+---------+--------+-------+------+----------+ |trip_id| rider|home_city|stop_seq| place| tag|fare_total| +-------+-------+---------+--------+-------+------+----------+ | T1| Anada| Mysuru| 1|Airport|pickup| 640.0| | T1| Anada| Mysuru| 1|Airport| toll| 640.0| | T1| Anada| Mysuru| 2| Palace| NULL| 640.0| | T2|Lakshmi| NULL| NULL| NULL| NULL| 85.0| | T3| Manoj| Kochi| NULL| NULL| NULL| NULL| +-------+-------+---------+--------+-------+------+----------+ stop rows with explode: 2 | with explode_outer: 4 explode versus explode_outer. With plain explode, trips T2 and T3 vanish (2 stop rows instead of 4), because an empty or null list produces no rows. explode_outer keeps them with nulls. Row counts multiply. T1 has two stops and the first has two tags, so T1 becomes three rows, and fare_total is repeated on all of them. Sum trip-level values before exploding, or the total triples. Bad JSON turns into nulls, silently. T3’s fare could not be parsed, and nothing failed. Count those nulls if they matter. Declare schemas in production rather than relying on inference, so a new or changed field is something you decided, not something you discover. 133. One tenant sends 90% of all requests. Compute per-tenant counts and average latency without one task doing all the work. A groupBy sends every row of a tenant to one task, so the big tenant becomes one very slow task. Spread it out in two steps: add a random bucket number, aggregate per tenant and bucket, then combine the buckets: requests = (spark.range(0, 1_000_000) .withColumn("tenant", F.when(F.col("id") % 10 < 9, F.lit("acme")) # one tenant: 90% .otherwise(F.concat(F.lit("t"), (F.col("id") % 300).cast("string")))) .withColumn("latency_ms", (F.col("id") % 389).cast("double"))) BUCKETS = 12 per_bucket = (requests .withColumn("bucket", (F.rand(17) * BUCKETS).cast("int")) .groupBy("tenant", "bucket") # step 1: the big tenant split 12 ways .agg(F.count("*").alias("n"), F.sum("latency_ms").alias("sum_ms"))) per_tenant = (per_bucket.groupBy("tenant") # step 2: combine the small partials .agg(F.sum("n").alias("requests"), F.sum("sum_ms").alias("sum_ms")) .withColumn("avg_ms", F.col("sum_ms") / F.col("requests"))) direct = requests.groupBy("tenant").agg(F.count("*").alias("requests"), F.avg("latency_ms").alias("avg_ms")) mismatches = per_tenant.join(direct, "tenant").filter( (per_tenant.requests != direct.requests) | (F.abs(per_tenant.avg_ms - direct.avg_ms) > 1e-9)).count() print("tenants:", per_tenant.count(), "| tenants that differ from a direct groupBy:", mismatches) per_tenant.filter("tenant = 'acme'").select("tenant", "requests", F.round("avg_ms", 3).alias("avg_ms")).show() rows_per_task = lambda df, cols: sorted(df.repartition(8, *cols).rdd.glom().map(len).collect(), reverse=True) bucketed = requests.withColumn("bucket", (F.rand(17) * BUCKETS).cast("int")) print("rows per shuffle partition, by tenant :", rows_per_task(requests, ["tenant"])) print("rows per shuffle partition, by tenant + bucket:", rows_per_task(bucketed, ["tenant", "bucket"])) tenants: 31 | tenants that differ from a direct groupBy: 0 +------+--------+-------+ |tenant|requests| avg_ms| +------+--------+-------+ | acme| 900000|193.984| +------+--------+-------+ rows per shuffle partition, by tenant : [906666, 30002, 20001, 13333, 10000, 9999, 6666, 3333] rows per shuffle partition, by tenant + bucket: [313289, 236779, 235586, 89404, 86843, 14520, 13609, 9970] Same answer: none of the 31 tenants differs from a direct groupBy, averages included. Smaller worst task: the largest shuffle partition falls from 906,666 rows to about 313,000. It is not 12 equal pieces, because 12 buckets hash into only 8 partitions and some collide; more buckets or more partitions even it out further. Only combinable measures split this way. Counts and sums combine across buckets, so the average is rebuilt as total ÷ count. An average of bucket averages would be wrong, and medians or exact distinct counts cannot be combined like this at all; use percentile_approx or a sketch (question 55). AQE’s skew handling (question 31) splits oversized partitions in joins only, which is why aggregations still need this by hand. 134. Validate invoices against rules kept in configuration, report every result, and block the release on serious failures. The checks themselves are simple; the design is the point. The rules are a list that could live in YAML or a table, each check type is one function, and a dictionary connects the two, so supporting a new kind of rule never touches the runner: invoices = spark.createDataFrame([ ("INV-7001", "V-1", 1200.0, "INR"), ("INV-7002", "V-2", 480.0, "INR"), ("INV-7003", None, 310.0, "INR"), ("INV-7002", "V-2", 480.0, "INR"), ("INV-7004", "V-1", 0.0, "USD"), ("INV-7005", "V-9", 75.0, "YEN"), ], "invoice_id STRING, vendor_id STRING, total DOUBLE, currency STRING") vendors = spark.createDataFrame([("V-1",), ("V-2",), ("V-3",)], "vendor_id STRING") RULES = [ # configuration: load from YAML or a table in a real job {"name": "invoice_id present", "check": "not_null", "column": "invoice_id", "severity": "block"}, {"name": "vendor_id present", "check": "not_null", "column": "vendor_id", "severity": "block"}, {"name": "invoice_id unique", "check": "unique", "column": "invoice_id", "severity": "block"}, {"name": "total above zero", "check": "min_exclusive", "column": "total", "min": 0, "severity": "block"}, {"name": "known currency", "check": "allowed", "column": "currency", "values": ["INR", "USD", "EUR"], "severity": "warn"}, {"name": "vendor on file", "check": "lookup", "column": "vendor_id", "ref": vendors, "ref_column": "vendor_id", "severity": "warn"}, ] def check_not_null(df, r): return df.filter(F.col(r["column"]).isNull()).count() def check_unique(df, r): return df.groupBy(r["column"]).count().filter("count > 1").agg(F.coalesce(F.sum("count"), F.lit(0))).first()[0] def check_min(df, r): return df.filter(F.col(r["column"]) <= r["min"]).count() def check_allowed(df, r): return df.filter(~F.col(r["column"]).isin(r["values"])).count() def check_lookup(df, r): present = df.filter(F.col(r["column"]).isNotNull()) return present.join(r["ref"], present[r["column"]] == r["ref"][r["ref_column"]], "left_anti").count() CHECKS = {"not_null": check_not_null, "unique": check_unique, "min_exclusive": check_min, "allowed": check_allowed, "lookup": check_lookup} # adding a check type: one line here def evaluate(df, rules): rows = df.count() results = [(r["name"], r["severity"], CHECKS[r["check"]](df, r), rows) for r in rules] return (spark.createDataFrame(results, "rule STRING, severity STRING, bad_rows LONG, rows LONG") .withColumn("ok", F.col("bad_rows") == 0)) report = evaluate(invoices, RULES) report.show(truncate=False) blocking = report.filter("NOT ok AND severity = 'block'").count() print("blocking failures:", blocking, "-> do not publish" if blocking else "-> publish") +------------------+--------+--------+----+-----+ |rule |severity|bad_rows|rows|ok | +------------------+--------+--------+----+-----+ |invoice_id present|block |0 |6 |true | |vendor_id present |block |1 |6 |false| |invoice_id unique |block |2 |6 |false| |total above zero |block |1 |6 |false| |known currency |warn |1 |6 |false| |vendor on file |warn |1 |6 |false| +------------------+--------+--------+----+-----+ blocking failures: 3 -> do not publish Six invoices, five failed rules: one missing vendor, one invoice number used twice (both copies counted, so 2), a zero total, an unrecognised currency, and a vendor that is not on file. Severity decides what happens next: block failures stop the release, warn failures are reported and alerted on. Worth saying in an interview: each rule here is a separate Spark job, so fold the counts into one aggregation pass when the rule list grows; store every report with its run id to see trends; and tools like Great Expectations or Deequ package the same idea. 135. Keep history for a product dimension with plain DataFrames: expire changed rows, add new versions, and handle two changes on one day. Question 51 does Type 2 with a Delta MERGE. Without one, rebuild the dimension from four pieces: rows that stay as they are, rows that expire today, new versions of changed products, and brand-new products. A fingerprint of the tracked columns tells changed from unchanged: dim = spark.createDataFrame([ (101, "P-10", "Kettle", "Kitchen", "2025-06-01", None, True), (102, "P-20", "Lantern", "Outdoor", "2025-08-20", None, True), ], "product_sk INT, product_id STRING, name STRING, category STRING, valid_from STRING, valid_to STRING, is_current BOOLEAN") \ .withColumn("valid_from", F.to_date("valid_from")).withColumn("valid_to", F.to_date("valid_to")) incoming = spark.createDataFrame([ ("P-10", "Kettle", "Appliances", "2026-10-27 08:00:00"), ("P-10", "Kettle", "Small appliances", "2026-10-27 17:30:00"), # re-categorised twice today ("P-20", "Lantern", "Outdoor", "2026-10-27 09:00:00"), # no change ("P-30", "Hammock", "Outdoor", "2026-10-27 10:00:00"), # brand new ], "product_id STRING, name STRING, category STRING, changed_at STRING").withColumn("changed_at", F.to_timestamp("changed_at")) TRACKED = ["name", "category"] # only these create a new version fingerprint = F.sha2(F.concat_ws("||", *[F.coalesce(F.col(c), F.lit("<null>")) for c in TRACKED]), 256) as_of = F.to_date(F.lit("2026-10-27")) today = dedup_latest(incoming, ["product_id"], [F.col("changed_at").desc()]).withColumn("fp", fingerprint) live = dim.filter("is_current").withColumn("fp", fingerprint) cmp = today.alias("n").join(live.alias("o"), "product_id", "left") changed = cmp.filter("o.product_sk IS NOT NULL AND n.fp <> o.fp") added = cmp.filter("o.product_sk IS NULL") expired = (dim.join(changed.select("product_id"), "product_id", "left_semi") .filter("is_current") .withColumn("valid_to", as_of).withColumn("is_current", F.lit(False))) kept = dim.join(expired.select("product_sk"), "product_sk", "left_anti") next_sk = dim.agg(F.max("product_sk")).first()[0] fresh = (changed.select("product_id", "n.name", "n.category").unionByName(added.select("product_id", "n.name", "n.category")) .withColumn("product_sk", F.lit(next_sk) + F.row_number().over(Window.orderBy("product_id"))) .withColumn("valid_from", as_of) .withColumn("valid_to", F.lit(None).cast("date")) .withColumn("is_current", F.lit(True))) kept.unionByName(expired).unionByName(fresh).orderBy("product_id", "valid_from").show() +----------+----------+-------+----------------+----------+----------+----------+ |product_sk|product_id| name| category|valid_from| valid_to|is_current| +----------+----------+-------+----------------+----------+----------+----------+ | 101| P-10| Kettle| Kitchen|2025-06-01|2026-10-27| false| | 103| P-10| Kettle|Small appliances|2026-10-27| NULL| true| | 102| P-20|Lantern| Outdoor|2025-08-20| NULL| true| | 104| P-30|Hammock| Outdoor|2026-10-27| NULL| true| +----------+----------+-------+----------------+----------+----------+----------+ P-10 was re-categorised twice today. Only the latest change survives the per-key reduction, so “Small appliances” becomes the new version and “Appliances” never appears. Whether every intra-day change deserves its own version is a question for the business. P-20 did not change, so its fingerprint matches and its row is untouched. P-30 is new and receives the next surrogate key. The fingerprint covers tracked columns only. Including something like a load timestamp would create a new version on every run. Rebuilding the whole dimension is fine at thousands or millions of rows; beyond that, MERGE (question 51) rewrites only the files holding changed products. 136. Count page views per country in 10-minute windows, accept events up to 15 minutes late, and write each window to Delta once. Question 40 shows watermarks with a memory sink; this is the production shape: a declared schema, a watermark, tumbling windows, append mode into Delta and a checkpoint. A folder of JSON files stands in for Kafka (question 38 reads Kafka), and maxFilesPerTrigger turns each file into its own micro-batch: src, out, chk = f"{BASE}/views_in", f"file://{BASE}/views_10min", f"{BASE}/chk_views" os.makedirs(src) schema = StructType([StructField("country", StringType()), StructField("views", DoubleType()), StructField("event_time", TimestampType())]) def land(name, rows): with open(f"{src}/{name}.json", "w") as fh: fh.writelines(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in rows) def run_stream(): agg = (spark.readStream.schema(schema).option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1).json(src) # schema is declared .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes") .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "country") .agg(F.count("*").alias("events"), F.sum("views").alias("views"))) q = (agg.writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append") .option("checkpointLocation", chk) # progress and state survive restarts .trigger(availableNow=True).start(out)) q.awaitTermination() return spark.read.format("delta").load(out).select("window.start", "country", "events", "views") \ .orderBy("start", "country") land("a", [{"country": "IN", "views": 3.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:01:00"}, {"country": "IN", "views": 1.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:07:00"}, {"country": "SG", "views": 2.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:09:00"}]) land("b", [{"country": "IN", "views": 4.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:33:00"}]) print("after the first run:"); run_stream().show(truncate=False) land("c", [{"country": "IN", "views": 50.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:05:00"}, # 28 minutes late {"country": "SG", "views": 1.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T19:02:00"}]) print("after the second run:"); run_stream().show(truncate=False) after the first run: +-------------------+-------+------+-----+ |start |country|events|views| +-------------------+-------+------+-----+ |2026-10-09 18:00:00|IN |2 |4.0 | |2026-10-09 18:00:00|SG |1 |2.0 | +-------------------+-------+------+-----+ after the second run: +-------------------+-------+------+-----+ |start |country|events|views| +-------------------+-------+------+-----+ |2026-10-09 18:00:00|IN |2 |4.0 | |2026-10-09 18:00:00|SG |1 |2.0 | |2026-10-09 18:30:00|IN |1 |4.0 | +-------------------+-------+------+-----+ First run. The 18:33 event pushed the watermark to 18:18, which closed the 18:00-18:10 windows, so they were written. Nothing later had closed yet. Second run. An Indian event from 18:05 arrived 28 minutes late. Its window was already closed and written, so the event was dropped and the table still shows 4.0 views, not 54.0. The 19:02 event moved the watermark to 18:47, which closed and wrote the 18:30 window; Singapore’s 19:00 window is still open. The trade-off of append mode: every window is written once and never revised, but only after the watermark passes it, so results lag by the window length plus the allowed lateness. update mode publishes earlier, partial numbers, and then needs a sink that can overwrite them, typically a MERGE inside foreachBatch. The checkpoint plus Delta’s per-batch commit is what makes the output exactly-once. 137. Keep the latest scan for each shipment at each warehouse, and explain why dropDuplicates is not enough. Partition by the key, order by recency, keep row 1. Written once as a function, it is reused by the upsert and SCD answers above: scans = spark.createDataFrame([ ("SHP-41", "BLR", "picked", "2026-10-12 08:10:00", 7), ("SHP-41", "BLR", "packed", "2026-10-12 09:45:00", 8), # the later scan wins ("SHP-41", "HYD", "in_transit", "2026-10-12 21:00:00", 9), # another warehouse: its own key ("SHP-52", "BLR", "packed", "2026-10-12 11:30:00", 3), ("SHP-52", "BLR", "on_hold", "2026-10-12 11:30:00", 4), # same second: the scanner sequence decides (None, "BLR", "picked", "2026-10-12 12:00:00", 5), # no shipment id ], "shipment_id STRING, warehouse STRING, status STRING, scanned_at STRING, scanner_seq INT") \ .withColumn("scanned_at", F.to_timestamp("scanned_at")) def dedup_latest(df, keys, order_by): """One row per key, the first by `order_by`. Make order_by unique per key, or ties are arbitrary.""" w = Window.partitionBy(*keys).orderBy(*order_by) return (df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w)) .filter("_rn = 1").drop("_rn")) current = dedup_latest(scans, ["shipment_id", "warehouse"], [F.col("scanned_at").desc(), F.col("scanner_seq").desc()]) current.orderBy("shipment_id", "warehouse").show() print("dropDuplicates on the same key also leaves", scans.dropDuplicates(["shipment_id", "warehouse"]).count(), "rows, with no rule for which one") +-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+ |shipment_id|warehouse| status| scanned_at|scanner_seq| +-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+ | NULL| BLR| picked|2026-10-12 12:00:00| 5| | SHP-41| BLR| packed|2026-10-12 09:45:00| 8| | SHP-41| HYD|in_transit|2026-10-12 21:00:00| 9| | SHP-52| BLR| on_hold|2026-10-12 11:30:00| 4| +-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+ dropDuplicates on the same key also leaves 4 rows, with no rule for which one SHP-41 has two scans at Bengaluru; the later one, packed, wins. Its Hyderabad scan is a different key, so it stays. SHP-52’s two scans have the same timestamp; scanner_seq breaks the tie, so the result is the same on every run. Without a tiebreaker the winner is whichever row Spark happens to see first. The scan with no shipment id forms its own group, because nulls are grouped together. Decide whether to keep it or send it to a rejects table. dropDuplicates(["shipment_id", "warehouse"]) also returns 4 rows, but makes no promise about which row survives, so it can change between runs. It is fine for rows that are identical in every column, and wrong for “keep the latest”. 138. Write a meter-reading loader you could leave running overnight: settings, structured logs, a rejects table, retries and a safe write. This one brings the earlier answers together, reusing upsert from question 130: @dataclass(frozen=True) class Settings: source: str target: str rejects: str business_date: str statuses: tuple = ("ok", "estimated") reject_limit: float = 0.3 write_attempts: int = 3 log = logging.getLogger("meter_loader") handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout) handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(message)s")) log.addHandler(handler); log.setLevel(logging.INFO); log.propagate = False def emit(step, **fields): # one JSON object per step: easy to query later log.info(json.dumps({"step": step, **fields}, sort_keys=True)) def retried(attempts, wait_s=0.2, on=(Exception,)): def deco(fn): @wraps(fn) def wrapper(*a, **kw): for n in range(1, attempts + 1): try: return fn(*a, **kw) except on as e: emit("retry", fn=fn.__name__, attempt=n, error=type(e).__name__) if n == attempts: raise time.sleep(wait_s * 2 ** (n - 1)) return wrapper return deco class Transient(Exception): pass hiccups = {"left": 1} # the first write attempt fails, as if a node was lost @retried(attempts=3, on=(Transient,)) def write_readings(df, s): if hiccups["left"]: hiccups["left"] -= 1 raise Transient("storage timeout") upsert(df, s.target, key="meter_id", version_col="read_at") def run(s): t0 = time.time() raw = spark.read.schema("meter_id STRING, kwh STRING, status STRING, read_at STRING, _bad_line STRING") \ .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_bad_line").json(s.source).cache() emit("read", rows=raw.count(), business_date=s.business_date) typed = raw.withColumn("kwh_num", F.col("kwh").cast("double")).withColumn("read_at", F.to_timestamp("read_at")) why = (F.when(F.col("_bad_line").isNotNull(), "unparseable_line") .when(F.col("meter_id").isNull(), "no_meter_id") .when(F.col("kwh_num").isNull(), "kwh_not_numeric") .when(F.col("kwh_num") < 0, "negative_kwh") .when(~F.col("status").isin(*s.statuses), "unknown_status")) tagged = typed.withColumn("why", why) good = tagged.filter("why IS NULL").select("meter_id", F.col("kwh_num").alias("kwh"), "status", "read_at") bad = tagged.filter("why IS NOT NULL") n_good, n_bad = good.count(), bad.count() emit("validate", accepted=n_good, rejected=n_bad, by_reason={r["why"]: r["count"] for r in bad.groupBy("why").count().collect()}) (bad.select(F.lit(s.business_date).alias("business_date"), "why", # raw kept for replay F.to_json(F.struct(*[c for c in raw.columns if c != "_bad_line"])).alias("raw"), "_bad_line") .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite") .option("replaceWhere", f"business_date = '{s.business_date}'").save(s.rejects)) if n_bad / max(n_good + n_bad, 1) > s.reject_limit: emit("stop", reject_share=round(n_bad / (n_good + n_bad), 3)) raise RuntimeError("reject share above the limit; target left untouched") write_readings(good, s) emit("finished", seconds=round(time.time() - t0, 1), target_rows=spark.read.format("delta").load(s.target).count()) readings_file = f"{BASE}/meters.json" with open(readings_file, "w") as fh: fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-1", "kwh": "14.2", "status": "ok", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n') fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-2", "kwh": "n/a", "status": "ok", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n') fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-3", "kwh": "9.8", "status": "tampered", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n') fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-4", "kwh": "3.1", "status": "ok"\n') for i in range(5, 13): fh.write(json.dumps({"meter_id": f"M-{i}", "kwh": f"{i * 1.5:.1f}", "status": "estimated", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}) + "\n") meter_table = f"file://{BASE}/meter_readings" spark.createDataFrame([("M-1", 13.9, "ok", "2026-10-27 06:00:00")], "meter_id STRING, kwh DOUBLE, status STRING, read_at STRING") \ .withColumn("read_at", F.to_timestamp("read_at")).write.format("delta").save(meter_table) s = Settings(source=f"file://{readings_file}", target=meter_table, rejects=f"file://{BASE}/meter_rejects", business_date="2026-10-28") run(s) try: run(Settings(**{**s.__dict__, "reject_limit": 0.1})) # a feed that is normally clean except RuntimeError as e: print("strict run:", e) spark.read.format("delta").load(s.rejects).select("why", "raw", "_bad_line").orderBy("why").show(truncate=60) spark.stop() {"business_date": "2026-10-28", "rows": 12, "step": "read"} {"accepted": 9, "by_reason": {"kwh_not_numeric": 1, "unknown_status": 1, "unparseable_line": 1}, "rejected": 3, "step": "validate"} {"attempt": 1, "error": "Transient", "fn": "write_readings", "step": "retry"} {"seconds": 5.4, "step": "finished", "target_rows": 9} {"business_date": "2026-10-28", "rows": 12, "step": "read"} {"accepted": 9, "by_reason": {"kwh_not_numeric": 1, "unknown_status": 1, "unparseable_line": 1}, "rejected": 3, "step": "validate"} {"reject_share": 0.25, "step": "stop"} strict run: reject share above the limit; target left untouched +----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+ | why| raw| _bad_line| +----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+ | kwh_not_numeric|{"meter_id":"M-2","kwh":"n/a","status":"ok","read_at":"20...| NULL| | unknown_status|{"meter_id":"M-3","kwh":"9.8","status":"tampered","read_a...| NULL| |unparseable_line| {}|{"meter_id": "M-4", "kwh": "3.1", "status": "ok"| +----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+ Walk the interviewer through it in this order: Settings in a frozen dataclass. Nothing is hard-coded in the logic, and the business date is passed in, so a backfill is the same call with an older date. One JSON log line per step, with counts. Last night’s rejects become a log query. Rejected rows go to a table, with the reason and the raw input (the truncated line survives intact in _bad_line). It is overwritten per business date, so a rerun replaces rather than duplicates it, and rows can be replayed after a fix. A limit on the reject share. Three bad rows out of twelve (25%) is tolerated at a 30% limit; at 10% the run stops before touching the target, because a sudden jump usually means the source changed. Retry only what can succeed on retry. The storage timeout on the first write was retried with backoff and succeeded; a bad row is never retried. A write that tolerates repetition. The upsert updated M-1 with its newer reading and added eight meters: 9 rows, however many times the job runs. Streaming and Kafka 139. Kafka partitions, consumer groups and ordering: how many consumers can read a topic in parallel, and what is ordered? A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log; each message gets an increasing offset within its partition. Ordering is per partition only. Messages with the same key go to the same partition (the default partitioner hashes the key), so per-key order holds and global order does not. A consumer group shares a topic’s partitions: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group. Parallelism is capped by the partition count, so 12 partitions and 20 consumers leave 8 idle. Adding or removing a consumer triggers a rebalance, which reassigns partitions. kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --create --topic payments \ --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2 kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --describe --group fraud-scorer # shows CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG for each partition Durability: with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write succeeds only when two replicas have it, so losing one broker loses no acknowledged data. Choosing the key is the design decision: key payments by account_id for per-account order, and watch for a hot key that overloads one partition (question 30’s skew, one layer earlier). Question 38’s run showed the hashing: with 3 partitions and keys A1, A2, A3, the final offsets were {'0': 4, '1': 2, '2': 0}. Partition 2 received nothing, because three keys do not spread evenly over three partitions. 140. Join two streams (ad impressions and clicks). What stops the join state from growing forever? A stream-stream join keeps both sides in state, waiting for a match. Bound it with a watermark on each side and a time-range condition in the join: imps = (spark.readStream.schema("ad_id STRING, imp_ts TIMESTAMP").json(f"{src}/impressions") .withWatermark("imp_ts", "2 hours")) clks = (spark.readStream.schema("click_ad_id STRING, click_ts TIMESTAMP").json(f"{src}/clicks") .withWatermark("click_ts", "3 hours")) joined = imps.join(clks, F.expr(""" click_ad_id = ad_id AND click_ts >= imp_ts AND click_ts <= imp_ts + interval 1 hour""")) q = (joined.writeStream.format("memory").queryName("ad_clicks") .option("checkpointLocation", chk).trigger(availableNow=True).start()) Three impressions at 10:00, 10:01 and 10:02; a click on a1 five minutes later, and a click on a2 89 minutes later: +-----+-------------------+-------------------+ |ad_id| imp_ts| click_ts| +-----+-------------------+-------------------+ | a1|2026-10-01 10:00:00|2026-10-01 10:05:00| +-----+-------------------+-------------------+ Only a1 matched: the a2 click is outside the one-hour range. The range condition plus the watermarks tell Spark when an impression can no longer match, so it can drop it from state. Without them the query still runs, but the state of an inner join grows forever. For outer joins, the watermark and range condition are mandatory, because Spark must know when to emit the unmatched row with nulls. Data modeling These build on questions 51 to 55. The data modeling guide covers each topic in depth with runnable examples. 141. Model a sales fact for five sales channels and three product hierarchies. What is the grain? Declare the grain first: one row per order line, the lowest level the sources record. Channel becomes a dimension, not five separate fact tables, so cross-channel totals are a plain GROUP BY: CREATE TABLE dim_channel ( channel_sk INT, channel_code STRING, -- web, app, store, marketplace, wholesale channel_type STRING -- direct / partner ); CREATE TABLE fact_order_line ( order_id STRING, -- degenerate dimension line_number INT, order_date_key INT, channel_sk INT, product_sk BIGINT, -- hierarchies live on dim_product customer_sk BIGINT, quantity INT, net_amount DECIMAL(12, 2) ); SELECT c.channel_code, p.category, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_channel c ON c.channel_sk = f.channel_sk JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_sk = f.product_sk GROUP BY c.channel_code, p.category; The three product hierarchies (category, brand, merchandising group) are attributes of dim_product, or separate hierarchy tables if they are ragged or change on their own schedule. A hierarchy describes the product, not the sale, so the fact holds only product_sk. If one channel reports at a coarser level (wholesale sends daily totals, not lines), do not mix it into the line fact. Build a second fact at the daily grain and conform the shared dimensions so the two can be compared. 142. Role-playing, junk and degenerate dimensions. Role-playing: one physical dimension used in several roles, exposed as views named for the role: CREATE VIEW dim_order_date AS SELECT date_key AS order_date_key, full_date AS order_date FROM dim_date; CREATE VIEW dim_ship_date AS SELECT date_key AS ship_date_key, full_date AS ship_date FROM dim_date; CREATE VIEW dim_delivery_date AS SELECT date_key AS delivery_date_key, full_date AS delivery_date FROM dim_date; Junk dimension: low-cardinality flags combined into one small dimension, one row per combination, so the fact holds one key instead of many flag columns: CREATE TABLE dim_order_flags AS SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY is_gift, payment_type, has_promo) AS order_flags_sk, is_gift, payment_type, has_promo FROM (SELECT DISTINCT is_gift, payment_type, has_promo FROM staging.orders) t; Degenerate dimension: a key with no dimension table, such as order_id on the fact. It groups lines into an order and traces back to the source, and has no attributes of its own to store. 143. What are conformed dimensions, and what is a bus matrix? A conformed dimension has the same keys, attribute names and meanings in every fact that uses it. Then “drilling across” two facts is valid: -- Sales and support tickets by the same customer segment WITH s AS (SELECT c.segment, SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer c USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY c.segment), t AS (SELECT c.segment, COUNT(*) AS tickets FROM fact_support_ticket f JOIN dim_customer c USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY c.segment) SELECT s.segment, s.revenue, t.tickets, t.tickets / (s.revenue / 1000) AS tickets_per_1k_revenue FROM s JOIN t USING (segment); Aggregate each fact separately, then join the results on the conformed attribute. Joining the two facts directly would fan out (question 82). The bus matrix is the planning grid: business processes as rows, dimensions as columns, and a mark where a process uses a dimension: date customer product store channel orders X X X X X shipments X X X X returns X X X X X support tickets X X X It shows which dimensions must be conformed before teams build facts on their own. Without it, each team builds its own customer dimension and the numbers stop agreeing. 144. SCD Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 6: how do you choose? Ask how the business reports history, per attribute: Type 1 when only the current value matters, or the change is a correction. History is restated. Type 2 when facts must report under the value valid at the time: sales by the region the customer was in when they bought. Type 6 when users need both “as was” and “as is” on the same row: Type 2 rows, plus a current_ column overwritten on every version. -- Type 6: after Ranga moves Pune -> Mumbai, both versions carry the current city customer_sk | customer_id | city | current_city | valid_from | valid_to | is_current 101 | C01 | Pune | Mumbai | 2026-01-01 | 2026-03-01 | false 102 | C01 | Mumbai | Mumbai | 2026-03-01 | NULL | true -- "as was": revenue by the city at purchase time SELECT d.city, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer d USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY d.city; -- "as is": the same facts by today's city, with no extra join SELECT d.current_city, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer d USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY d.current_city; The choice is per attribute, not per table: email can be Type 1 while loyalty_tier is Type 2 in the same dimension. Question 51 has the Type 2 MERGE. 145. A fact arrives before its dimension row (an early-arriving fact). What do you load? Never drop the fact and never load a NULL key. The standard answer is an inferred member: insert a placeholder dimension row with the business key, then overwrite it in place when the real row arrives: -- 1. Before loading facts: create placeholders for unknown business keys INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_sk, customer_id, city, is_inferred, valid_from, is_current) SELECT next_sk(), s.customer_id, 'Unknown', true, s.order_date, true FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS order_date FROM staging.orders GROUP BY customer_id) s LEFT ANTI JOIN dim_customer d ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id; -- 2. When the real customer row arrives: a Type 1 overwrite of the placeholder, -- even in a Type 2 dimension, so the facts' keys stay valid MERGE INTO dim_customer t USING staging.customers s ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id AND t.is_inferred WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET city = s.city, is_inferred = false; (next_sk() stands for your surrogate-key generator, such as an identity column.) The alternative is pointing the fact at a reserved unknown member (-1) and reprocessing the fact later. The inferred member avoids that reprocessing. Monitor how many inferred rows are never completed. 146. One big table (OBT) vs a star schema in a lakehouse. An OBT pre-joins the fact with its dimension attributes: CREATE TABLE gold.sales_obt USING delta AS SELECT f.order_id, f.order_date_key, f.quantity, f.net_amount, c.segment, c.city, p.category, p.brand, ch.channel_code FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_sk = f.customer_sk JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_sk = f.product_sk JOIN dim_channel ch ON ch.channel_sk = f.channel_sk; Columnar formats read only the columns a query needs and compress repeated values well, so wide tables are much cheaper than they were in a row store, and dashboards get join-free SQL. What an OBT costs: a Type 1 dimension change means rewriting every fact row that carries the attribute; the history semantics are frozen when the table is built; and every new attribute is a backfill. A defensible answer keeps the star as the source of truth and derives OBTs for specific dashboards, rebuilt from the star whenever needed. System design Expect one system design round at most product companies. The 2026 guides describe it as the round that carries the most weight. The follow-ups are predictable: why this storage layer, what you ruled out, how backfill works, what breaks when a source changes, and what it costs over time. 147. Design a pipeline that ingests 1 TB of clickstream a day and serves dashboards at under 2 seconds P95. Start with the numbers: 1 TB a day is about 12 MB/s on average, so plan for 3 to 5 times that at peak. Then the layers: SDK / web ──► Kafka (partition by user_id) ──► stream job ──► bronze table │ (append, raw) ▼ silver: deduplicated, sessionized events │ ▼ gold: pre-aggregated by minute/hour × dimension ──► serving store (OLAP engine) The key decision is that dashboards never scan raw events. Two seconds at P95 comes from pre-aggregated gold tables, or from a real-time OLAP store (Druid, Pinot, ClickHouse), not from a lake query over a terabyte. The gold step is a windowed aggregate: events = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.clicks") .withWatermark("event_ts", "15 minutes") .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"])) per_minute = (events .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "1 minute"), "page", "country") .agg(F.count("*").alias("views"), F.approx_count_distinct("user_id").alias("users"))) (per_minute.writeStream.outputMode("append") .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://lake/_chk/clicks_per_minute") .trigger(processingTime="1 minute") .toTable("gold.clicks_per_minute")) Cover deduplication by event ID, late events with a watermark, a schema registry for the event contract, partitioning by event date, and compaction of the small files that streaming writes (question 36). The follow-ups: the Kafka partition count comes from peak throughput per partition and consumer parallelism; and a day is replayed from bronze, not from Kafka, once Kafka’s retention has passed. 148. Backfill nine months of history after a logic fix, without double counting and without stopping the daily job. Make every run partition-scoped and overwrite-based, so a backfill is just the normal job run with old dates: from datetime import date, timedelta from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor def run_day(d): df = transform(spark.read.table("silver.orders").filter(F.col("order_date") == d)) (df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite") .option("replaceWhere", f"order_date = '{d}'") # replaces exactly one day .saveAsTable("gold_shadow.daily_sales")) # a copy, not the live table return d days = [date(2026, 1, 1) + timedelta(n) for n in range(273)] with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool: # throttle: the daily job still runs for d in pool.map(run_day, reversed(days)): # newest months first print("done", d) Write to a shadow table first, reconcile its counts and totals against the live table, then swap. Throttle with a small worker pool so the backfill does not starve the daily SLA. Freeze the inputs: read a fixed snapshot of silver (VERSION AS OF), not a table that is still changing. The trap: appending recomputed data on top of the old output. That is the double count. Overwrite-by-partition makes reruns safe, including a rerun of the backfill itself. 149. An upstream API changes a field from a string to an object, and the pipeline starts failing. What do you do in the next hour? In order: Stop the damage. Pause the job, or let it fail closed. Do not let it write partial or mis-parsed data into tables consumers read. Keep the raw data. Make sure bronze still lands raw payloads, so nothing is lost while you fix the parser. Tell people: which tables are stale, since when, and when you will update them next. Fix forward: parse both shapes, and route anything unparseable to quarantine. Replay from bronze for the affected window, then reconcile the counts. Step 4 in PySpark, when customer changed from "C01" to {"id": "C01", "tier": "gold"}: raw = spark.read.table("bronze.orders_raw") # payload kept as a string parsed = raw.select( F.get_json_object("payload", "$.order_id").alias("order_id"), F.coalesce( F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer.id"), # new shape: object F.when(~F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer").startswith("{"), F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer")) # old shape: plain string ).alias("customer_id"), "payload") parsed.filter("customer_id IS NULL").write.mode("append").saveAsTable("quarantine.orders") parsed.filter("customer_id IS NOT NULL").drop("payload").createOrReplaceTempView("fixed") One payload of each shape, plus one with no customer: +--------+-----------+ |order_id|customer_id| +--------+-----------+ | o1| C01| | o2| C02| | o3| NULL| +--------+-----------+ Afterwards: a schema contract with the producer, a schema check at ingestion that alerts before the transform fails, and a test with the new payload. 150. Design CDC replication from a PostgreSQL OLTP database into a lakehouse table. PostgreSQL WAL ──► Debezium (logical replication slot) ──► Kafka topic per table │ initial snapshot ─────────────────────────────────────┤ ▼ Spark: latest change per key by LSN, then MERGE The Debezium connector, registered with Kafka Connect: { "name": "orders-cdc", "config": { "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector", "plugin.name": "pgoutput", "database.hostname": "orders-db", "database.port": "5432", "database.user": "debezium", "database.password": "${file:/secrets/db.properties:password}", "database.dbname": "shop", "topic.prefix": "shop", "table.include.list": "public.orders", "slot.name": "orders_cdc", "snapshot.mode": "initial" } } The apply step keeps the newest change per key and ignores anything older than what the target already has: w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("lsn")) latest = (changes.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1").drop("rn")) (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders").alias("t") .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id") .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn") .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="s.op <> 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn", set={"status": "s.status", "lsn": "s.lsn"}) .whenNotMatchedInsert(condition="s.op <> 'd'", values={"order_id": "s.order_id", "status": "s.status", "lsn": "s.lsn"}) .execute()) The target starts with orders 1 and 2 at LSN 100. Five changes arrive out of order: two updates to order 1 (LSN 103 and 105), a delete of order 2 at 104, a stale update of order 2 at 99, and a new order 3: +--------+-------+---+ |order_id| status|lsn| +--------+-------+---+ | 1|shipped|105| | 3| placed|106| +--------+-------+---+ Order 1 took the LSN 105 update, not 103. Order 2 was deleted, because the newest change for it (104) is the delete, and the stale LSN 99 update lost the ROW_NUMBER. Order 3 was inserted. The operational risk to name: a replication slot that nobody consumes keeps WAL on the primary until its disk fills. Monitor slot lag: SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS retained_wal FROM pg_replication_slots; The data modeling guide runs an idempotent CDC apply end to end, including what a late event does after a hard delete. 151. Estimate storage and cost at one, three and ten years for a 500 GB-a-day source. Interviewers want arithmetic, stated assumptions and the levers that change the result: raw_gb_per_day = 500 compression = 5 # assumption: measure it on a sample layers = 2.2 # bronze + silver + a smaller gold retained_versions = 1.1 # time travel keeps some old files alive usd_per_gb_month = 0.023 # object storage, standard class for years in (1, 3, 10): tb = raw_gb_per_day * 365 * years / compression * layers * retained_versions / 1024 print(f"{years:>2} years: {tb:6.0f} TB stored, about ${tb * 1024 * usd_per_gb_month:,.0f} a month") 1 years: 86 TB stored, about $2,032 a month 3 years: 259 TB stored, about $6,095 a month 10 years: 863 TB stored, about $20,316 a month Then the levers: lifecycle rules that move old bronze to colder storage classes (question 75), a retention policy per layer, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup, and aggregating old detail nobody queries. Compute usually costs more than storage, so mention incremental processing, which avoids recomputing history every day. 152. Design an event deduplication layer for at-least-once delivery at billions of events a day. At-least-once delivery makes duplicates normal, so deduplication is a design component, not a cleanup job. Two layers: deduped = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.events") .withWatermark("event_ts", "2 hours") # longest realistic redelivery .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"])) # layer 1: bounded state def upsert(batch_df, batch_id): # layer 2: idempotent sink (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.events").alias("t") .merge(batch_df.alias("s"), "t.event_date = s.event_date AND t.event_id = s.event_id") .whenNotMatchedInsertAll() .execute()) deduped.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert).option("checkpointLocation", chk).start() Key: a producer-assigned event ID. Without one, hash the business fields, and accept that two identical genuine events will merge. Window: state with a watermark, sized to the longest redelivery delay. Question 38 showed it catching a producer retry inside one batch and resent events across runs. Sink: the MERGE catches duplicates that arrive after the state has expired. Measure: track the duplicate rate. A sudden rise usually means a producer retry storm, not more traffic. Airflow These DAGs were loaded with DagBag and the fan-out DAG was test-run with airflow dags test on Airflow 3.1.0. 153. How do you make an Airflow DAG idempotent? Each task run must process a fixed slice of data and produce the same output however many times it runs. Question 74’s DAG shows all three rules: Use the data interval, not the clock. The task takes data_interval_start and data_interval_end from the run context instead of calling datetime.now(). Rerunning last Tuesday then processes last Tuesday. Overwrite the slice the task owns (INSERT OVERWRITE ... PARTITION), or MERGE on a key. Never append. Keep tasks atomic. Write to staging and swap, so a failed attempt leaves nothing for the retry to trip over. @task def load_partition(data_interval_start=None, data_interval_end=None): # Airflow fills these from the run being executed run_sql(f""" INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE sales.orders PARTITION (order_date = '{data_interval_start:%Y-%m-%d}') SELECT * FROM staging.orders WHERE event_ts >= '{data_interval_start}' AND event_ts < '{data_interval_end}' """) The trap: a task that “loads everything since the last run” using a watermark stored outside Airflow. A manual rerun of an old interval then loads whatever is new today, not that interval’s data. 154. catchup, backfill, and what happens when you deploy a DAG with a start_date in the past. With catchup=True, the scheduler creates a run for every interval between start_date and now that has not run. Deploying a daily DAG with a start_date a year ago creates 365 runs at once. With catchup=False, only the latest interval runs. Set it on every DAG. The default comes from catchup_by_default, which Airflow 3 changed from True to False, so the same DAG file behaves differently after an upgrade. The loaded DAGs confirm the setting: from airflow.models.dagbag import DagBag bag = DagBag("/opt/airflow/dags", include_examples=False) print("import errors:", bag.import_errors) for dag_id, dag in sorted(bag.dags.items()): print(dag_id, "catchup=", dag.catchup, "tasks=", [t.task_id for t in dag.tasks]) import errors: {} daily_orders catchup= False tasks= ['wait_for_file', 'load_partition'] file_fanout catchup= False tasks= ['list_files', 'process', 'publish'] orders_report catchup= False tasks= ['build_report'] Run deliberate backfills with the CLI, throttled: airflow backfill create --dag-id daily_orders \ --from-date 2026-01-01 --to-date 2026-09-30 --max-active-runs 3 Airflow 3 runs backfills inside the scheduler; earlier versions ran them in a separate CLI process that died with your terminal. The DagBag check above is also worth putting in CI, so a DAG that fails to import never reaches production. 155. Sensors: poke vs reschedule vs deferrable, and why sensors can deadlock a cluster. from airflow.providers.standard.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor FileSensor(task_id="poke", filepath=path, mode="poke", poke_interval=60) # holds a slot FileSensor(task_id="reschedule", filepath=path, mode="reschedule", poke_interval=300) # frees it between checks FileSensor(task_id="deferred", filepath=path, deferrable=True, timeout=6 * 3600) # hands the wait to the triggerer Poke holds a worker slot for the whole wait. Reschedule releases the slot between checks. Deferrable hands the wait to the triggerer process, which watches thousands of waits asynchronously, and uses no worker slot until the condition fires. FileSensor in Airflow 3.1 accepts deferrable=True. If many poke-mode sensors wait on late files, they can occupy every worker slot, and the tasks that would produce those files can never start. Use deferrable or reschedule mode for long waits, always set a timeout, and decide what a timeout means: fail and alert, or soft_fail=True to skip. 156. What is XCom for, and what should you never put in it? Show dynamic task mapping. XCom passes small values between tasks: a path, a row count, a batch ID. The TaskFlow API pushes a task’s return value automatically. Dynamic task mapping creates one task instance per input at runtime: from airflow.sdk import DAG, Asset, task orders_clean = Asset("s3://lake/silver/orders") with DAG(dag_id="file_fanout", schedule=None, start_date=datetime(2026, 10, 1)) as dag: @task def list_files() -> list[str]: # Return paths, never the data: XComs live in the metadata database. return [f"s3://landing/orders/part-{i}.json" for i in range(3)] @task def process(path: str) -> int: print(f"processing {path}") return 100 # a row count is a fine XCom @task(outlets=[orders_clean]) def publish(counts: list[int]) -> int: return sum(counts) publish(process.expand(path=list_files())) # one mapped task per file airflow dags test file_fanout ran three mapped process instances (map_index 0, 1 and 2), one per path, and publish received the list of their counts. Never pass datasets through XCom. Values are stored in the metadata database by default, so large ones bloat it and slow the scheduler and UI. Write data to storage and pass its location. A custom XCom backend can store large values in object storage if you truly need them. 157. What changed in Airflow 3, and what does an interviewer expect you to know about it? Airflow 3.0 was released in April 2025. The changes that come up: Assets replace Datasets for data-aware scheduling. In question 156, publish declares outlets=[orders_clean], and this DAG runs whenever that asset is updated, with no timetable: with DAG(dag_id="orders_report", schedule=[orders_clean], start_date=datetime(2026, 10, 1)): @task def build_report(): print("runs whenever s3://lake/silver/orders is updated") build_report() A new authoring import: from airflow.sdk import DAG, task, Asset. DAG versioning: the UI shows which version of the DAG code each run used. Task SDK and execution API: tasks talk to the API server instead of connecting to the metadata database directly, which is what makes remote and multi-language execution possible. Scheduler-managed backfills (question 154). Removals: SubDAGs (use TaskGroups), SLA callbacks (deadline alerts arrived in later 3.x releases), and the execution_date context key (use logical_date). catchup_by_default is now False. Databricks Most Databricks features run only on Databricks, so the code here was checked against the Databricks documentation rather than run. The exception is liquid clustering, which open-source Delta Lake 3.3 also supports, and which ran on Spark 3.5.9. 158. Liquid clustering vs partitioning vs Z-order. When do you use which? Partitioning fixes a directory layout at creation. Good for one low-cardinality filter column (date) on a very large table; bad for anything else, and changing it means rewriting the table. Z-order (OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY) co-locates values inside partitions, but every run rewrites everything again, and the columns are not recorded on the table. Liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY) records the clustering columns on the table, clusters data incrementally on OPTIMIZE, and lets you change the columns without rewriting existing data. spark.sql(f"""CREATE TABLE delta.`{lc}` (event_id BIGINT, user_id BIGINT, event_date DATE) USING delta CLUSTER BY (user_id, event_date)""") # ... 8 appends ... spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE delta.`{lc}`").select("metrics.numFilesAdded", "metrics.numFilesRemoved").show() print(spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`{lc}`").select("clusteringColumns").first()) +-------------+---------------+ |numFilesAdded|numFilesRemoved| +-------------+---------------+ | 1| 8| +-------------+---------------+ Row(clusteringColumns=['user_id', 'event_date']) Changing the clustering key is a metadata operation: spark.sql("CREATE TABLE gold_cpd USING delta CLUSTER BY (customer_id) AS SELECT ...") spark.sql("ALTER TABLE gold_cpd CLUSTER BY (orders)") Row(clusteringColumns=['customer_id']) after ALTER: Row(clusteringColumns=['orders']) New writes and the next OPTIMIZE use the new key; old files are reclustered gradually. On Databricks, CLUSTER BY AUTO lets the platform choose the columns from the query history. Liquid clustering cannot be combined with PARTITIONED BY or ZORDER BY on the same table. Use it for new tables by default, and keep partitioning only for very large tables with one dominant date filter and a retention policy that drops whole partitions. 159. Build a bronze-silver-gold pipeline with data-quality rules in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables). You declare the tables and their rules; the platform works out the order, creates the tables, manages checkpoints and retries, and records every expectation’s pass and fail counts in the pipeline event log. from pyspark import pipelines as dp from pyspark.sql import functions as F @dp.table(comment="Raw orders, as delivered") def bronze_orders(): return (spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") .load("/Volumes/prod/landing/orders/")) @dp.table(comment="Typed, valid orders") @dp.expect("has_customer", "customer_id IS NOT NULL") # keep, but count failures @dp.expect_or_drop("valid_amount", "amount >= 0") # drop failing rows @dp.expect_or_fail("has_order_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL") # stop the update def silver_orders(): return (spark.readStream.table("bronze_orders") .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(12,2)")) .withColumn("order_date", F.to_date("order_ts"))) @dp.materialized_view(comment="Revenue per day") def gold_daily_revenue(): return (spark.read.table("silver_orders") .groupBy("order_date").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))) @dp.table over a streaming read is a streaming table: it processes each input row once, incrementally. @dp.materialized_view over a batch read is recomputed, incrementally where the platform can, to always match its query. Expectations: expect records failures and keeps the row, expect_or_drop removes the row, expect_or_fail fails the update. Group several with @dp.expect_all({...}). from pyspark import pipelines as dp is the current import. Older code uses import dlt with the same decorators (@dlt.table, @dlt.expect_or_drop), which still works. 160. Apply a CDC feed as SCD Type 2 in a Databricks pipeline, without writing the MERGE yourself. create_auto_cdc_flow (formerly apply_changes) handles ordering, deletes and history: from pyspark import pipelines as dp from pyspark.sql.functions import col, expr dp.create_streaming_table("customers_history") dp.create_auto_cdc_flow( target="customers_history", source="customers_cdc", # a streaming source of change rows keys=["customer_id"], sequence_by=col("lsn"), # resolves out-of-order changes apply_as_deletes=expr("op = 'DELETE'"), except_column_list=["op", "lsn"], stored_as_scd_type="2", # or 1 for latest-only ) sequence_by does what the ROW_NUMBER by LSN did in question 150: a change with a lower sequence than the stored one cannot overwrite it. With stored_as_scd_type="2", the target gets __START_AT and __END_AT columns, which are question 51’s effective_date and end_date. Interviewers ask this to see whether you know what it replaces. Be able to write the MERGE by hand as well (question 51), because that is what AUTO CDC does, and it is what you need on any engine without it. 161. Unity Catalog: grant analysts read access, restrict rows by region, and mask emails. Unity Catalog has a three-level namespace, catalog.schema.table, and a grant at each level. Reading a table needs all three: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod TO `analysts`; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod.sales TO `analysts`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders TO `analysts`; Row filter: a SQL function returning a boolean, attached to the table: CREATE FUNCTION prod.sales.region_filter(region STRING) RETURN IF(is_account_group_member('sales_admins'), true, region = 'IN'); ALTER TABLE prod.sales.orders SET ROW FILTER prod.sales.region_filter ON (region); Column mask: a function that returns the value to show: CREATE FUNCTION prod.sales.mask_email(email STRING) RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('pii_readers') THEN email ELSE regexp_replace(email, '^[^@]+', '***') END; ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK prod.sales.mask_email; Both apply to every query from every engine that goes through Unity Catalog, so there is no view to keep in sync and no way around them from a notebook. Grant to groups, never to individuals, and audit access through system.access.audit. 162. All-purpose compute vs job compute vs serverless vs SQL warehouses, and what Photon changes. All-purpose compute: interactive clusters for notebooks, shared by people. The most expensive DBU rate. Never run scheduled production jobs on it. Job compute: a cluster created for one job run and terminated after it. A cheaper rate, isolated from other work, and the right default for scheduled pipelines. Serverless (jobs, notebooks, pipelines): no cluster to configure, and start-up in seconds. You trade control over instance types and Spark configuration for zero idle cost and no tuning. SQL warehouses: compute for SQL and BI tools, with auto-stop and scaling by concurrency. A job definition that uses job compute, from an Asset Bundle (question 164): job_clusters: - job_cluster_key: main new_cluster: spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12 # an LTS runtime node_type_id: i3.xlarge autoscale: {min_workers: 2, max_workers: 8} runtime_engine: PHOTON Photon is Databricks’ native, vectorized C++ engine for Spark SQL and DataFrame operations. It speeds up scans, joins and aggregations over Delta and Parquet, and costs a higher DBU rate. It does not accelerate Python UDFs or RDD code, so check a job’s plan for operators that fall back before paying for it. 163. Databricks spend doubled this month. How do you find out why? Billable usage is in the system.billing.usage system table, one row per usage record, with the job or warehouse that caused it: -- DBUs by product and SKU, this month vs last SELECT date_trunc('month', usage_date) AS month, billing_origin_product, sku_name, SUM(usage_quantity) AS dbus FROM system.billing.usage WHERE usage_date >= date_trunc('month', add_months(current_date(), -1)) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY month, dbus DESC; -- The jobs that grew the most SELECT usage_metadata.job_id, SUM(CASE WHEN usage_date >= date_trunc('month', current_date()) THEN usage_quantity END) AS this_month, SUM(CASE WHEN usage_date < date_trunc('month', current_date()) THEN usage_quantity END) AS last_month FROM system.billing.usage WHERE usage_metadata.job_id IS NOT NULL AND usage_date >= date_trunc('month', add_months(current_date(), -1)) GROUP BY usage_metadata.job_id ORDER BY this_month - COALESCE(last_month, 0) DESC LIMIT 20; The usual causes are: production jobs moved onto all-purpose clusters, clusters with no auto-termination, a job whose input grew (check its run duration), and Photon or serverless switched on without comparing the cost. Prevent a repeat with cluster policies (enforce auto-termination, allowed node types and tags) and budgets with alerts. Tag every job with a team, so custom_tags can attribute the cost. 164. How do you deploy Databricks jobs through CI/CD? Databricks Asset Bundles describe jobs, pipelines and their code as YAML in the repository, deployed per environment with the Databricks CLI: # databricks.yml bundle: name: orders resources: jobs: orders_daily: name: orders-daily schedule: quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 2 * * ?" timezone_id: Asia/Kolkata tasks: - task_key: load job_cluster_key: main python_wheel_task: package_name: orders entry_point: load libraries: - whl: ./dist/*.whl job_clusters: - job_cluster_key: main new_cluster: spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12 node_type_id: i3.xlarge num_workers: 2 targets: dev: mode: development # prefixes names, pauses schedules default: true prod: mode: production workspace: host: https://prod.cloud.databricks.com databricks bundle validate databricks bundle deploy -t dev # every pull request databricks bundle run -t dev orders_daily databricks bundle deploy -t prod # on merge to main, from CI with a service principal The points to make: code and job definitions are reviewed together, dev deployments are isolated per developer, production deploys only from CI with a service principal (not a person’s token), and unit tests run on the wheel before deploy. Snowflake Snowflake SQL cannot run outside Snowflake, so this code was checked against the Snowflake documentation rather than executed. 165. What is a Snowflake micro-partition, and how does clustering affect query performance? Snowflake stores every table as micro-partitions: immutable, columnar units of 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, created automatically in load order. For each one it keeps metadata, including every column’s min and max. A filter skips micro-partitions whose range cannot match. That is pruning, the main performance lever, and it works only when ranges do not overlap much. Data loaded in date order prunes well on date and badly on customer_id. -- How well is the table clustered on the column queries filter by? SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('sales.orders', '(customer_id)'); -- Is pruning working? Compare partitions scanned with partitions total. SELECT query_id, partitions_scanned, partitions_total, ROUND(100 * partitions_scanned / NULLIF(partitions_total, 0), 1) AS pct_scanned FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history WHERE query_text ILIKE '%sales.orders%' AND start_time > DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) ORDER BY partitions_scanned DESC LIMIT 20; -- Define a clustering key: Automatic Clustering reorganizes in the background ALTER TABLE sales.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id, order_date); Automatic Clustering costs credits, so use a clustering key only on large tables (multi-terabyte) with a dominant filter that pruning currently misses. For point lookups on high-cardinality columns, the search optimization service (ALTER TABLE ... ADD SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON EQUALITY(customer_id)) is the alternative. 166. Permanent vs transient vs temporary tables in Snowflake. CREATE TABLE sales.orders (...); -- Time Travel 1 day (up to 90 on Enterprise) + 7-day Fail-safe CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE staging.orders (...); -- Time Travel 0 or 1 day, no Fail-safe CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_orders (...); -- this session only, 0 or 1 day, no Fail-safe ALTER TABLE sales.orders SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 30; Use transient tables for staging and intermediate data that can be rebuilt. Fail-safe storage is billed, so a staging table that is rewritten every hour as a permanent table pays for seven days of old versions that nobody will ever restore. A transient database or schema makes every table in it transient by default. 167. Snowflake streams vs tasks: build incremental ELT inside Snowflake. A stream tracks the changes to a table since its offset. A task runs SQL on a schedule. Together they give incremental ELT: CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM raw.orders_stream ON TABLE raw.orders; CREATE OR REPLACE TASK etl.merge_orders WAREHOUSE = etl_wh SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE' WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('raw.orders_stream') -- skip runs with nothing to do AS MERGE INTO core.orders t USING (SELECT * FROM raw.orders_stream WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT') s ON t.order_id = s.order_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET status = s.status, amount = s.amount, updated_at = s.updated_at WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, status, amount, updated_at) VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.amount, s.updated_at); ALTER TASK etl.merge_orders RESUME; -- tasks are created suspended The stream exposes METADATA$ACTION and METADATA$ISUPDATE. An update appears as a DELETE row plus an INSERT row, both with METADATA$ISUPDATE = TRUE, which is why the MERGE reads only the INSERT side. Consuming the stream in a DML statement advances its offset when the transaction commits, so a failed MERGE leaves the changes for the next run. The WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA clause means a run with no changes does not start the warehouse, which is the cost point interviewers look for. Dynamic tables (question 172) are the declarative alternative. 168. A Snowflake virtual warehouse is expensive. How do you tell whether it is the right size? Read the evidence before changing the size: SELECT warehouse_name, COUNT(*) AS queries, ROUND(AVG(total_elapsed_time) / 1000, 1) AS avg_s, SUM(IFF(bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage > 0, 1, 0)) AS remote_spills, SUM(IFF(bytes_spilled_to_local_storage > 0, 1, 0)) AS local_spills, ROUND(AVG(queued_overload_time) / 1000, 1) AS avg_queued_s FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history WHERE start_time > DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) GROUP BY warehouse_name ORDER BY queries DESC; Spilling (local, and worse, remote) means queries do not fit in memory: scale up a size. Queuing with short queries means too much concurrency: scale out with a multi-cluster warehouse, not up. Long idle time between sparse queries means auto-suspend is too long. Billing is per second with a 60-second minimum each time the warehouse resumes. Poor pruning (question 165) means the query or the layout is the problem, and no size fixes it. ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1 MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3 SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD'; CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR bi_monthly WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 500 TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND; ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = bi_monthly; Put ELT, BI and ad hoc work on separate warehouses, so each can be sized and attributed on its own. 169. COPY INTO vs Snowpipe vs Snowpipe Streaming: how do files get into Snowflake? COPY INTO is a batch load you run on a warehouse. It remembers which files it loaded for 64 days and skips them, so rerunning it is safe: CREATE STAGE raw.orders_stage URL = 's3://landing/orders/' STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_landing FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON); COPY INTO raw.orders (payload, file_name, loaded_at) FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM @raw.orders_stage) ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE'; -- skip bad rows, keep going -- What failed, and why SELECT * FROM TABLE(VALIDATE(raw.orders, JOB_ID => '_last')); Snowpipe runs the same COPY automatically when a file lands, triggered by cloud storage event notifications, on Snowflake-managed serverless compute rather than your warehouse: CREATE PIPE raw.orders_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS COPY INTO raw.orders (payload, file_name, loaded_at) FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM @raw.orders_stage); SELECT SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS('raw.orders_pipe'); Snowpipe Streaming writes rows directly through an SDK or the Kafka connector, with no files at all, for latency in seconds. Choose by arrival pattern: scheduled batches use COPY INTO, files trickling in all day use Snowpipe, and event streams use Snowpipe Streaming. Thousands of tiny files load inefficiently with either file-based path; Snowflake’s guidance is files of roughly 100 to 250 MB compressed. 170. Query nested JSON in Snowflake with VARIANT and FLATTEN. Land JSON in a VARIANT column, then query it with path notation and casts: CREATE TABLE raw.orders (payload VARIANT); SELECT payload:order_id::STRING AS order_id, payload:customer.city::STRING AS city, -- nested object payload:items[0].sku::STRING AS first_sku, -- array index ARRAY_SIZE(payload:items) AS item_count FROM raw.orders; LATERAL FLATTEN turns an array into rows, one per element: SELECT o.payload:order_id::STRING AS order_id, i.index AS line_number, i.value:sku::STRING AS sku, i.value:qty::INT AS qty FROM raw.orders o, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => o.payload:items) i; Two traps: a path that does not exist returns NULL, not an error, so a typo in a field name silently produces empty columns; and without the ::STRING cast, strings come back as JSON with quotes. Flatten into typed silver tables once, rather than parsing the VARIANT in every dashboard query. 171. Zero-copy cloning, Time Travel and UNDROP: someone ran a bad UPDATE an hour ago. Recover it. Time Travel reads a table as it was: -- What did the table look like before the bad statement? SELECT * FROM core.orders BEFORE (STATEMENT => '01b2c3d4-0000-1234-0000-000000000abc'); SELECT * FROM core.orders AT (OFFSET => -3600); -- one hour ago Recover by cloning the old version and swapping it in. A clone shares the original’s micro-partitions, so it is created instantly and costs no storage until either side changes: CREATE TABLE core.orders_restored CLONE core.orders AT (OFFSET => -3600); ALTER TABLE core.orders SWAP WITH core.orders_restored; -- atomic UNDROP brings back a dropped table, schema or database within its Time Travel retention: DROP TABLE core.orders; UNDROP TABLE core.orders; Cloning a whole database is also how teams give every developer a full-size test environment in seconds: CREATE DATABASE dev_asha CLONE prod;. After the retention period ends, Fail-safe keeps the data for another 7 days, but only Snowflake support can recover from it. 172. Dynamic tables vs streams and tasks vs materialized views. A dynamic table is a query plus a freshness target.
