Snowflake refreshes it, incrementally when it can: CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE core.daily_revenue TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes' WAREHOUSE = etl_wh REFRESH_MODE = AUTO AS SELECT order_date, region, SUM(amount) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM core.orders GROUP BY order_date, region; Dynamic tables: declarative pipelines. You state the result and the maximum lag; Snowflake schedules refreshes and chains dependent dynamic tables. TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM refreshes a table only when a table that depends on it needs fresh data. Streams and tasks (question 167): imperative. Use them when you need procedural logic, side effects, or control over exactly what happens to each change. Materialized views: a single table, with restrictions (no joins), maintained automatically. Best for speeding up a repeated query on one large table. REFRESH_MODE = AUTO falls back to a full refresh when the query cannot be maintained incrementally. Check the refresh mode Snowflake chose with SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES, because a “dynamic” table that fully refreshes every 15 minutes over a large table is an expensive surprise. 173. Snowflake's three caches: why did the same query run in 50 ms and then in 40 seconds? Result cache (cloud services layer): an identical query returns the stored result with no warehouse at all, for 24 hours (each reuse extends it, up to 31 days), as long as the underlying data has not changed and the query has no non-deterministic functions such as CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(). Warehouse (local disk) cache: micro-partitions read by recent queries stay on the warehouse’s SSDs while it runs. It is lost when the warehouse suspends. Metadata: COUNT(*), MIN and MAX on a column can be answered from micro-partition metadata without scanning. ALTER SESSION SET USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE; -- turn the result cache off to benchmark honestly The 50 ms run hit the result cache. The 40-second run came after new data landed (invalidating the result cache) on a warehouse that had just resumed (an empty local cache). Benchmarks that do not account for this measure the caches, not the query. There is a cost angle too: a very short AUTO_SUSPEND saves credits but throws away the local cache every time. 174. Role-based access, masking policies and row access policies in Snowflake. Privileges go to roles, roles go to users, and roles can be granted to other roles to form a hierarchy: CREATE ROLE analyst; GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE prod TO ROLE analyst; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA prod.sales TO ROLE analyst; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA prod.sales TO ROLE analyst; GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA prod.sales TO ROLE analyst; -- tables created later GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE sysadmin; -- keep the hierarchy connected GRANT ROLE analyst TO USER ranga; Masking policy for a column: CREATE MASKING POLICY pii.email_mask AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING -> CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val ELSE REGEXP_REPLACE(val, '^[^@]+', '***') END; ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET MASKING POLICY pii.email_mask; Row access policy, driven by a mapping table so access is data, not code: CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY sec.region_policy AS (region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN -> EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sec.role_regions m WHERE m.role_name = CURRENT_ROLE() AND m.region = region); ALTER TABLE prod.sales.orders ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY sec.region_policy ON (region); FUTURE grants are the detail people miss: without them, every new table needs a new grant. IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION also covers roles inherited through the hierarchy, which CURRENT_ROLE() does not. dbt The dbt answers ran on dbt-core 1.10 with the DuckDB adapter, the same way they would on Snowflake or Databricks, with one adapter difference noted in the first answer. 175. dbt incremental models: how do they work, and what goes wrong? An incremental model builds the full table on the first run. On later runs is_incremental() is true, and the model selects only new or changed rows: -- models/fct_orders.sql {{ config( materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', incremental_strategy='delete+insert', on_schema_change='fail' ) }} select order_id, customer_id, status, amount, updated_at from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} {% if is_incremental() %} -- Look back one day so a late row with an older updated_at is not skipped. where updated_at > (select max(updated_at) - interval 1 day from {{ this }}) {% endif %} The second run brings an update to order 1, a new order 4, and a late order 5 whose updated_at (08:00 on 1 October) is older than the table’s latest (10:00). The same run with and without the lookback: with 1-day lookback -> order ids: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] without lookback -> order ids: [1, 2, 3, 4] Without the lookback, order 5 is skipped, and nothing reports it. With a unique_key, the overlap the lookback creates re-processes some rows harmlessly, and order 1 is updated in place instead of duplicated. Three things the run itself taught: Strategies depend on the adapter. DuckDB rejected merge with “The incremental strategy ‘merge’ is not valid for this adapter”, so this ran with delete+insert. Snowflake and Databricks support merge, and use it by default. Contracts constrain incremental models. With contract: {enforced: true}, dbt refused to parse the project until on_schema_change was append_new_columns or fail. A logic change does not fix history until you run dbt run --full-refresh -s fct_orders. 176. dbt snapshots and dbt tests. A snapshot implements SCD Type 2 on a source. In dbt 1.9 and later it is configured in YAML: # snapshots/customers.yml snapshots: - name: customers_snapshot relation: ref('raw_customers') config: unique_key: customer_id strategy: timestamp updated_at: updated_at After customer 10 moved from Pune to Mumbai and dbt snapshot ran again: customers_snapshot: (10, 'Pune', datetime(2026, 9, 1, 0, 0), datetime(2026, 10, 2, 0, 0)) (10, 'Mumbai', datetime(2026, 10, 2, 0, 0), None) (11, 'Delhi', datetime(2026, 9, 1, 0, 0), None) (12, 'Chennai', datetime(2026, 9, 15, 0, 0), None) dbt_valid_to closed the Pune row and the Mumbai row is current. A snapshot sees only the state at each run, so two changes between runs record only the last one. CDC catches every change; a snapshot does not. Tests are queries that must return zero rows. Generic tests are declared in YAML, alongside a model contract: # models/schema.yml models: - name: fct_orders config: contract: enforced: true columns: - name: order_id data_type: integer constraints: [{type: not_null}] data_tests: [unique, not_null] - name: customer_id data_type: integer data_tests: - not_null - relationships: arguments: {to: ref('raw_customers'), field: customer_id} - name: status data_type: varchar data_tests: - accepted_values: arguments: {values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'cancelled']} A singular test is a SQL file: -- tests/assert_no_negative_amounts.sql select * from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} where amount < 0 Done. PASS=6 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 TOTAL=6 Put unique and not_null on every model’s grain key: it is the cheapest protection against the fan-out in question 82. 177. ref vs source, materializations, and how you structure a dbt project. source() points at a raw table that dbt does not build, declared in YAML so dbt can test it and check its freshness. ref() points at another model. dbt builds the dependency graph from the ref calls, runs models in order, and swaps in the right schema per environment. # models/staging/sources.yml sources: - name: shop schema: raw loaded_at_field: _loaded_at freshness: warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour} error_after: {count: 24, period: hour} tables: - name: orders -- models/staging/stg_orders.sql (view: cheap, always current) select order_id, customer_id, lower(status) as status, cast(amount as decimal(10, 2)) as amount, cast(updated_at as timestamp) as updated_at from {{ source('shop', 'orders') }} Materializations: view for light staging models, table for small marts rebuilt each run, incremental for large facts (question 175), and ephemeral for a CTE inlined into its consumers. The usual layout: staging (one model per source table: rename, cast, nothing else), intermediate (joins and business logic), and marts (facts and dimensions for consumers). Run dbt source freshness before dbt build, so a stale source fails the run instead of publishing stale numbers. 178. Run dbt in CI without rebuilding the whole project on every pull request. “Slim CI” builds only the models a pull request changed, plus everything downstream of them, and reads unchanged parents from production: # Production's manifest.json, saved by the last prod deploy dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci state:modified+: models whose code or config changed, and the + adds their children. --defer --state: any parent that was not rebuilt is read from production instead of the empty CI schema. dbt build: runs models, tests, snapshots and seeds in dependency order, so a failing test stops its children. Write CI into its own schema per pull request, drop it when the pull request closes, and run dbt build --select state:modified+ with --fail-fast so the first broken test fails the check quickly. Data quality and observability 179. What do you monitor on a production table, and where do the alerts go? Five signals cover most incidents: freshness, volume, schema, distribution and lineage. The first four are a query each: from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone def table_health(table, ts_col, key_col, expected_cols): df = spark.read.table(table) today = df.filter(F.col(ts_col) >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), 0)) stats = df.agg(F.max(ts_col).alias("latest"), F.avg(F.col(key_col).isNull().cast("int")).alias("null_rate")).first() history = (df.filter(F.col(ts_col) >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), 28)) .groupBy(F.to_date(ts_col).alias("d")).count()) usual = history.agg(F.percentile_approx("count", 0.5).alias("median")).first()["median"] return { "fresh": stats["latest"] >= datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=6), "volume": today.count() >= 0.5 * (usual or 0), # half the usual day is suspicious "schema": set(df.columns) == set(expected_cols), "nulls": (stats["null_rate"] or 0) < 0.01, } print(table_health("orders_t", "order_ts", "customer_id", ["order_id", "customer_id", "order_ts"])) On a test table with 100 orders a day for four weeks, 30 so far today, and a missing customer_id on every fiftieth row: {'fresh': True, 'volume': False, 'schema': True, 'nulls': False} Fresh and schema pass. Volume fails because 30 is below half of the usual 100, and nulls fail because 2% of keys are missing against a 1% threshold. Run the volume check after the day’s expected load time, or it fires every morning. Lineage answers “who is affected” when a check fails (question 62). Alerts go to the team that owns the table, with the table name, the failed check, expected and actual values, and a runbook link. Page only for broken SLAs on critical tables; send a channel message for the rest. An alert that nobody acts on should be fixed or deleted, because alert fatigue hides the real one. 180. What is the write-audit-publish (WAP) pattern? Show it on Iceberg. Write new data where consumers cannot see it, audit it, and publish it atomically only if the checks pass. Iceberg branches make this a few lines. This ran on Iceberg 1.11 with Spark 3.5.9: spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.db.orders (order_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE) USING iceberg " "TBLPROPERTIES ('write.wap.enabled' = 'true')") def write_audit_publish(batch, branch): spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lake.db.orders CREATE BRANCH IF NOT EXISTS {branch}") spark.conf.set("spark.wap.branch", branch) # writes go to the branch batch.writeTo("lake.db.orders").append() spark.conf.unset("spark.wap.branch") staged = spark.read.option("branch", branch).table("lake.db.orders") bad = staged.filter("amount < 0 OR order_id IS NULL").count() print(f"{branch}: main rows={spark.table('lake.db.orders').count()}, " f"branch rows={staged.count()}, failed checks={bad}") if bad: spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lake.db.orders DROP BRANCH {branch}") # discard return "rejected" spark.sql(f"CALL lake.system.fast_forward('db.orders', 'main', '{branch}')") spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lake.db.orders DROP BRANCH {branch}") return "published" audit_1: main rows=2, branch rows=4, failed checks=0 published audit_2: main rows=4, branch rows=5, failed checks=1 rejected main rows now: [1, 2, 3, 4] While the first batch sat on audit_1, readers of main still saw 2 rows. It passed and was fast-forwarded in one commit. The second batch failed its check, so its branch was dropped and main never saw order 5. On Delta there are no branches, so write to a staging table, check it, and MERGE or INSERT into the target in one commit. In dbt, build into a separate schema and swap. The cost is the extra latency and the storage for the staged data. 181. A producer team wants to rename a column you consume. How does a data contract handle it? A data contract is a versioned specification of a dataset (schema, meaning, quality guarantees, SLA, owner) that is checked automatically in the producer’s CI, so a breaking change fails their build before it reaches you: # contracts/orders.yml, owned by the orders team dataset: sales.orders version: 2.1.0 owner: orders-team@company.com sla: {freshness_hours: 2} columns: - {name: order_id, type: string, nullable: false, unique: true} - {name: customer_id, type: string, nullable: false} - {name: amount, type: decimal(12,2), nullable: false, checks: ["amount >= 0"]} - {name: cust_id, type: string, deprecated: true, replaced_by: customer_id, remove_after: 2026-12-31} import yaml def breaking_changes(old_path, new_path): old = {c["name"]: c for c in yaml.safe_load(open(old_path))["columns"]} new = {c["name"]: c for c in yaml.safe_load(open(new_path))["columns"]} removed = [n for n in old if n not in new] retyped = [n for n in old if n in new and old[n]["type"] != new[n]["type"]] return removed + retyped # CI fails the producer's PR if this is not empty print("breaking:", breaking_changes("contracts/v1.yml", "contracts/v2.yml")) Version 2 of a test contract renamed cust_id to customer_id and changed amount from decimal(12,2) to double: breaking: ['cust_id', 'amount'] A rename is a breaking change, so the process is: add the new column, keep publishing the old one marked deprecated for an agreed period (cust_id above), tell consumers, and remove it in a new major version. Question 59 covers the consumer side. LLM and AI data pipelines These are newer. They appear in 2026 interview guides for teams that feed models or call LLMs inside pipelines. 182. Design a pipeline that processes 10,000 documents a day through an LLM, within rate limits, retries and a cost budget. Treat the model as a slow, rate-limited, metered external API. The core loop, run against a fake model that rate-limits every fourth call: import hashlib, random, time PROMPT_VERSION = "summarize-v3" MODEL = "small-model" cache = {} # in production: a table keyed by the same hash dead_letter, spent_tokens = [], 0 DAILY_TOKEN_BUDGET = 1_000 def cache_key(doc_id, text): content = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest() return f"{doc_id}:{content}:{PROMPT_VERSION}:{MODEL}" def process(doc_id, text, max_retries=5): global spent_tokens key = cache_key(doc_id, text) if key in cache: return "cached" if spent_tokens >= DAILY_TOKEN_BUDGET: return "deferred (budget)" for attempt in range(max_retries): try: out = llm.summarize(text, MODEL) break except RateLimited: time.sleep(min(0.01 * 2 ** attempt, 0.1) + random.uniform(0, 0.005)) else: dead_letter.append(doc_id) return "dead-lettered" if not isinstance(out.get("summary"), str): # validate before storing dead_letter.append(doc_id) return "invalid output" spent_tokens += out["tokens"] cache[key] = {**out, "prompt_version": PROMPT_VERSION, "model": MODEL} return "processed" first = [process(d, t) for d, t in docs.items()] # 12 documents docs["d1"] += " restated" # one document changed second = [process(d, t) for d, t in docs.items()] run 1: {'deferred (budget)': 2, 'processed': 10} run 2: {'cached': 9, 'deferred (budget)': 3} model calls: 13 | tokens spent: 1042 Idempotent and cached: the key is document ID + content hash + prompt version + model, so the second run re-used 9 results and paid only for what changed. Changing the prompt or the model invalidates exactly the right entries. Rate limits: retries with backoff and jitter absorbed the 429s. In production, size a worker pool to the provider’s request and token limits, not to the document count, and send repeat failures to a dead-letter queue. Budget: the run stopped calling the model at the budget and deferred the rest to tomorrow. The flaw the run exposed: 1,042 tokens were spent against a budget of 1,000, because the check happens before a call whose cost is only known after it. Reserve an estimate before the call (prompt tokens plus the output limit) and settle the difference afterwards, and the overshoot goes away. 183. Keep a vector index in sync with a source table of documents. This is CDC again, with an embedding step: import hashlib def chunks(doc_id, text, size=800, overlap=100): step = size - overlap for i, start in enumerate(range(0, max(len(text) - overlap, 1), step)): yield {"chunk_id": f"{doc_id}:{i}", # deterministic: same doc, same ids "doc_id": doc_id, "text": text[start:start + size]} def sync(changes, index, embed, model_version): for c in changes: # from a change feed or a hash diff if c["op"] == "delete": index.delete(filter={"doc_id": c["doc_id"]}) # the step most often forgotten continue new_hash = hashlib.sha256(c["text"].encode()).hexdigest() if index.get_doc_hash(c["doc_id"]) == new_hash: continue # unchanged: no embedding cost index.delete(filter={"doc_id": c["doc_id"]}) # replace, do not add for ch in chunks(c["doc_id"], c["text"]): index.upsert(id=ch["chunk_id"], vector=embed(ch["text"]), metadata={**ch, "doc_hash": new_hash, "model": model_version}) Detect changes with a change feed or a content hash, and re-embed only new or changed documents. Chunk deterministically, so a re-embed replaces a document’s chunks instead of adding to them. Delete first: a shorter new version has fewer chunks, and the old extra ones would linger. Propagate deletes. A document deleted at the source must leave the index, or retrieval keeps returning it. Version the embedding model. A new model needs a full re-embed into a new index, then a cutover, because vectors from two models cannot be compared. (index and embed stand for your vector store client and embedding call.) How to prepare from this list Start with the frequency table. Window functions, skew, idempotency, late data and incremental loads appear at most companies. Being solid on those five covers most rounds. Prepare by company type. For product companies, practise designing systems out loud and coding without an IDE. For services and consulting firms, know Azure Data Factory and Databricks operationally, implement SCD Type 2 from memory, and prepare the managerial stories. Answer scenarios with evidence. For every “it became slow” or “the numbers are wrong” question, the structure is the same: what changed, where you look, what you found, what you fixed, and how you verified it. That structure is what these interviews reward. Then drill by component. Once the company-tagged questions are solid, use the component section to cover the rounds your target companies run: Java or Scala for JVM-heavy teams, Snowflake and dbt for analytics-engineering roles, and system design for every senior role. Run the code, then change one thing. Every answer has the code and the output it produced. Load the sample tables, run the query, then break it on purpose: remove the tiebreaker, drop the calendar join, delete the checkpoint. Seeing the wrong answer appear is what makes the trap stick. Do not memorise answers. Interviewers change one condition (“now the key is null”, “now there is no timestamp”) and watch whether the answer adapts. Every outline above names the mechanism so you can reason from it. References Spark SQL performance tuning for AQE, join strategies and partition settings Spark configuration for memory and shuffle defaults Structured Streaming programming guide for watermarks, checkpoints and output semantics Delta Lake documentation for the transaction log, MERGE, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM Data engineering interview questions and answers for 2026 (Dataquest) for the round types and question styles used in the component section Data engineer interview questions 2026 (KORE1) for the system design follow-ups, Snowflake and backfill scenarios Data engineering interview prep 2026 (DEV Community) for the LLM-pipeline design prompt Snowflake micro-partitions and data clustering and Snowflake storage costs for Time Travel and Fail-safe dbt incremental models and dbt snapshots Apache Airflow 3 release notes for assets, DAG versioning and the removed features Java HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap API documentation PostgreSQL window functions and window call syntax for the default frame behind questions 4 and 84 Apache Iceberg branching and tagging for the write-audit-publish answer Apache Kafka documentation for partitions, consumer groups and producer idempotence Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines Python reference, expectations and AUTO CDC Auto Loader schema inference and evolution Databricks billable usage system table and query history system table Snowflake CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE Top Apache Spark interview questions for 200 Spark questions answered in depth Data modeling for data engineers for grain, SCD and fact types Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Kafka, Apache Hudi, Apache Iceberg, Apache Airflow, Apache Parquet, Apache ORC, Apache Avro and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries. Delta Lake is a trademark of the Linux Foundation. Databricks, Unity Catalog, Lakeflow and Photon are trademarks of Databricks, Inc. Azure, Synapse and Power BI are trademarks of Microsoft Corporation. BigQuery and Google Cloud are trademarks of Google LLC. Amazon S3, Amazon Kinesis and DynamoDB are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc. or its affiliates. Snowflake and Snowpipe are trademarks of Snowflake Inc. PostgreSQL is a trademark of the PostgreSQL Community Association of Canada. DuckDB is a trademark of the DuckDB Foundation. Python is a trademark of the Python Software Foundation. dbt is a trademark of dbt Labs, Inc. Java and Oracle are trademarks of Oracle and/or its affiliates. Company names are used only to identify where questions were reported.

entry.title: Apache Iceberg 1.12.0: what’s new, breaking changes, and upgrade guide

link.title: Apache Iceberg 1.12.0: what’s new, breaking changes, and upgrade guide

entry.content:
• 1. What’s new in 1.12.0
    • 1.1 Geospatial types arrive
    • 1.2 Hilbert clustering alongside Z-order
    • 1.3 Flink: equality deletes become deletion vectors
    • 1.4 Format v4 groundwork
    • 1.5 Variant, v3 interoperability, and encryption
    • 1.6 Scan planning, metrics, and maintenance
    • 1.7 Kafka Connect stops hiding failures
    • 1.8 REST catalog: protocol and operational changes
    • 1.9 Security and supply-chain work
  • 2. Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 for Java and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0
  • 3. Breaking changes
    • 3.1 Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 support removed
    • 3.2 Position deletes with row data (PDWR) cannot be written
    • 3.3 Deprecated methods removed
    • 3.4 Old S3 signer classes removed
  • 4. Migrating from 1.11 to 1.12
    • 4.1 Pre-upgrade inventory
    • 4.2 Position deletes with row data (PDWR)
    • 4.3 Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 migration
    • 4.4 Deprecated API removals
    • 4.5 Testing checklist
  • 5. Upgrade sequence in one page
  • 6. Quick reference
  • Key takeaways
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 is a substantial release: 777 commits from 142 contributors.
  • Geospatial types (geometry and geography) arrive as first-class types, stored as WKB, with Spark 4.1 supporting them end to end.
  • Hilbert-curve clustering joins Z-order as a rewrite_data_files sort strategy; benchmark before adopting.
  • Flink gains a maintenance task that converts equality deletes to deletion vectors, cutting read cost for upsert pipelines.
  • Format version 4 plumbing is everywhere in the code, but V4 is not production-ready. Do not set format-version=4 on real tables.
  • Breaking: Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 support are removed; PDWR can no longer be written, and old S3 signer classes are gone.
  • Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 for Java and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0 are separate releases. Validate Rust encryption, Variant, v3 scans, and REST API changes independently.
  • Upgrade by table behavior, not by dependency file. The PDWR and Spark 3.4 changes need a plan before you bump.

1. What’s new in 1.12.0

1.1 Geospatial types arrive

Iceberg now has first-class geometry and geography types, stored as WKB (Well-Known Binary). Both Avro and Parquet support reading and writing them with self-describing logical types. Spark 4.1 supports them end to end, including row-level DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE.

Until now, spatial data in Iceberg meant a binary or string column plus a convention your team had to remember. Native types let engines and catalogs know what the column actually holds. This is a meaningful step for teams working with location data, mapping, or any spatial analytics workload.

Behavior change to watch: GeometryType and GeographyType now include the resolved CRS (Coordinate Reference System) and edge algorithm in their toString() output. A plain geometry now prints as geometry(OGC:CRS84), and geography prints as geography(OGC:CRS84, spherical). If you have tests or tooling that compare type strings, they may need updating. The community decided to keep this change because equal types printing differently looked like a bug, and function definition IDs built from parameter type strings would otherwise treat them as different overloads.

1.2 Hilbert clustering alongside Z-order

rewrite_data_files gains a second space-filling curve. Z-order is still there, and now you can also cluster on a Hilbert curve. Hilbert curves usually keep nearby values closer together than Z-order does, which can mean tighter file-level min/max statistics when you filter on several columns at once.

-- Existing: Z-order clustering
CALL my_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.events',
  strategy => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'zorder(device_id, event_ts)'
);

-- New in 1.12: Hilbert curve clustering
CALL my_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.events',
  strategy => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'hilbert(device_id, event_ts)'
);

Important details:

  • hilbert() has no options of its own. Each column contributes its full 8-byte primitive width to the index, so Z-order knobs like var-length-contribution and max-output-size do not apply.
  • You cannot combine hilbert() with zorder() in the same sort order.
  • Do not assume Hilbert always wins. Benchmark it on your real query patterns before switching.

1.3 Flink: equality deletes become deletion vectors

This may be the most useful change for streaming teams. Flink upsert pipelines typically write equality deletes, which are cheap to write but expensive to read because every reader must join them against data files. The new ConvertEqualityDeletes maintenance task turns those into row-position deletion vectors (DVs), which readers can apply cheaply.

How it works: the Flink IcebergSink writes data files and equality deletes to a staging branch. The converter then resolves the deletes and commits the data files plus DVs to the target branch (usually main).

// Flink TableMaintenance, Iceberg 1.12
.add(ConvertEqualityDeletes.builder()
    .stagingBranch("staging")
    .equalityFieldColumns(ImmutableList.of("id"))
    .scheduleOnEqDeleteFileCount(10)
    .parallelism(4))

Requirements and caveats:

  • Requires table format version 3 or higher.
  • Does not support row lineage yet.
  • equalityFieldColumns must match the columns your writer uses.
  • The task keeps a primary-key index in Flink state; RocksDB is recommended.
  • Avoid running other continuous writers against the target branch, or conversion cycles can keep losing the commit race.

1.4 Format v4 groundwork

Iceberg 1.12 contains a lot of code labeled v4, but format version 4 is not ready for production tables. This is implementation groundwork that shows where the format is heading.

What is present in the code:

  • Relative paths in the evolving specification, and utilities for converting absolute locations to relative ones. This can make table metadata less tied to one bucket or storage prefix.
  • Parquet or Avro manifests (instead of Avro-only), which can bring richer types and reader tooling to manifest data.
  • Content-statistics structures and filters, carrying structured index and average-size information alongside tracked files.
  • Tracked-file builders and adapters, plus a v4 manifest reader.
  • A draft Mumbling Bitmap specification and a read-only implementation.
  • EntryStatus.MODIFIED and TrackingBuilder status derivation, expressing changes that do not fit the older added/existing/deleted model cleanly.

What you should not do:

  • Do not set format-version=4 on production tables.
  • Do not build application code that parses V4 structures.
  • Do not build a roadmap around draft field names.

The useful action today is to keep table movement and metadata assumptions out of application code, and follow the specification through later releases.

1.5 Variant, v3 interoperability, and encryption

Iceberg 1.12 fills in several engine paths for v3 features. Spark adds vectorized Parquet reads for Variant; Flink, Kafka Connect, and generic record writers gain Variant shredding paths. Java also strengthens v3 support for geometry and geography, row lineage, deletion vectors, and encrypted metadata. These features are useful only when every client that touches a table can interpret them. A table opening successfully is not proof that each engine supports every feature in it.

Before enabling a v3 feature, test the actual writer-reader combinations in your stack. Include schema evolution, nulls, decimal edge cases, and failure recovery. Keep the table format upgrade separate from the library upgrade so a compatibility failure has a clear cause.

1.6 Scan planning, metrics, and maintenance

The less visible changes in 1.12 may save more time than the headline features.

  • Partition-statistics scans can now project columns and apply filters, reducing the amount of metadata an optimizer must read.
  • Snapshot expiration correctly reads delete manifests in cases that previously went wrong.
  • A scan-based action removes dangling delete files.
  • RESTMetricsReporter.report() no longer blocks the calling thread, so emitting metrics cannot stall the work they describe. Still monitor queue size, delivery failures, and dropped reports.
  • Adaptive split-sizing options are documented, making it easier to balance planning overhead against parallelism.

Reader and file-format fixes cover Arrow integer-to-long promotion, dictionary-encoded INT96 timestamps with offsets, large decimals, decimal default values, end-of-file handling in object-store streams, Parquet row-group size tracking, and faster decimal handling that avoids unnecessary BigInteger conversions.

1.7 Kafka Connect stops hiding failures

Kafka Connect’s most important change is simple: commit failures are surfaced instead of silently swallowed.

  • Adds a metric for partial commit failures.
  • Bounded retries for transient commit exceptions.
  • Fixes rebalance scenarios that could commit files from a prior attempt.
  • Tracks control-topic offsets as a high-water mark.

Schema and conversion fixes cover null-valued records after a schema change, UUID conversion from Avro, decimal inference, MongoDB timestamp and date arrays, and Variant shredding. Removed deprecated members in TableReference and IcebergWriterResult may affect custom transforms or extensions at compile time.

1.8 REST catalog: protocol and operational changes

Iceberg 1.12 expands the REST catalog contract. The OpenAPI model adds table-unregister and function list/load endpoints, Variant types, catalog object identifiers, labels, and remote-signing configuration. Path segments now use RFC 3986 percent-encoding, fixing interoperability for namespaces and object names with reserved characters. Spark can delegate DROP TABLE PURGE to the REST catalog so the server can enforce storage-deletion policy.

The changes affect both compatibility and operations:

  • Check capability negotiation. Confirm that the deployed catalog server and any proxy implement the endpoints and request/response shapes your Java or Rust client needs. Do not infer support from a product name or version string alone.
  • Test names end to end. Exercise reserved characters through client, proxy, and server. Inconsistent decoding can address the wrong object or make it unreachable.
  • Review authorization. Test permissions for unregister, function metadata operations, remote signing, and purge delegation.
  • Define deletion ownership. Unregister removes the catalog registration but leaves files behind; purge requests file deletion. Record the table metadata location and recovery procedure before either operation.
  • Drill purge failures. Verify behavior when storage deletion is denied, partially succeeds, or times out. Establish whether the table remains registered, whether cleanup can be retried, and where the action is audited.
  • Check authentication refresh. Exercise OAuth token refresh, SigV4/assumed-role signing, and retries against the actual catalog implementation.

Test Java 1.12.0 and Rust 0.11.0 clients against the same catalog where both are deployed. Their independent release versions do not guarantee identical REST feature support.

1.9 Security and supply-chain work

  • The project published an Iceberg security model describing trust boundaries across catalogs, clients, storage, credentials, and metadata.
  • CI now makes vulnerability scanning blocking on relevant pull requests.
  • Jackson versions were aligned and updated to address reported vulnerabilities.
  • OAuth token refresh keeps optional parameters during non-exchange refreshes.
  • AWS REST signing can use assumed-role credentials.
  • RemoteSigningConfig implements the formalized remote signing spec, and old S3 signer classes are removed.

A library upgrade does not secure an Iceberg deployment by itself. Use the security model to review who can alter catalog metadata, who can request temporary storage credentials, who can delete files, where tokens are cached, and how audit events connect catalog actions to object-store actions.

2. Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 for Java and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0

These are companion releases in the Iceberg ecosystem, not matching version numbers for the same library. Java Iceberg 1.12.0 and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0 have independent release artifacts, APIs, and feature coverage. Upgrade the implementations separately, then validate their interaction wherever they share a catalog or table. The linked release coverage highlights end-to-end table encryption, stronger v3 reads, Variant support, row-lineage metadata, and REST catalog changes. For teams with Rust readers or writers, these can close important cross-engine gaps, but validate the final release artifacts and changelog before adopting them.

The Rust changes to review include:

  • Encryption: Rust reads and writes encrypted data, manifests, manifest lists, and Puffin files, with AES-256 support and a KMS factory integration. Test encrypted files written by Rust with Java readers, and vice versa, including key rotation and missing-key failures.
  • V3 scans: Rust adds deletion-vector decoding/application, Variant support, row-lineage metadata columns, and additional metadata columns. Test tables containing each feature with your actual catalog, storage, and other engines.
  • REST authentication: the AuthManager / AuthSession API changes authentication setup. Review OAuth2 and SigV4 configuration and confirm the client respects endpoints advertised by GET /v1/config.
  • API and behavior changes: review lazy table-property parsing, validated FileScanTask construction, write.metadata.path, and the GCS host property change. Rebuild downstream Rust applications and integration crates.
  • DataFusion: check the DataFusion version line required by the selected Rust release and track the integration’s separate release lifecycle.

The key upgrade rule is cross-engine testing. A file accepted by the Rust writer must also be readable by every Java, Spark, Flink, and query-engine client that shares the table. Test both directions before enabling new table features in production.

3. Breaking changes

This is the section to share with whoever owns your Spark and Flink jobs. Several removals land in 1.12.0, and they break code, not just deprecate it.

3.1 Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 support removed

PR #14122 removes the Spark 3.4 runtime entirely. The 1.12.0 Java artifacts support Spark 3.5, 4.0, and 4.1, with version bumps to Spark 3.5.9, 4.0.4, and 4.1.3. Spark 4.2 is excluded from the source and binary artifacts, even though its module is present on the project main branch.

Flink 2.0 support is also removed. Iceberg 1.12 adds Flink 2.2 and 2.3 while retaining Flink 1.20 and 2.1. Inventory both batch and streaming jobs, then test the exact Flink/Iceberg pair. For stateful jobs, include savepoint restore, checkpoint recovery, serializers, and commit behavior—not only compilation.

3.2 Position deletes with row data (PDWR) cannot be written

PR #17706 removes the feature the community deprecated in 1.11. The rewrite_position_delete_files and rewrite_table_path actions now fail with an explicit exception on files that still carry row data.

This was a deliberate community decision. At the August 26 sync, the group agreed that table owners should make explicit decisions about existing PDWR rather than having maintenance actions silently drop the row column.

3.3 Deprecated methods removed

  • Deprecated SparkTableUtil methods in Spark 4.0 and 4.1 are removed.
  • SparkFilters is deprecated in favor of SparkV2Filters.

3.4 Old S3 signer classes removed

PR #17627 drops deprecated AWS signer classes and properties. The new RemoteSigningConfig implementation follows the formalized remote signing spec.

4. Migrating from 1.11 to 1.12

Upgrade by table behavior, not by dependency file. The following sequence catches the failures most likely to escape a basic smoke test.

4.1 Pre-upgrade inventory

Build an engine and feature inventory before touching anything:

Item What to record  
  Engine clients Every Spark, Flink, Kafka Connect, Python, Rust, query-engine, and maintenance client that touches each catalog
  Runtime versions Spark, Flink, and other engine versions in use; flag Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0
  Iceberg library versions Current version on each client; track Java and Rust release tracks independently
  Client feature support Which readers/writers support Variant, deletion vectors, row lineage, geo types, and encryption
  Catalog client REST, Hive, Glue, JDBC, Nessie, or other
  Authentication method OAuth2, SigV4, assumed-role, or other
  REST catalog behavior Supported endpoints, path encoding, unregister/purge semantics, and server/client versions
  File I/O implementation S3, GCS, ADLS, HDFS, or other
  Table format versions V1, V2, V3 for each table
  Delete-file strategies Copy-on-write vs merge-on-read; position vs equality deletes

This inventory tells you which breaking changes affect you and which do not.

4.2 Position deletes with row data (PDWR)

If you still run V2 tables with position deletes that include row data, your maintenance jobs will start failing after the upgrade. You have two ways out.

Option A: upgrade to V3 and rewrite as deletion vectors.

-- Upgrade table format version
ALTER TABLE prod.db.trips SET TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3');

-- Then rewrite position delete files (now allowed on V3)
CALL prod.system.rewrite_position_delete_files(table => 'db.trips');

Option B: stay on V2 and let data compaction fold those deletes into data files.

-- Run data compaction to rewrite position deletes into data files
CALL prod.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.trips',
  strategy => 'sort'
);

Pick one before you upgrade, not after the first failed job.

How to find affected tables:

-- Query position deletes across tables to find PDWR
SELECT * FROM prod.db.trips.position_deletes LIMIT 10;
-- If the row column is populated, this table has PDWR

4.3 Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 migration

If any job runs Spark 3.4 or Flink 2.0, move it to a supported runtime before upgrading that integration to Iceberg 1.12.0. For Flink, the supported lines are 1.20, 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3.

Recommended path:

  1. Upgrade Spark 3.4 jobs to Spark 3.5.x first (3.5.9 is the 1.12.0 baseline). Upgrade Flink 2.0 jobs to a supported Flink line.
  2. Run engine and state-recovery tests on the new runtime.
  3. Then upgrade the Iceberg integration to 1.12.0.

Spark 4.2 users should stay on Iceberg 1.11.x until a later Iceberg release adds official 4.2 artifacts. Do not treat Flink 2.0 as supported by substituting a neighboring runtime artifact.

4.4 Deprecated API removals

Search your codebase for:

  • SparkTableUtil method calls (in Spark 4.0/4.1 projects)
  • SparkFilters usage (replace with SparkV2Filters)
  • Any code referencing removed S3 signer classes or properties

These fail at compile time, not runtime, so a full build catches them.

4.5 Testing checklist

After upgrading in staging, run these targeted tests:

Test area Why it matters
Arrow integer-to-long promotion Fixed in 1.12; verify with affected types
Dictionary-encoded INT96 timestamps with offsets Fixed in 1.12
Large decimals Fixed in 1.12
Decimal default values Fixed in 1.12
End-of-file handling in object-store streams Fixed in 1.12
Parquet row-group size tracking Fixed in 1.12
Kafka Connect commit failures Force a catalog commit failure and confirm it is reported
Kafka Connect rebalance Trigger a task rebalance during a pending commit
Kafka Connect restart Restart from a known control-topic offset
Geospatial types (if used) Verify toString() behavior change does not break tests

For Rust clients, compile against the target release and test REST authentication, metadata paths, GCS configuration, encrypted file interoperability, and v3 scans. For every shared table, verify that each active client can read all features written by the others.

For Kafka Connect specifically, the release notes recommend three forced-failure drills: make a catalog commit fail, trigger a task rebalance during a pending commit, and restart from a known control-topic offset. Confirm the connector reports the failure, avoids duplicate table data, and resumes from the expected point.

5. Upgrade sequence in one page

The order that catches the failures most likely to escape a smoke test:

  1. Build an engine and feature inventory. List every Spark, Flink, Kafka Connect, Python, Rust, query-engine, and maintenance client that touches each catalog. Record its runtime version, Iceberg library version, catalog client, authentication method, and file I/O implementation.
  2. Inventory table format versions and delete-file strategies. Any V2 table writing PDWR needs a plan before upgrade.
  3. Test the specific changes that matter to your tables. Arrow integer-to-long promotion, dictionary-encoded INT96 timestamps with offsets, large decimals, decimal default values, end-of-file handling in object-store streams, Parquet row-group size tracking.
  4. Force failure drills on Kafka Connect. Make a catalog commit fail, trigger a task rebalance during a pending commit, restart from a known control-topic offset. Confirm the connector reports the failure, avoids duplicate table data, and resumes from the expected point.

6. Quick reference

Feature Status in 1.12.0 Action required
Geospatial types Available None unless using spatial data
Hilbert clustering Available Benchmark before adopting
Flink equality-delete conversion Available Requires V3 table; read docs first
Format V4 Not production-ready Do not use format-version=4
PDWR Removed Migrate V2 tables or compact
Spark 3.4 Removed Upgrade to Spark 3.5+
Flink 2.0 Removed Upgrade to Flink 1.20, 2.1, 2.2, or 2.3
Spark 4.2 Excluded from release Stay on Iceberg 1.11.x
Old S3 signers Removed Update to RemoteSigningConfig
Kafka Connect commit failures Now surfaced Force failure drills after upgrade
Iceberg Rust 0.11 Separate client release; encryption and v3 support expanded Rebuild Rust apps and run cross-engine compatibility tests
REST catalog additions New endpoints, path encoding, and optional server-side purge Test authorization, names with reserved characters, and failure recovery

Key takeaways

Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 for Java and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0 are separate releases that reward coordinated planning. Upgrade each client deliberately, and validate shared tables and REST catalog behavior across both implementations. Geospatial types and Hilbert clustering are worth testing; Flink equality-delete conversion is worth evaluating for streaming CDC pipelines. Plan for the Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 removals, along with the PDWR maintenance boundary, before upgrading.

The V4 code is worth watching, not using. The specification work on relative paths, Parquet manifests, and content statistics shows where the format is heading, but setting format-version=4 on production tables today is not a supported path.

When you move off this release, re-check the format version range first, then the defaults in the properties table, then whether SparkProcedures has grown: procedures are the part of the surface that changes most between releases.

References

  • Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 release notes
  • Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 GitHub release
  • Dremio: Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 what’s new, breaking changes, and upgrade guide
  • Dremio: preview of upcoming Apache Iceberg 1.12 and Iceberg Rust 0.11
  • Apache Mail Archives: PDWR handling discussion
  • Apache Iceberg on LinkedIn: 1.12.0 announcement
  • Apache Hudi on Spark: the complete cheat sheet
  • Apache Iceberg on Spark: the complete cheat sheet

Trademarks

Apache Iceberg, Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Apache Hive, Apache Parquet, Apache Avro, Apache Hudi, Apache Polaris (incubating) and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries. Delta Lake is a trademark of the Linux Foundation.

Use the security model to review who can alter catalog metadata, who can request temporary storage credentials, who can delete files, where tokens are cached, and how audit events connect catalog actions to object-store actions. 2. Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 for Java and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0 These are companion releases in the Iceberg ecosystem, not matching version numbers for the same library. Java Iceberg 1.12.0 and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0 have independent release artifacts, APIs, and feature coverage. Upgrade the implementations separately, then validate their interaction wherever they share a catalog or table. The linked release coverage highlights end-to-end table encryption, stronger v3 reads, Variant support, row-lineage metadata, and REST catalog changes. For teams with Rust readers or writers, these can close important cross-engine gaps, but validate the final release artifacts and changelog before adopting them. The Rust changes to review include: Encryption: Rust reads and writes encrypted data, manifests, manifest lists, and Puffin files, with AES-256 support and a KMS factory integration. Test encrypted files written by Rust with Java readers, and vice versa, including key rotation and missing-key failures. V3 scans: Rust adds deletion-vector decoding/application, Variant support, row-lineage metadata columns, and additional metadata columns. Test tables containing each feature with your actual catalog, storage, and other engines. REST authentication: the AuthManager / AuthSession API changes authentication setup. Review OAuth2 and SigV4 configuration and confirm the client respects endpoints advertised by GET /v1/config. API and behavior changes: review lazy table-property parsing, validated FileScanTask construction, write.metadata.path, and the GCS host property change. Rebuild downstream Rust applications and integration crates. DataFusion: check the DataFusion version line required by the selected Rust release and track the integration’s separate release lifecycle. The key upgrade rule is cross-engine testing. A file accepted by the Rust writer must also be readable by every Java, Spark, Flink, and query-engine client that shares the table. Test both directions before enabling new table features in production. 3. Breaking changes This is the section to share with whoever owns your Spark and Flink jobs. Several removals land in 1.12.0, and they break code, not just deprecate it. 3.1 Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 support removed PR #14122 removes the Spark 3.4 runtime entirely. The 1.12.0 Java artifacts support Spark 3.5, 4.0, and 4.1, with version bumps to Spark 3.5.9, 4.0.4, and 4.1.3. Spark 4.2 is excluded from the source and binary artifacts, even though its module is present on the project main branch. Flink 2.0 support is also removed. Iceberg 1.12 adds Flink 2.2 and 2.3 while retaining Flink 1.20 and 2.1. Inventory both batch and streaming jobs, then test the exact Flink/Iceberg pair. For stateful jobs, include savepoint restore, checkpoint recovery, serializers, and commit behavior—not only compilation. 3.2 Position deletes with row data (PDWR) cannot be written PR #17706 removes the feature the community deprecated in 1.11. The rewrite_position_delete_files and rewrite_table_path actions now fail with an explicit exception on files that still carry row data. This was a deliberate community decision. At the August 26 sync, the group agreed that table owners should make explicit decisions about existing PDWR rather than having maintenance actions silently drop the row column. 3.3 Deprecated methods removed Deprecated SparkTableUtil methods in Spark 4.0 and 4.1 are removed. SparkFilters is deprecated in favor of SparkV2Filters. 3.4 Old S3 signer classes removed PR #17627 drops deprecated AWS signer classes and properties. The new RemoteSigningConfig implementation follows the formalized remote signing spec. 4. Migrating from 1.11 to 1.12 Upgrade by table behavior, not by dependency file. The following sequence catches the failures most likely to escape a basic smoke test. 4.1 Pre-upgrade inventory Build an engine and feature inventory before touching anything: Item What to record Engine clients Every Spark, Flink, Kafka Connect, Python, Rust, query-engine, and maintenance client that touches each catalog Runtime versions Spark, Flink, and other engine versions in use; flag Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 Iceberg library versions Current version on each client; track Java and Rust release tracks independently Client feature support Which readers/writers support Variant, deletion vectors, row lineage, geo types, and encryption Catalog client REST, Hive, Glue, JDBC, Nessie, or other Authentication method OAuth2, SigV4, assumed-role, or other REST catalog behavior Supported endpoints, path encoding, unregister/purge semantics, and server/client versions File I/O implementation S3, GCS, ADLS, HDFS, or other Table format versions V1, V2, V3 for each table Delete-file strategies Copy-on-write vs merge-on-read; position vs equality deletes This inventory tells you which breaking changes affect you and which do not. 4.2 Position deletes with row data (PDWR) If you still run V2 tables with position deletes that include row data, your maintenance jobs will start failing after the upgrade. You have two ways out. Option A: upgrade to V3 and rewrite as deletion vectors. -- Upgrade table format version ALTER TABLE prod.db.trips SET TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3'); -- Then rewrite position delete files (now allowed on V3) CALL prod.system.rewrite_position_delete_files(table => 'db.trips'); Option B: stay on V2 and let data compaction fold those deletes into data files. -- Run data compaction to rewrite position deletes into data files CALL prod.system.rewrite_data_files( table => 'db.trips', strategy => 'sort' ); Pick one before you upgrade, not after the first failed job. How to find affected tables: -- Query position deletes across tables to find PDWR SELECT * FROM prod.db.trips.position_deletes LIMIT 10; -- If the row column is populated, this table has PDWR 4.3 Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 migration If any job runs Spark 3.4 or Flink 2.0, move it to a supported runtime before upgrading that integration to Iceberg 1.12.0. For Flink, the supported lines are 1.20, 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3. Recommended path: Upgrade Spark 3.4 jobs to Spark 3.5.x first (3.5.9 is the 1.12.0 baseline). Upgrade Flink 2.0 jobs to a supported Flink line. Run engine and state-recovery tests on the new runtime. Then upgrade the Iceberg integration to 1.12.0. Spark 4.2 users should stay on Iceberg 1.11.x until a later Iceberg release adds official 4.2 artifacts. Do not treat Flink 2.0 as supported by substituting a neighboring runtime artifact. 4.4 Deprecated API removals Search your codebase for: SparkTableUtil method calls (in Spark 4.0/4.1 projects) SparkFilters usage (replace with SparkV2Filters) Any code referencing removed S3 signer classes or properties These fail at compile time, not runtime, so a full build catches them. 4.5 Testing checklist After upgrading in staging, run these targeted tests: Test area Why it matters Arrow integer-to-long promotion Fixed in 1.12; verify with affected types Dictionary-encoded INT96 timestamps with offsets Fixed in 1.12 Large decimals Fixed in 1.12 Decimal default values Fixed in 1.12 End-of-file handling in object-store streams Fixed in 1.12 Parquet row-group size tracking Fixed in 1.12 Kafka Connect commit failures Force a catalog commit failure and confirm it is reported Kafka Connect rebalance Trigger a task rebalance during a pending commit Kafka Connect restart Restart from a known control-topic offset Geospatial types (if used) Verify toString() behavior change does not break tests For Rust clients, compile against the target release and test REST authentication, metadata paths, GCS configuration, encrypted file interoperability, and v3 scans. For every shared table, verify that each active client can read all features written by the others. For Kafka Connect specifically, the release notes recommend three forced-failure drills: make a catalog commit fail, trigger a task rebalance during a pending commit, and restart from a known control-topic offset. Confirm the connector reports the failure, avoids duplicate table data, and resumes from the expected point. 5. Upgrade sequence in one page The order that catches the failures most likely to escape a smoke test: Build an engine and feature inventory. List every Spark, Flink, Kafka Connect, Python, Rust, query-engine, and maintenance client that touches each catalog. Record its runtime version, Iceberg library version, catalog client, authentication method, and file I/O implementation. Inventory table format versions and delete-file strategies. Any V2 table writing PDWR needs a plan before upgrade. Test the specific changes that matter to your tables. Arrow integer-to-long promotion, dictionary-encoded INT96 timestamps with offsets, large decimals, decimal default values, end-of-file handling in object-store streams, Parquet row-group size tracking. Force failure drills on Kafka Connect. Make a catalog commit fail, trigger a task rebalance during a pending commit, restart from a known control-topic offset. Confirm the connector reports the failure, avoids duplicate table data, and resumes from the expected point. 6. Quick reference Feature Status in 1.12.0 Action required Geospatial types Available None unless using spatial data Hilbert clustering Available Benchmark before adopting Flink equality-delete conversion Available Requires V3 table; read docs first Format V4 Not production-ready Do not use format-version=4 PDWR Removed Migrate V2 tables or compact Spark 3.4 Removed Upgrade to Spark 3.5+ Flink 2.0 Removed Upgrade to Flink 1.20, 2.1, 2.2, or 2.3 Spark 4.2 Excluded from release Stay on Iceberg 1.11.x Old S3 signers Removed Update to RemoteSigningConfig Kafka Connect commit failures Now surfaced Force failure drills after upgrade Iceberg Rust 0.11 Separate client release; encryption and v3 support expanded Rebuild Rust apps and run cross-engine compatibility tests REST catalog additions New endpoints, path encoding, and optional server-side purge Test authorization, names with reserved characters, and failure recovery Key takeaways Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 for Java and Iceberg Rust 0.11.0 are separate releases that reward coordinated planning. Upgrade each client deliberately, and validate shared tables and REST catalog behavior across both implementations. Geospatial types and Hilbert clustering are worth testing; Flink equality-delete conversion is worth evaluating for streaming CDC pipelines. Plan for the Spark 3.4 and Flink 2.0 removals, along with the PDWR maintenance boundary, before upgrading. The V4 code is worth watching, not using. The specification work on relative paths, Parquet manifests, and content statistics shows where the format is heading, but setting format-version=4 on production tables today is not a supported path. When you move off this release, re-check the format version range first, then the defaults in the properties table, then whether SparkProcedures has grown: procedures are the part of the surface that changes most between releases. References Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 release notes Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 GitHub release Dremio: Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 what’s new, breaking changes, and upgrade guide Dremio: preview of upcoming Apache Iceberg 1.12 and Iceberg Rust 0.11 Apache Mail Archives: PDWR handling discussion Apache Iceberg on LinkedIn: 1.12.0 announcement Apache Hudi on Spark: the complete cheat sheet Apache Iceberg on Spark: the complete cheat sheet Trademarks Apache Iceberg, Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Apache Hive, Apache Parquet, Apache Avro, Apache Hudi, Apache Polaris (incubating) and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries. Delta Lake is a trademark of the Linux Foundation.

entry.title: Data Modeling for Data Engineers: From Foundations to Lakehouse Design

link.title: Data Modeling for Data Engineers: From Foundations to Lakehouse Design

entry.content:

      • Second normal form (2NF)

    • 2.2 Dimensional modeling core: fact tables vs. dimension tables
      • 2.2.1 Choose the fact-table shape
      • 2.2.2 Choose a serving model for its consumers
    • 2.3 Schema topologies: star schema vs. snowflake schema
    • 2.4 Data Vault 2.0: hubs, links, and satellites
