Writing the contract down per layer is what stops the labels from turning into three copies of the same table: Bronze Silver Gold Holds Source-shaped records plus ingestion metadata Typed, deduplicated, conformed detail Facts, dimensions and serving aggregates Grain One row per received record One row per business entity or event Declared per table Write pattern Append only MERGE by business key and source position MERGE, or overwrite of affected partitions Schema Loose: raw payload plus envelope Enforced and versioned Published contract with an owner Retention Long enough to replay any downstream bug As needed by marts and auditing As agreed with consumers Rebuilt from The source (often impossible) Bronze Silver Readers Platform engineers, replay jobs Data engineers, data scientists Analysts, BI, applications Typical test Source positions contiguous, nothing dropped Duplicate, reject and null counts Grain, coverage and measure reconciliation Read the “Rebuilt from” row as the reason for the whole pattern. Silver and gold can be recomputed after a logic fix because bronze still holds what arrived. Bronze usually cannot be recomputed, because the source has moved on. That is why bronze retention is the setting to argue about, not the number of layers. How each table format implements the writes. The pattern is format neutral, but the silver upsert is where the formats differ most: Layer write Apache Iceberg Apache Hudi Delta Lake Bronze append INSERT INTO or append insert or bulk_insert operation append mode Silver upsert by key MERGE INTO upsert, with a record key and a precombine (ordering) field that keeps the newest version MERGE INTO Incremental read of silver Incremental read between snapshots (appends only) Incremental query from a commit instant Change data feed Gold refresh MERGE INTO, or dynamic partition overwrite upsert, or insert_overwrite MERGE INTO, or replaceWhere Hudi’s ordering field resolves two versions of the same key inside the write itself, so an out-of-order CDC batch does not need a separate deduplication step. Iceberg and Delta leave that to the MERGE condition, as in the s.lsn > t.source_lsn guard of section 3.2. The incremental-read row decides how cheaply gold can follow silver: Iceberg’s incremental read returns only appended rows, so a silver table that is updated in place needs a full or partition-level re-read, or a changelog view, instead. Common anti-patterns. Three copies of everything. Materializing every source table three times triples storage and commits without adding a recovery point. Skip a layer when it adds no new contract. Gold as a synonym for aggregated. A detailed fact_order_line is gold if it is the published contract; an aggregate built for one dashboard may not deserve a permanent table at all. Bronze with short retention. If bronze keeps seven days and a silver bug is found after thirty, there is nothing to replay from. Size retention to the time it takes to notice a defect, not to storage cost alone. Silver as a dumping ground. Silver without enforced keys and types pushes cleansing into every gold job, so each mart cleans differently. Layers per team instead of per contract. Bronze, silver and gold describe data quality, not organizational ownership; ownership belongs to each table’s contract (see the data mesh discussion in section 4.2). 3.4 Schema evolution and data contracts In plain terms. A data contract is the promise a producer makes to its consumers: these columns, with these types and meanings, changed only by these rules. Schema evolution is how a table changes shape without breaking the people who read it. A schema contract is more than a list of field names. It should state field types, nullability, meaning, units, valid values, key semantics, event-time meaning, privacy classification, and compatibility expectations. Version the contract and identify an owner who can approve changes. Adding a nullable field is often compatible, depending on the consumer. Ask what null means for old rows, and which contract version adds the field. Renaming a field is not automatically compatible. Ask whether it is the same semantic field or a new definition, and provide a migration alias or a transition period. Widening a numeric type is often compatible if values keep their meaning. Ask whether the target engine supports the widening, and whether every producer can write it. Narrowing or reinterpreting a type is usually breaking. Plan the backfill, the validation, and the consumer migration. Changing a metric definition is semantically breaking even when the SQL type does not change. Version the metric or publish a new one, because schema compatibility cannot preserve meaning. Parquet readers may infer different schemas from different files. Spark supports schema merging, but it is disabled by default because collecting schemas across files has a cost. For table formats, schema and partition evolution are metadata operations with format-specific compatibility rules. Validate the logical contract before accepting either change. A contract can be as small as a reviewed YAML file next to the pipeline code. What matters is that each line is something a test can check: dataset: gold.fact_order_line owner: sales-data-team version: 2 grain: one row per product line on an accepted customer order primary_key: [order_id, line_number] columns: - {name: order_id, type: string, nullable: false} - {name: line_number, type: int, nullable: false} - {name: order_date_key, type: int, nullable: false} - {name: customer_sk, type: int, nullable: false, references: dim_customer.customer_sk, unknown_member: -1} - {name: product_sk, type: int, nullable: false, references: dim_product.product_sk, unknown_member: -1} - {name: net_amount, type: decimal(12,2), nullable: false, rule: gross_amount - discount_amount, currency: USD} compatibility: backward # add nullable columns only; renames need a new version freshness: loaded by 06:00 UTC daily 3.5 Hands-on: build the fact table end to end The example starts with curated order lines and customer change records. It derives end-exclusive customer validity ranges, resolves the customer version at order time, joins the product dimension, and creates one fact row per order line. It uses in-memory fixtures and local Spark; it does not write to the playground’s shared Hive or MinIO tables. order to customer version 101 and the February order to version 102. The unknown source IDs still produce a fact row, using the explicit unknown key -1. The four input lines remain four fact rows, and the reconciled net amount is 56.00. This is a batch build from already curated source rows, not a complete CDC ingestion framework. In production, deduplicate replayed events by a source sequence or version before building dimensions and facts. If the source only exposes current state, it cannot reconstruct changes that happened between polls; use its change log or another history source when those changes matter. 3.6 Production failures: where models lie A join changes the grain Suppose one order line joins to two customer records because the Type 2 join uses only customer_id. Its quantity and revenue are now counted twice. Add an explicit uniqueness test for the fact key, and check that each fact matches at most one version of each dimension. A total that still looks plausible is not evidence that the join is correct. The SCD demo in section 3.1 shows the exact numbers: 2 rows become 4, and 29.00 becomes 58.00. A late dimension arrives after its fact An order can arrive before its customer record, or a customer history update can be delayed. Mapping the fact immediately to an unknown key preserves the row, but may leave it associated with the unknown member permanently. Track which unknown reason was used, define a repair or restatement policy, and reprocess the affected facts when the dimension arrives. “Use key -1” is a referential-integrity technique, not a late-arrival strategy by itself. A common repair is the inferred member: when the fact arrives, insert a placeholder dimension row for the new business key with a real surrogate key and a flag such as is_inferred = true. The fact references that key immediately. When the real customer record arrives, update the placeholder’s attributes in place, typically as a Type 1 change, and clear the flag. No fact needs rewriting, because its surrogate key was right from the start. An event timestamp is mistaken for valid time updated_at may mean when the source row was last written, while a business effective date says when the new value became true. Those clocks answer different questions. If a retroactive correction is effective on January 1 but arrives on February 10, record both the business-valid interval and the warehouse observation time when audit requirements call for bitemporal history. Do not silently substitute ingestion time for business time. Retries make “append” mean duplicate At-least-once delivery can replay a batch after a timeout. Appending blindly turns one order line into two rows. Define an idempotency key at the business grain, keep source offsets or batch IDs as operational metadata, and choose whether corrections update a current-state fact or create explicit adjustment events. A table format’s atomic commit does not automatically make a pipeline idempotent. A hard delete forgets that a key ever existed The CDC demo in section 3.2 shows it: after a physical delete, a late event older than the delete is applied as a fresh insert, and a deleted customer returns. Keep tombstones for at least the maximum delivery lateness. A many-to-many bridge inflates measures If an order is attributed to multiple campaigns or a customer belongs to multiple households, joining the bridge to the fact can repeat revenue. Use the bridge only with a documented filter or allocation rule. If sales must be allocated, store allocation weights whose sum is one for each fact at the appropriate time and test that invariant. A changing definition masquerades as a schema change Renaming a column is not the same as changing what it means. “Net sales” might exclude shipping in one definition and include it in another. Schema evolution can safely add or rename physical fields in formats that track field identity, but it cannot decide whether old and new metric definitions can be summed. Version semantic contracts or publish a new measure when the business meaning changes. Part 3 interview questions 1. Explain SCD Types 0, 1, 2 and 3 with one customer. Customer C01 moves from Gold to Silver. Type 0 keeps Gold forever. Type 1 overwrites it to Silver, so past sales now report as Silver. Type 2 closes the Gold row (valid_to = 2025-02-01, is_current = false) and inserts a Silver row with a new surrogate key, so past sales stay Gold. Type 3 keeps Silver in segment and Gold in previous_segment, which gives one step of history. Say that the type is chosen per attribute: email can be Type 1 while segment is Type 2 in the same table. 2. How do you implement SCD Type 2 with a single MERGE? Stage each changed record twice. One copy has merge_key = customer_id, matches the current version, and the WHEN MATCHED branch closes it by setting valid_to and is_current = false. The other copy has merge_key = NULL, so it never matches, and the WHEN NOT MATCHED branch inserts it as the new current version. New customers appear only once with a real key and are inserted. Because it is one MERGE, Iceberg or Delta commits it atomically, as section 3.1 shows. 3. Why use half-open intervals [valid_from, valid_to) for Type 2? With closed intervals, an event exactly on the boundary timestamp matches both the old and the new version and is counted twice. Half-open intervals make valid_to of one version equal valid_from of the next, and a >=/< predicate matches exactly one. Use a far-future valid_to such as 9999-12-31 rather than NULL, so the same predicate works for the current row. 4. What is the difference between log-based, trigger-based and query-based CDC? Log-based reads the database’s write-ahead log or binlog. It sees every insert, update and delete in commit order with little load on the source, but needs log retention and replication privileges. Trigger-based writes changes to an audit table from triggers, adding cost to every source transaction. Query-based polls WHERE updated_at > last_watermark. It is simple but misses hard deletes and intermediate updates, and breaks on late or equal timestamps. 5. How do you make a CDC pipeline idempotent? Carry the source log position (LSN, binlog offset, or Kafka offset) with every event. Deduplicate on (key, position), keep only the latest position per key in each batch, and apply with a MERGE whose update and delete branches require source.position > target.position. Then a replayed batch or an older straggler is a no-op. Keep tombstones rather than hard deletes if late events are possible, or a deleted key can be resurrected. 6. What is a late-arriving dimension, and how do you handle it? A fact arrives referencing a business key the dimension does not have yet. Either map it to an unknown member (-1) and reprocess later, or insert an inferred member: a placeholder dimension row with a real surrogate key and is_inferred = true, filled in when the real record arrives. The inferred member avoids rewriting facts. The opposite case, a late-arriving fact, needs the Type 2 lookup on the fact’s event time, not its arrival time. 7. Describe bronze, silver and gold. Is gold always aggregated? Bronze keeps raw, source-faithful records plus ingestion metadata, for replay and audit. Silver holds validated, typed, deduplicated detail. Gold publishes business-facing models: facts, dimensions and aggregates. Gold is not necessarily aggregated; a detailed fact_order_line is a gold table. The labels do not define grain, so every table still declares one. 8. What makes a schema change breaking? Removing or renaming a field, narrowing a type, changing nullability from optional to required, or changing what a field means. Adding a nullable field is usually compatible. A changed metric definition is semantically breaking even if the schema is identical, so it needs a new version or a new name. 9. When would you choose log-based CDC over query-based CDC? When the consumer needs every committed change in commit order: hard deletes must propagate, a Type 2 dimension or audit trail needs intermediate states, freshness is seconds, or polling scans would load a busy primary. Query-based CDC sees only the state at each poll, so a row inserted and deleted between two polls never appears, and an updated_at high-water mark can skip a long transaction that committed late with an earlier timestamp. Choose query-based when log access is impossible, rows are insert-only or soft-deleted, and minutes to hours of latency are fine. Mention the cost of log-based CDC: a stalled PostgreSQL replication slot retains WAL on the primary until someone acts. 10. What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve? The dual-write problem. If a service updates its database and then publishes to Kafka, a crash between the two loses or invents an event. With an outbox, the service writes the business row and an event row in one local transaction, and log-based CDC publishes the outbox table. The event exists if and only if the transaction committed, and consumers receive a domain event such as OrderPaid rather than inferring intent from column diffs. Part 4: Architectural Paradigms & Governance The model sits inside a platform and an organization. Processing topology decides how results are refreshed; ownership decides who defines and supports the contract; metadata makes its meaning and dependencies discoverable. None of these choices replaces the need to define a correct row grain. 4.1 Data processing topologies: Lambda architecture vs. Kappa architecture In plain terms. Lambda runs two pipelines, a slow, complete batch one and a fast, approximate streaming one, and merges their answers. Kappa runs one streaming pipeline and, when the logic changes, replays the stored event log through the new version. Both patterns address the tension between low-latency updates and the ability to recompute results after code or business rules change. Lambda architecture: two paths, merged at read time Nathan Marz described Lambda around one idea: keep an immutable master dataset, and treat every view as a function of it that can be recomputed. Batch recomputation is complete and correct but slow, so a second, faster path covers the hours the batch has not reached yet. +--------------------------------+ +-----> | batch layer | | | immutable master dataset | | | full recompute (Spark, Hive) | | +---------------+----------------+ | | batch views (complete up to T) events ------+ v (Kafka) | +-------------+ | | serving / |---> query = batch(<=T) | | merge | + speed(>T) | +-------------+ | ^ | +---------------+----------------+ +-----> | speed layer | | incremental, recent data only | | (Flink, Spark Streaming) | +--------------------------------+ Step by step: Every event is appended to the master dataset and, at the same time, delivered to the speed layer. The batch layer periodically recomputes its views from the whole master dataset, so each run is complete up to a cut-off time T. The speed layer maintains incremental views only for events after T. Its state is disposable: when the next batch run covers those events, that part of the speed view is dropped. The serving layer answers a query by merging the batch view up to T with the speed view after T. The mechanism that makes Lambda correct is step 3. An error in the speed layer lives only until the next batch run overwrites it, so the fast path is allowed to be approximate. This is why early Lambda systems accepted probabilistic structures such as HyperLogLog in the speed layer. The cost is that the same business rule exists twice, written for two engines with different semantics for time, joins and late data. When the batch view and the speed view disagree at the T boundary, the dashboard shows a visible jump each time the batch completes. Every rule change means two deployments and a reconciliation test between them. Kappa architecture: one path, replayed Jay Kreps proposed Kappa in Questioning the Lambda Architecture as a response to that duplication: if the stream processor can reprocess history, there is no need for a separate batch system. retained, replayable log (Kafka) events ---> [ o0 | o1 | o2 | ............................ | oN ] | | | replay from offset 0 | live tail v v +-------------+ +-------------+ | job v2 | catches up, then tails | job v1 | | (new logic) | | (current) | +------+------+ +------+------+ | | v v output_v2 -- reconcile, then switch --> output_v1 readers, drop output_v1 (readers today) Step by step: All events go to one log, retained long enough to cover the longest rebuild window. Kafka keeps it with time-based retention, log compaction for keyed state, or tiered storage that offloads old segments to object storage. One streaming job (v1) consumes the log and maintains the output. To change the logic, start job v2 as a new consumer group from the earliest retained offset, writing to a new output table. When v2 has caught up and its output reconciles against v1, point readers at v2’s output (a view swap or a catalog pointer) and stop v1. The mechanism that makes Kappa correct is that the log is the system of record and the output is a cache derived from it. A bug fix is a replay, not a patch to two code bases. The cost moves from duplicated code to replay capacity and retention. Replaying a year of events through a stateful job needs enough parallelism to catch up in an acceptable time, enough state backend capacity for the joins and windows the job keeps, and enough log retention to start from. A replay also needs deterministic logic: if v2 reads a dimension “as of now” while processing year-old events, its output differs from what v1 produced at the time. Lambda vs. Kappa side by side Dimension Lambda Kappa Processing paths Batch and speed, merged at serving One streaming path Business logic Written twice Written once Reprocessing Batch recompute from the master dataset Replay the log through a new job version Source of truth Immutable master dataset (files) Retained log, possibly archived to object storage Correctness of recent data Approximate until the next batch run As correct as the streaming job Operational cost Two engines, two deployments, reconciliation Log retention, replay capacity, state size Typical failure Batch and speed views disagree at the boundary Retention shorter than the rebuild window Fits best Complex batch-only logic, heavy ML features, legacy Hadoop estates Event-driven products, CDC pipelines, uniform logic Which one to choose Choose Kappa when the events can be retained, in the log or archived from it, for as long as the longest rebuild you will need, when one engine can express all the logic, and when replay capacity is affordable. Most CDC- and event-driven pipelines fit here. Choose Lambda when part of the logic can only run as a full batch computation, for example a model retrained over all history or a join against data that arrives only as daily files, and the business also needs sub-minute views of the same metric. Accept the second code path knowingly, and test the boundary between the two views. The lakehouse blurs the line. Table formats provide incremental reads (Hudi incremental queries, Delta change data feed, Iceberg incremental reads of appended snapshots), so one Spark or Flink job can process new commits continuously, while the same code runs a bounded backfill over older partitions. That is Kappa’s single code path with a table, rather than only the log, as the replayable history. The table becomes the long-term archive that the log’s retention could not afford, and the log only needs to hold data until it is committed. Kappa is not “streaming instead of batch” in every system. A bounded historical replay is still a batch-shaped workload even if it uses the same stream processor and code. If a source log retains only a few days, an arbitrary multi-year rebuild cannot be performed from that log alone. Keep an immutable archive or another reconstruction source when the business requires longer reprocessing windows. For the sales model, separate arrival time from business event time. A late sale must join to a customer version valid at order_ts, not to the dimension row that happened to be current when the stream processed it. A replay must produce the same fact key and measure or write into a versioned output and switch readers after reconciliation. 4.2 Decentralized vs. centralized: data mesh vs. data fabric In plain terms. Data mesh is about people: each business domain owns and publishes its data as a product. Data fabric is about technology: a connected metadata and integration layer that lets you find and access data wherever it lives. A company can use both. Data mesh is primarily a way to organize analytical ownership around business domains and data products. Data fabric is a broad architectural approach for connecting, governing, and discovering data across systems, often through shared metadata and integration capabilities. They describe different axes and can coexist; neither is a single product or a table schema. Who owns and serves a domain dataset? In a data mesh, the domain team owns the data product and its quality interface. In a data fabric, shared capabilities connect assets across owners and systems. What is centralized? A mesh centralizes platform capabilities and federated interoperability rules. A fabric may centralize metadata, integration, governance, and access automation. What is the main engineering risk? In a mesh, every domain invents incompatible keys, definitions, and SLOs. In a fabric, a central catalog or virtualization layer promises semantics it cannot enforce. What does it mean for the model? A mesh publishes a documented schema, owner, keys, and change policy per product. A fabric keeps source, logical, and physical metadata discoverable across platforms. Centralize what creates interoperability: identity domains, schema compatibility policy, security classifications, and shared dimensions where their definitions truly match. Decentralize domain-specific meaning and delivery ownership. If two domains both use a field called customer_id, that name alone does not prove they identify the same entity. Data mesh rests on four principles from its original description: domain ownership, data as a product, a self-serve data platform, and federated computational governance. The fourth is the one modeling depends on, because it is where shared keys and conformed dimensions are agreed. 4.3 Metadata and data lineage: the nervous system of a platform In plain terms. Metadata is data about data: what a column means, who owns the table, when it last loaded. Lineage is the family tree: which sources and jobs produced this table, and which dashboards depend on it. Metadata describes data and how it is operated. At minimum, distinguish: Structural metadata: names, types, nullability, keys, and schema versions. Business metadata: definitions, owner, domain, sensitivity, and allowed use. Operational metadata: freshness, row counts, quality results, source offsets, and failed runs. Lineage: directed relationships from source datasets through jobs and runs to output datasets. Lineage answers different questions from a catalog. A catalog helps find and understand a dataset; lineage explains where it came from and which consumers may be affected by a change. OpenLineage models jobs, runs, input datasets, output datasets, and extensible facets. A production contract should capture the source version/offset and model version that produced a snapshot, not just the code repository name. postgres.shop.orders ──> job: cdc_ingest ──> bronze.order_events │ job: build_silver v dim_customer ──────────> job: build_fact ──> gold.fact_order_line ──> revenue dashboard Impact analysis walks right: change orders.amount -> who breaks? Root-cause analysis walks left: dashboard is wrong -> which job, which run? Metadata is useful only if it is emitted and maintained. Define stable dataset identifiers across environments, include schema and quality facets, and connect run IDs to orchestrator logs. For regulated data, lineage records do not replace access control or retention policy; they make those policies and their effects auditable. Part 4 interview questions 1. Lambda vs Kappa: which would you pick for a new platform? Kappa when the source events can be retained (in Kafka with long retention, or archived to object storage) for as long as the longest rebuild window, and one engine can serve both live processing and replay. Lambda when a batch recompute must use data or logic the stream cannot, and you accept maintaining the same rules twice and reconciling them. Most modern lakehouse designs land close to Kappa, with incremental processing on table formats. 2. Data mesh vs data fabric: are they alternatives? No. Mesh is an organizational model in which domains own data products. Fabric is a technical layer of shared metadata, integration and access automation. A mesh still needs federated governance for shared keys and contracts, and a fabric can provide the discovery and policy tooling for it. 3. What is data lineage, and how would you use it during an incident? Lineage is the graph from source datasets through jobs and runs to outputs. During an incident, walk upstream from the wrong dashboard to find which job run changed the data and what its inputs were. Before a change, walk downstream to list every consumer that will be affected. Column-level lineage narrows this from tables to fields. 4. Event time vs processing time: why does a model care? Event time is when the business event happened; processing time is when the pipeline saw it. Type 2 lookups, daily partitions and late-data handling must use event time, or a late order is attributed to the wrong customer version and the wrong day. Keep both: processing time is useful for audits and freshness monitoring. 5. How do you deploy a logic change in a Kappa pipeline without downtime? Start the new job version as a new consumer group from the earliest retained offset, writing to a new output table, while the old job keeps serving. When the new job has caught up to the live tail, reconcile the two outputs on counts and key measures, then switch readers with a view or catalog pointer and stop the old job. Preconditions: the log (or its archive) covers the rebuild window, the logic is deterministic on replay, so dimensions are looked up as of event time, and there is enough capacity to catch up in time. 6. Why is the speed layer in Lambda allowed to be approximate? Because its output is temporary. Each batch run recomputes the views from the immutable master dataset up to a cut-off time, and the speed layer’s results for that period are discarded. An error in the fast path therefore lives only until the next batch completes. The price is that the same rule exists in two engines, and the two views can disagree at the boundary. Part 5: Database Performance & System Scaling Performance work starts from the physical execution plan and the data shape, not from a list of fashionable techniques. Indexes, partitions, sort order, and sharding solve different problems and carry different write and operating costs. 5.1 Indexing mechanics: B-trees, bitmaps, hash, clustered vs. non-clustered In plain terms. An index is the index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find “Iceberg”, you look it up and jump to page 212. It speeds up reads, but every new page added to the book means updating the index too. An index is an access structure that helps an engine find rows without examining every data page. Its useful operators depend on the index type and engine. B-tree Fits equality, ranges, and ordered scans on sortable values. It adds write amplification and storage, and a low-selectivity predicate may still scan the table. Hash Fits equality lookups in engines that support hash indexes. It cannot serve a range or an ordered scan. Bitmap Fits low-cardinality analytic predicates in engines that implement bitmap indexes. Update and concurrency behavior are engine-specific, so it is not a general OLTP index. GIN and inverted indexes Fit membership tests on arrays, tokens, and other multi-valued structures. Index size and update cost can be high, and the supported operators depend on the engine. BRIN and min-max summaries Fit large ranges that are physically correlated with the column, such as append-ordered timestamps. The summaries are coarse, so they return false-positive blocks that still need filtering. Run it: when PostgreSQL uses an index, and when it does not. indexes.sql builds 200,000 orders with three indexes: a B-tree on a selective column, a B-tree on a column where one value covers 90% of rows, and a BRIN index on an append-ordered timestamp. -- 200,000 orders: 2,000 customers, one status that covers 90% of rows, -- and order times that only ever increase. CREATE TABLE orders_big AS SELECT g AS order_id, 'C' || lpad((g % 2000)::text, 4, '0') AS customer_id, CASE WHEN g % 10 = 0 THEN 'CANCELLED' ELSE 'COMPLETE' END AS status, timestamptz '2025-01-01' + g * interval '1 minute' AS ordered_at, (g % 500)::numeric(10, 2) AS amount FROM generate_series(1, 200000) AS g; CREATE INDEX orders_big_customer_btree ON orders_big (customer_id); CREATE INDEX orders_big_status_btree ON orders_big (status); CREATE INDEX orders_big_ordered_brin ON orders_big USING brin (ordered_at); ANALYZE orders_big; -- Selective: about 100 of 200,000 rows. EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM orders_big WHERE customer_id = 'C0042'; -- Not selective: 90% of the table. The index exists and is ignored. EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM orders_big WHERE status = 'COMPLETE'; -- A one-day range on an append-ordered column: the tiny BRIN index is enough. EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM orders_big WHERE ordered_at >= '2025-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2025-02-02'; SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size FROM pg_class WHERE relname LIKE 'orders_big%' ORDER BY relname; EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) prints the chosen plan without costs or timings: Bitmap Heap Scan on orders_big Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 'C0042'::text) -> Bitmap Index Scan on orders_big_customer_btree Index Cond: (customer_id = 'C0042'::text) Seq Scan on orders_big Filter: (status = 'COMPLETE'::text) Aggregate -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders_big Recheck Cond: ((ordered_at >= '2025-02-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone) AND ...) -> Bitmap Index Scan on orders_big_ordered_brin Index Cond: ((ordered_at >= '2025-02-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone) AND ...) relname | size ---------------------------+--------- orders_big | 14 MB orders_big_customer_btree | 1352 kB orders_big_ordered_brin | 24 kB orders_big_status_btree | 1400 kB The three plans are the lesson. The selective lookup, about 100 of 200,000 rows, uses the B-tree. The status = 'COMPLETE' filter matches 90% of the table, so the planner reads the table sequentially and ignores an index that still costs 1,352 kB of storage and slows every insert. The BRIN index answers a one-day range at 24 kB, about 1/56 of the B-tree’s size, because the timestamps increase with physical row order. That correlation is the whole condition: on randomly ordered data a BRIN summary would match nearly every block range. “Clustered” and “non-clustered” are not portable physical promises. In SQL Server, a clustered index defines the row-storage order and a table has one; non-clustered indexes are separate lookup structures. PostgreSQL’s CLUSTER rewrites a table in index order as a one-time operation; later inserts and updates do not continuously preserve that order. State the database when using these terms. Open table formats add file- and manifest-level pruning, not a general B-tree over every row. Iceberg can use partition transforms and per-file metrics to skip files; Delta Lake can collect data-skipping statistics and supports Z-ordering. These mechanisms reduce files or row groups read, but do not replace a primary-key index for point lookups in a relational database. Oracle’s bitmap-index implementation is aimed at read-heavy analytic workloads: updating an indexed value can lock the bitmap entry representing many rows. Do not carry bitmap-index advice from a star-schema warehouse into a high-concurrency transactional workload without checking that engine’s locking and write behavior. 5.2 The query optimization playbook for large databases In plain terms. Do not guess why a query is slow. Ask the engine for its plan, find the step that reads or moves the most data, and change one thing at a time. Use the same loop across engines: state the expected access path, inspect the actual plan, measure input and output cardinalities, then change one thing. Validate both semantics and cost after the change. Reduce bytes read. Project only required columns, push predicates to the source, and make date/time filters use the model’s declared timezone. Check selectivity and statistics. A predicate on a very common value may make a sequential scan cheaper than random index lookups, as the status plan above shows. Refresh statistics after major loads. Join at the intended grain. Check uniqueness on the dimension side and inspect join estimates versus actual rows. A faster many-to-many join that multiplies measures is still incorrect. Look for avoidable exchanges and sorts. Partitioning, bucketing, clustering, and broadcast are workload-dependent; none is automatically beneficial for every query. Inspect skew and the long tail. Average task time can hide one hot partition. Compare per-partition rows/bytes and the maximum against the median. Tune only after the plan explains the bottleneck. Memory, parallelism, compaction, and file sizing are different controls; increasing one may move cost to shuffle, storage, or planning. In PostgreSQL, use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) carefully: it executes the statement and can run writes or expensive functions. In Spark, compare the physical plan with executed SQL metrics; an initial adaptive plan may change after shuffle statistics arrive. Do not copy one engine’s plan vocabulary onto another. 5.3 Key considerations for designing scalable database systems Choose keys for identity and distribution separately. A sequential surrogate can be an effective dimension key but a hotspot for a distributed write path; a random UUID may spread writes while increasing key size and reducing locality. Avoid hot partitions. Tenant, date, or status keys can be extremely skewed. Measure the distribution before choosing a partition key, shard count, or hash strategy. Specify uniqueness scope. A key unique inside one shard may not be globally unique. If consumers join across shards, provide a collision-safe global identity or an explicit compound key. Account for cross-boundary operations. A join, transaction, or update that spans shards has coordination cost. Data locality helps only when the query’s filters align with the distribution key. Make replay and migration part of the design. Preserve source offsets, support rebuilds into a new table, and define how consumers switch to the validated version. Set growth and retention policy. Unbounded event retention, indexes, snapshots, and CDC logs all consume storage and can affect recovery time. Scale is a workload property, not just row count. Include concurrent readers, write rate, skew, latency objectives, and correction/replay windows in the design envelope. 5.4 Partitioning, sharding, and Z-order In plain terms. Partitioning splits one table into folders, such as one per day, so a query for one day opens one folder. Sharding splits data across separate database servers. Z-ordering sorts data inside files so that rows with similar values on several columns sit close together. These words are often used interchangeably, but they refer to distinct mechanisms: Database partitioning splits one logical table into child partitions managed by one database. It prunes ranges or lists, manages lifecycle, and isolates hot data. Too many partitions raise planning and metadata cost, and uniqueness constraints may have to include the partition key. Sharding splits data across independent database instances or nodes. It scales capacity and isolates failure and load. The costs are cross-shard joins, cross-shard transactions, global uniqueness, and rebalancing. File partitioning groups files into directories or table partition specs in a lake. It skips files for common predicates and limits the scope of maintenance. High-cardinality partitions create small files and metadata overhead. Z-ordering is a multi-dimensional locality layout in table formats that support it. It clusters values so file-level statistics can skip more data. It costs a rewrite, its effect drops as more columns are added, and it is implementation-specific. For Iceberg, partition transforms such as days(order_ts) keep the logical timestamp column separate from the physical partition values, and partition specs can evolve. Delta Lake documents ZORDER BY as a mechanism to colocate related values for data skipping. Do not label an Iceberg sort order as Z-order or assume every lakehouse reader interprets a vendor-specific layout command. Partition only when the table size and query pattern justify it. A predicate on a source date can enable pruning without asking every query writer to duplicate a hand-maintained event_date column. Verify pruning in the engine plan and monitor file counts after the write. Run it: hidden partitioning and pruning. layout_demo.py writes 10,000 order lines over ten days into an Iceberg table partitioned by days(order_ts), queries one day by filtering on order_ts itself, and reads how many data files the scan opened. It then evolves the partition spec to monthly without rewriting anything: """Hidden partitioning on an Iceberg fact table, and what the planner prunes. The table is partitioned by days(order_ts). Queries filter on order_ts itself; nobody writes a separate order_date column. """ from pyspark.sql import SparkSession spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("layout-demo") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm.type", "hadoop") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm.warehouse", "file:///tmp/dm_blog/warehouse") .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC") .getOrCreate()) spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS dm.sales") spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dm.sales.fact_order_line PURGE") spark.sql(""" CREATE TABLE dm.sales.fact_order_line ( order_id STRING, line_number INT, customer_sk BIGINT, product_sk BIGINT, order_ts TIMESTAMP, quantity INT, net_amount DECIMAL(12, 2) ) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(order_ts)) """) # 10,000 order lines spread evenly over ten days of January. spark.sql(""" INSERT INTO dm.sales.fact_order_line SELECT concat('O', id DIV 2) AS order_id, CAST(id % 2 + 1 AS INT) AS line_number, id % 500 AS customer_sk, id % 40 AS product_sk, TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01' + make_interval(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, id * 86.4) AS order_ts, CAST(id % 5 + 1 AS INT) AS quantity, CAST(id % 100 AS DECIMAL(12, 2)) AS net_amount FROM range(10000) """) spark.sql(""" SELECT partition.order_ts_day AS day, record_count, file_count FROM dm.sales.fact_order_line.partitions ORDER BY day """).show() one_day = """ SELECT sum(net_amount) FROM dm.sales.fact_order_line WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-03' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-01-04' """ plan = spark.sql("EXPLAIN " + one_day).first()[0] print([line.strip() for line in plan.splitlines() if "BatchScan" in line][0]) def scan_metrics(df): """Iceberg's BatchScan metrics, as the Spark UI SQL tab shows them. This reaches into the JVM plan through py4j, which is internal API; it is here only to print the numbers without opening the UI. """ df.collect() stack = [df._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan()] while stack: node = stack.pop() if node.nodeName().startswith("BatchScan"): m = node.metrics() return {k: m.apply(k).value() for k in ("resultDataFiles", "skippedDataFiles")} children = node.children().iterator() while children.hasNext(): stack.append(children.next()) spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false") # keep the scan node visible metrics = scan_metrics(spark.sql(one_day)) print("files read vs skipped:", metrics) assert metrics == {"resultDataFiles": 1, "skippedDataFiles": 9} assert spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM dm.sales.fact_order_line.partitions").first()[0] == 10 # Partition evolution: switch new data to monthly partitions, no rewrite. spark.sql("ALTER TABLE dm.sales.fact_order_line " "REPLACE PARTITION FIELD days(order_ts) WITH months(order_ts)") spark.sql(""" INSERT INTO dm.sales.fact_order_line VALUES ('O9001', 1, 1, 1, TIMESTAMP '2025-02-14 09:00:00', 1, 10.00) """) spark.sql(""" SELECT spec_id, count(*) AS files FROM dm.sales.fact_order_line.files GROUP BY spec_id ORDER BY spec_id """).show() print("PASS: 10 day partitions, then a monthly spec added without a rewrite") spark.stop() +----------+------------+----------+ | day|record_count|file_count| +----------+------------+----------+ |2025-01-01| 1000| 1| |2025-01-02| 1000| 1| ... 7 more days, 1,000 records and 1 file each ... |2025-01-10| 1000| 1| +----------+------------+----------+ +- BatchScan dm.sales.fact_order_line[order_ts#63, net_amount#65] dm.sales.fact_order_line (branch=null) [filters=order_ts IS NOT NULL, order_ts >= 1735862400000000, order_ts < 1735948800000000, groupedBy=] RuntimeFilters: [] files read vs skipped: {'resultDataFiles': 1, 'skippedDataFiles': 9} +-------+-----+ |spec_id|files| +-------+-----+ | 0| 10| | 1| 1| +-------+-----+ PASS: 10 day partitions, then a monthly spec added without a rewrite The query never mentions a partition column. Iceberg converts the order_ts range into the days partition values, reads them from the manifests, and opens 1 of 10 files. The two numbers come from Iceberg’s own scan metrics, which the Spark UI shows on the BatchScan node. After REPLACE PARTITION FIELD, the ten old files keep spec_id 0 and the new February file is written with spec_id 1; no existing file was rewritten, and queries still filter on order_ts alone. 5.5 ACID vs. BASE and the CAP theorem in modeling In plain terms. ACID is the bank-transfer promise: money leaves one account and arrives in the other, or neither happens. BASE accepts that copies of the data may briefly disagree, in exchange for staying available. CAP says that when the network between servers breaks, a distributed system must choose between answering with possibly stale data and refusing to answer. ACID describes transaction properties: atomicity, consistency with declared constraints, isolation, and durability. BASE is a broad descriptive design slogan—basically available, soft state, eventually consistent—not a competing SQL transaction standard. A system can use ACID transactions for an individual write while exposing asynchronously refreshed read models elsewhere. The two meanings of “consistency” must not be conflated. ACID consistency means a committed transaction preserves application/database invariants. The C in CAP concerns whether distributed reads observe a single up-to-date copy. CAP’s trade-off applies when communication is partitioned: a system cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability for every request during that partition. It does not say a normal distributed system must choose only two properties at all times. For data models, make the trade visible to consumers. Is a dashboard allowed to read a replica behind the source? Can independent partitions accept writes that may conflict? How will those writes be reconciled, and which business invariants must never be violated? “Eventually consistent” is not a recovery plan; name the lag bound, conflict rule, and reconciliation owner. 5.6 Physical layout: schema versus stored bytes The star schema says how records relate and what they mean. Physical layout says how bytes are stored and found. Keep those decisions separate so a new partition strategy does not force consumers to rewrite their SQL. Customer history. The model decides one row per customer version and validity interval. The physical layer decides how to sort or cluster files to help common customer and time lookups. Sales fact. The model decides one row per order line. The physical layer decides whether to partition by a coarse date transform, once data volume justifies it. Schema change. The model decides to add sales_channel with a defined meaning and a default or backfill policy. The physical layer evolves the table schema, knowing old files may not contain the new field. Query filters. The model decides that queries use order_date_key and dimensional keys consistently. The physical layer picks file format, partition transforms, and clustering from measured queries. Do not partition a large table by a high-cardinality business key such as customer_id. That tends to create many small directories and files while doing little to reduce scans. A coarse event-date transform is often a better starting point, but the correct choice follows query predicates, file sizes, and write frequency. Apache Iceberg supports hidden partitioning and partition evolution, so a logical filter on the source timestamp can remain stable as the physical partition spec changes. Evolution avoids requiring consumers to filter on hand-maintained partition columns; it does not remove the need to measure pruning or file counts. Schema-on-read formats also need explicit schema discipline. Spark’s Parquet schema merge is disabled by default because merging file schemas has a cost. Do not rely on a random file’s inferred schema to define a production model. Publish an explicit contract, validate incoming schemas, and make compatible evolution deliberate. 5.7 Put model contracts into tests Every published fact or dimension should have checks that express its contract: Grain uniqueness. (order_id, line_number) appears at most once in the transaction fact. Non-null keys. Every required fact foreign key resolves to a real member or to an explicit unknown member. Dimension uniqueness. One dimension surrogate key identifies one row. Type 2 intervals. Versions for one business key never overlap, so an event-time lookup matches at most one version. Change ordering. A later-arriving source version never overwrites a newer accepted source sequence. Measure reconciliation. Fact net amount equals gross less discount, under the declared currency and rounding rules. Batch idempotency. Replaying the same input changes neither row counts nor totals. Delete semantics. A source delete is retained, invalidated, or stored as a tombstone, by an explicit policy. The demos in this guide implement most of these as plain assert statements: grain uniqueness and unknown-member coverage in section 3.5, Type 2 non-overlap in section 3.1, change ordering and replay idempotency in section 3.2. In a production pipeline the same checks run as data-quality tests after each load and fail the publish step. Also test volume and operations: rows rejected, unknown-member rates, late arrival age, duplicate source keys, fact-to-source reconciliation, file counts, and model freshness. Alert thresholds should distinguish a newly sparse source from a broken join. A practical design sequence: identify the business process; write the grain as a sentence; inspect the source’s keys and change semantics; choose transaction, periodic, or accumulating facts; define dimensions and history; specify measures and their aggregation rules; publish the logical contract; then choose the storage layout and test the invariants. Revisit the physical layout when measured access patterns change, not every time a new report is requested. Part 5 interview questions 1. Why might a database ignore an index on a filtered column? Because the predicate is not selective. If the filter matches a large share of the table, following the index means many random page reads, which costs more than one sequential scan. In the PostgreSQL demo, status = 'COMPLETE' matches 90% of rows and the planner chooses Seq Scan despite a B-tree on status. Stale statistics, functions applied to the column, and type mismatches can also prevent index use. 2. B-tree vs bitmap vs BRIN: when would you use each? B-tree for selective equality and range lookups, the default for OLTP. Bitmap indexes (in engines such as Oracle) for low-cardinality columns in read-heavy analytic tables, not for concurrent updates. BRIN for very large tables whose physical order follows the column, such as append-only event time, where a tiny summary index skips most blocks. The demo’s BRIN index is 24 kB against 1,352 kB for a B-tree on the same table. 3. Partitioning vs sharding vs bucketing vs Z-ordering. Partitioning splits one table into parts that queries can skip, inside one system. Sharding spreads data across independent servers to scale capacity, at the cost of cross-shard joins and transactions. Bucketing (in Spark/Hive) hashes rows into a fixed number of files per partition, so joins on the bucket key can avoid a shuffle. Z-ordering (in Delta, for example) sorts rows by several columns at once to improve file-level min/max skipping. 4. How do you choose a partition column for a lakehouse fact table? From the predicates queries actually use, usually event date. Prefer low to moderate cardinality so each partition holds well-sized files, and never a high-cardinality key such as customer_id. In Iceberg, use a transform such as days(order_ts) so queries filter on the real column, and evolve the spec later if volume changes. Verify pruning in the scan metrics, as the layout demo does: 1 file read, 9 skipped. 5. Explain the CAP theorem correctly. During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error response). When there is no partition, it can provide both. CAP’s C is not the C of ACID, which means preserving declared invariants inside a transaction. 6. What data quality tests would you put on a fact table? Grain uniqueness on the declared key, foreign keys that resolve to a real or unknown member, no NULL in required keys, reconciliation of totals against the source, idempotency (a replay changes nothing), freshness, and volume anomaly checks. For a Type 2 dimension, add a no-overlap test and exactly one current row per business key. Part 6: Database Lifecycle & Tooling Mechanics Models move in both directions. Forward engineering turns agreed semantics into schemas, constraints, migrations, and pipelines. Reverse engineering starts from deployed objects and reconstructs their declared structure. Neither direction can infer all the business meaning without people and source documentation. 6.1 Forward engineering vs. reverse engineering In plain terms. Forward engineering is building the house from the blueprint. Reverse engineering is drawing the blueprint by measuring a house that already exists, and then asking the owners why that one wall is there. Forward engineering starts from business requirements and a conceptual or logical model. It produces DDL, migration scripts, constraints, transformations, and test contracts. Review whether the design matches what the sources can deliver and what the queries need. Reverse engineering starts from existing schemas, views, constraints, and observed data. It produces an inventory, an ER diagram, a candidate model, and a dependency graph. Review the grain, hidden application rules, temporal meaning, and undocumented exceptions, because none of them are in the catalog. Treat deployed schema changes as versioned migrations. A change record should state the contract version, compatibility impact, rollout order, validation, and backfill plan. For a breaking rename, an expand-and-contract rollout can add the new field, dual-write or backfill, migrate consumers, verify the old field is unused, and only then remove it. A rollback script cannot always recover dropped or reinterpreted data, so the recovery plan may be a forward repair rather than a literal inverse migration. Expand-and-contract rename: cust_no -> customer_id step 1 expand add customer_id (nullable) readers: cust_no step 2 migrate backfill + dual-write both columns readers: either step 3 switch move every consumer to customer_id readers: customer_id step 4 verify query logs show no reads of cust_no step 5 contract drop cust_no 6.2 How reverse engineering works under the hood For a relational database, an introspection tool reads the system catalog or standard information schema. It collects columns and types, nullability, defaults, primary/unique/foreign keys, indexes, views, and dependencies. It then maps declared foreign keys to relationship edges and can infer candidate cardinality from uniqueness and nullability constraints. The distinction between declared and observed is important. A declared foreign key is evidence of an enforced relationship. A frequent join in query logs is only a candidate relationship. A missing foreign key might mean a performance choice, a cross-system relationship, or simply an integrity gap; reverse engineering cannot decide which explanation is correct. The following read-only PostgreSQL queries list visible columns and declared foreign-key column mappings. information_schema is SQL-standard and portable; pg_catalog is PostgreSQL-specific and exposes engine details that the standard views do not. Run them against the dm_blog database after normalization.sql, and they recover the 3NF schema and its four foreign keys. SELECT table_schema, table_name, ordinal_position, column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = ANY (current_schemas(false)) ORDER BY table_schema, table_name, ordinal_position; SELECT source_ns.nspname AS source_schema, source_table.relname AS source_table, constraint_row.conname AS constraint_name, source_column.attname AS source_column, target_ns.nspname AS target_schema, target_table.relname AS target_table, target_column.attname AS target_column, source_key.ordinality AS key_position FROM pg_constraint AS constraint_row JOIN pg_class AS source_table ON source_table.oid = constraint_row.conrelid JOIN pg_namespace AS source_ns ON source_ns.oid = source_table.relnamespace JOIN pg_class AS target_table ON target_table.oid = constraint_row.confrelid JOIN pg_namespace AS target_ns ON target_ns.oid = target_table.relnamespace JOIN LATERAL unnest(constraint_row.conkey) WITH ORDINALITY AS source_key(attnum, ordinality) ON true JOIN LATERAL unnest(constraint_row.confkey) WITH ORDINALITY AS target_key(attnum, ordinality) ON target_key.ordinality = source_key.ordinality JOIN pg_attribute AS source_column ON source_column.attrelid = source_table.oid AND source_column.attnum = source_key.attnum JOIN pg_attribute AS target_column ON target_column.attrelid = target_table.oid AND target_column.attnum = target_key.attnum WHERE constraint_row.contype = 'f' AND source_ns.nspname = ANY (current_schemas(false)) ORDER BY source_schema, source_table, constraint_name, key_position; The second query returns one row per foreign-key column (schema columns trimmed here), which is exactly the edge list of the normalization diagram in section 2.1: source_table | constraint_name | source_column | target_table | target_column --------------+------------------------------+---------------+--------------+--------------- customer | customer_postal_code_fkey | postal_code | postal_area | postal_code order_line | order_line_order_id_fkey | order_id | sales_order | order_id order_line | order_line_product_id_fkey | product_id | product | product_id sales_order | sales_order_customer_id_fkey | customer_id | customer | customer_id Those queries reveal declared structure, not an ER model ready for publication. Continue by sampling value distributions, checking whether candidate keys are actually unique, examining null rates and orphan rows, and asking the source owners what the fields mean. Then compare the recovered schema to the desired conceptual model: legacy schemas often encode implementation history rather than current business boundaries. Part 6 interview questions 1. How would you rename a column used by twenty downstream jobs without downtime? Expand and contract. Add the new column, backfill it, and dual-write both. Migrate consumers one by one while both exist. Confirm from query logs or lineage that nothing reads the old column, then drop it. In Iceberg, a rename is a metadata-only change because columns are tracked by field ID, but your consumers’ SQL still breaks, so the rollout plan is the same. 2. You inherit an undocumented database. How do you model it? Read the catalog (information_schema, pg_catalog) for tables, types, keys and declared foreign keys. Profile the data: test candidate keys for uniqueness, measure null rates, and look for orphan rows. Mine query logs for frequent joins, which suggest undeclared relationships. Then interview the owners about grain, time semantics and exceptions, and write a conceptual model of how the business works, not of how the tables happen to look. Interview scenario round: design questions Interviewers for senior roles usually stop asking definitions and hand you a business. These five scenarios cover the patterns above. For each, say the grain sentence first; most of the score is in that sentence. 1. Design the analytical model for a ride-hailing company. Grain: one row per completed or cancelled trip, in fact_trip. Dimensions: dim_rider, dim_driver (Type 2 on rating tier and vehicle), dim_location used twice as pickup and drop-off (role-playing), dim_date and dim_time. Measures: fare, tip, distance, duration, surge multiplier (non-additive; store base and surge amounts instead). Driver online hours are a different process, so they get their own fact, such as fact_driver_session or a daily periodic snapshot of driver activity. Partition fact_trip by days(pickup_ts). 2. Model subscription revenue so that monthly recurring revenue (MRR) is easy to report. Keep fact_subscription_event as a transaction fact, with one row per start, upgrade, downgrade or cancel. Add fact_subscription_monthly, a periodic snapshot with one row per subscription per month holding MRR and status. MRR is semi-additive: sum it across customers within a month, never across months. Churn and expansion come from comparing consecutive snapshots. The customer dimension is Type 2 on plan and segment, so cohort reports use the plan at the time. 3. Track e-commerce orders from placement to delivery and report average delivery time. An accumulating snapshot: one row per order with ordered_ts, paid_ts, shipped_ts and delivered_ts, and the lag measures between them, updated in place as each milestone arrives (a MERGE keyed on order_id). Use role-playing date keys for each milestone. Keep the line-level transaction fact for revenue; the two facts answer different questions and share conformed dimensions. 4. Build a CDC pipeline from PostgreSQL to a lakehouse with a Type 2 customer dimension. Debezium reads the WAL and publishes snapshot plus change events to Kafka. Land them unchanged in a bronze Iceberg table with key, op, LSN and payload. In silver, deduplicate on (key, lsn) and keep the latest event per key per batch. Apply a current-state MERGE guarded by lsn > target_lsn, with tombstones for deletes. Build dim_customer with the two-row staging MERGE from section 3.1, using the source’s business effective time for valid_from. Test replay idempotency, Type 2 non-overlap, and key coverage before publishing gold. 5. The revenue dashboard shows double yesterday's number. How do you debug it? Check grain before tuning anything. First, run uniqueness on the fact key; if there are duplicates, check whether a retry appended a batch twice (non-idempotent load). Second, check each dimension join: count rows before and after; a Type 2 join on the business key alone, or a bridge without weights, multiplies rows. Third, compare against the source total for the same event-time window. Then walk the lineage upstream to the job run that changed. The demos in this guide reproduce two of these causes exactly. Key takeaways Modeling is the work of making data interpretable without making every consumer rediscover how it was produced. Start with a row-level business contract, preserve the identity and relevant history of each dimension, and keep facts at a consistent grain. Then prove the contract with data tests. The durable distinctions are simple: The business key identifies an entity; the surrogate key identifies a warehouse row or historical version. Event time says when a business event occurred; processing time says when the platform handled it. A logical model defines grain and relationships; a physical table layout defines where bytes land and which files a query can skip. Atomic commits protect table metadata; idempotent transformations protect business outcomes when inputs are replayed. When a total changes unexpectedly, verify grain and join cardinality before tuning Spark. When history looks wrong, verify validity intervals and event time before changing a table format. Those checks find modeling errors closer to their cause than another layer of SQL can. For interview preparation, practise saying each idea at three depths: the one-sentence “in plain terms” version, the mechanism with its trade-off, and a concrete number from one of the demos. That last step is what separates a memorized answer from one that has been run. References Declaring the grain and fact tables for grain discipline and transaction, periodic snapshot, and accumulating snapshot patterns Design Tip #152: SCD Types 0, 4, 5, 6 and 7 and Slowly Changing Dimensions for Type 0–6 behavior and historical change policies Understand star schema for fact and dimension responsibilities, surrogate keys, and Type 1/2 examples UC Berkeley CS 186 database design notes for ER constraints, functional dependencies, BCNF, and lossless decomposition Oracle SQL Tuning Guide: optimizer access paths for B-tree, bitmap, table-cluster, and optimizer access-path behavior in Oracle DataVault4dbt staging for a practical Data Vault staging implementation Data lakehouse overview for the broad platform comparison Medallion architecture for bronze, silver, and gold layer responsibilities and operational guidance dbt snapshots for a practical implementation of Type 2 history over mutable source tables Debezium PostgreSQL connector for snapshot-plus-log CDC, keys, operation envelopes, source positions, and delete/tombstone events Spark 3.5.9 CREATE TABLE USING and Parquet data source behavior for Spark table DDL, partition discovery, and Parquet schema merging Iceberg 1.11.0 schema and partition evolution and partitioning for separating logical columns from physical layout Iceberg 1.11.0 Spark writes for MERGE INTO semantics, and Spark DDL for REPLACE PARTITION FIELD Delta Lake Z-ordering and data skipping for a format-specific example of file-level locality PostgreSQL index types, BRIN indexes, CLUSTER, partitioning, and information schema for the engine-specific indexing, storage, and reverse-engineering examples Spark SQL performance tuning for query-plan and adaptive-execution tuning concepts Data Mesh Principles and Logical Architecture, IBM data mesh, and IBM data fabric for the distinct ownership and integration concerns Questioning the Lambda Architecture for the dual-path cost and replay-centered alternative How to beat the CAP theorem for the original batch, speed and serving layer design of the Lambda architecture KIP-405: Kafka Tiered Storage for keeping long log history in object storage, the retention side of Kappa Debezium MySQL connector for the binlog_format = ROW requirement and binlog-based capture PostgreSQL replication settings for max_slot_wal_keep_size and WAL retained by replication slots Debezium outbox event router and incremental snapshots for the outbox and backfill-while-streaming patterns Kafka Connect JDBC source connector for query-based capture modes (incrementing, timestamp, and both) and their limits Iceberg 1.11.0 incremental read, Hudi incremental query, and Delta Lake change data feed for reading only what changed between commits CAP Twelve Years Later for the partition-time scope of CAP and its distinction from ACID consistency OpenLineage facets for run, job, dataset, and extensible lineage metadata Run every demo on this blog locally for the public Spark and lakehouse playground setup Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, Apache Hadoop, Apache Parquet and Apache are either
